Month 3 Q&A - Networking, OS and Distributed Data

Weeks 9 to 12. The month that fills the degree-shaped gap. 44 questions.

Covers: Weeks 9-12. Networking, operating systems, replication and partitioning, caching, and messaging. Plus the first three system designs.

Read this on the train. You do not need a laptop, a compiler or two free hours - that is the whole point of these files. Each question has the answer you would say, the reason it is true, and the mistake to avoid. Read one question or twenty; it works either way.

How to use this on a bad week

• 20 minutes on a train: read the five questions in the box below. Nothing else.

• Reading is not learning. After each question, close the file and say the answer out loud once. On a train, mouth it silently - it still works. If you cannot, read it again and move on. You will meet it again.

• Mark what you could not say. Put it in the WEAK tab of the tracker when you get home. That is the only homework.

• This replaces nothing. The tracker still runs the plan. This is what you do with the hours the plan cannot use - the commute, the wait, the evening you are too tired to code.

If you only have 20 minutes, read these five

# Question
1 What happens when you type a URL and press enter?
2 Why does TLS use both asymmetric and symmetric cryptography?
3 Why does async I/O not need a thread while waiting?
4 Why does consistent hashing beat modulo hashing?
5 Why is exactly-once delivery a myth, and what do you do instead?

What this file answers

Everything in the Month 3 checkpoint. This is the material a CS degree gives people and you were never taught - which is why it is also the material that most changes how senior you sound.

PART A - Networking

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q1. What happens when you type a URL and press enter?

Say this. DNS resolution turns the hostname into an IP - browser cache, OS cache, resolver, then root, TLD and authoritative servers if needed. Then a TCP three-way handshake to that IP, and a TLS handshake on top if it is HTTPS. Then the HTTP request goes out, usually to a load balancer, which picks a backend. The application handles it, probably hitting a cache and a database. The response comes back, the browser parses the HTML and fires more requests for CSS, JS and images, often from a CDN.

Why. Every layer exists to hide a failure or a cost from the layer above: DNS hides IP changes, TCP hides packet loss, TLS hides eavesdropping, the load balancer hides individual servers.

Watch out. This is the single most-asked systems question. Practise it as a five-minute narration and know where you would go deeper if pushed - the handshakes are the usual follow-up.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q2. Walk through DNS resolution.

Say this. Check the browser cache, then the OS cache, then ask the configured recursive resolver. If the resolver has nothing cached it asks a root server, which points to the TLD server for .com, which points to the authoritative nameserver for the domain, which returns the record. Everything is cached along the way for the TTL.

Why. The hierarchy exists so no single server has to know everything, and caching means the full walk almost never happens - most lookups are answered from a cache within a millisecond.

Watch out. TTL is why DNS changes are slow to take effect: you cannot recall a cached answer. Lowering the TTL before a planned migration is the standard trick.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q3. Explain the TCP three-way handshake, and what reliability costs.

Say this. SYN from the client with an initial sequence number, SYN-ACK from the server with its own, ACK from the client. Now both sides know the other is reachable and have agreed sequence numbers. The cost is one full round trip before any data flows - and with TLS on top, two or three.

Why. Reliability comes from sequence numbers plus acknowledgements plus retransmission: the sender keeps data until it is acknowledged and resends if not. That guarantees delivery and order, at the cost of latency and head-of-line blocking.

Watch out. This is why connection reuse matters so much. Keep-alive, connection pooling and HTTP/2 all exist to avoid paying the handshake repeatedly.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q4. Flow control or congestion control - what is the difference?

Say this. Flow control protects the receiver: the receive window says how much unacknowledged data it can buffer. Congestion control protects the network: slow start and congestion avoidance grow the sending rate gradually and back off on packet loss.

Why. They solve different overload problems. A fast sender can overwhelm a slow receiver even on a perfect network, and a network can be congested even when every receiver is fast.

Watch out. Slow start is why the first few hundred milliseconds of a connection are slower than the steady state - another reason to reuse connections.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q5. What is head-of-line blocking, and how did HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 address it?

Say this. One slow or lost item blocks everything behind it. In HTTP/1.1 a single connection handles one request at a time, so a slow response blocks the queue. HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one connection, which fixes it at the HTTP layer - but a lost TCP packet still stalls every stream, because TCP guarantees order. HTTP/3 moves to QUIC over UDP, where each stream is independently ordered, so loss affects only its own stream.

Why. HTTP/1.1 pipelining tried to fix this and failed because responses still had to come back in request order. Multiplexing works because responses carry stream IDs and can be interleaved.

Watch out. "HTTP/2 fixed head-of-line blocking" is only half true - it fixed it at the HTTP layer and left it at the TCP layer. Saying both halves is the strong answer.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q6. Why does TLS use both asymmetric and symmetric cryptography?

Say this. Asymmetric crypto lets two parties who have never met agree a shared secret and verify identity, but it is slow. Symmetric crypto is fast but needs a shared key. So TLS uses asymmetric during the handshake to authenticate the server and establish a session key, then switches to symmetric for the actual data.

Why. It is the only way to get both properties: you cannot bootstrap trust with symmetric crypto because there is no pre-shared key, and you cannot afford asymmetric for every byte.

Watch out. The certificate is what makes the asymmetric half meaningful - it binds the public key to a hostname, vouched for by a CA the client already trusts.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q7. What does HTTPS not protect?

Say this. It does not hide which server you are talking to - the IP is visible, and the hostname is visible in SNI unless encrypted client hello is in use. It does not hide traffic volume or timing. It does not protect you if the endpoint itself is malicious or compromised, and it does nothing about what happens to the data after it arrives.

Why. TLS secures the channel, not the parties. Confidentiality and integrity in transit is the entire promise.

Watch out. A good extra: it does not protect against a compromised or coerced certificate authority, which is why certificate pinning and transparency logs exist.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q8. Explain CORS and preflight.

Say this. A browser blocks a page on origin A from reading a response from origin B unless B opts in with Access-Control-Allow-Origin. For anything beyond a simple request - a custom header, or a method other than GET/POST/HEAD - the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight asking what is permitted, and only sends the real request if the answer allows it.

Why. It is a browser-enforced policy protecting users, not a server security mechanism. The server is perfectly reachable by anything that is not a browser.

Watch out. Two common mistakes: CORS middleware registered after routing, so preflights never reach it; and wildcard origin with credentials, which the spec forbids outright.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q9. Why is scaling WebSockets harder than scaling HTTP?

Say this. HTTP is stateless, so any server can handle any request and a load balancer can send it anywhere. A WebSocket is a long-lived stateful connection pinned to one server. So a message for a user connected to server B is useless if it arrives at server A - you need a backplane like Redis so any server can publish to any connection, plus sticky sessions for the initial handshake.

Why. The connection is the state. Every scaling technique that relies on statelessness stops applying.

Watch out. You lived this with SignalR in VCDoctor. Mention the backplane and what happens to messages during a reconnect - that second part is what makes it a real answer.

PART B - Operating systems

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q10. Process or thread - what actually differs at the OS level?

Say this. A process has its own virtual address space, its own file handles and its own page tables. Threads inside a process share all of that and have only their own stack, registers and program counter. So creating a thread is far cheaper, and communication between threads is just shared memory - which is also why it is dangerous.

Why. Isolation is the point of a process. One crashing process cannot corrupt another; one crashing thread takes down the whole process.

Watch out. This connects directly to Month 1: a thread's stack is where your value-type locals live, which is why each thread reserves around a megabyte.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q11. Why is a context switch expensive?

Say this. The kernel saves the registers and stack pointer, switches page tables, and restores the other thread. That is maybe a microsecond of direct cost - but the real cost is indirect: the CPU caches and the TLB are now full of the wrong data, so the new thread runs slowly until they warm up again.

Why. Modern CPUs are fast only because of cache locality. A context switch destroys locality, and the recovery costs far more than the switch itself.

Watch out. This is the deep reason the thread pool exists and why more threads than cores makes things slower. It ties the OS layer to the .NET layer.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q12. What is virtual memory and why does it exist?

Say this. Every process sees a contiguous private address space; the OS maps those virtual addresses to physical pages through page tables, with the TLB caching recent translations. It exists for isolation - one process cannot address another's memory - and to allow the total memory in use to exceed physical RAM by paging to disk.

Why. It also allows lazy allocation: memory is reserved cheaply and only backed by physical pages when touched. That is why a process can reserve a gigabyte and use ten megabytes.

Watch out. A page fault is not an error. It is the normal mechanism for bringing a page in. Only a hard fault, requiring a disk read, is slow - and constant hard faults is thrashing.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q13. Where does the OS scheduler end and the .NET scheduler begin?

Say this. The OS schedules threads onto cores using preemptive time slices and priorities. The .NET thread pool schedules work items onto its threads, with a queue per thread and work stealing between them. So there are two layers: .NET decides which work item a pool thread picks up, the OS decides when that thread actually runs.

Why. The layering exists because a work item is much cheaper than a thread. .NET can queue a million work items; the OS cannot host a million threads.

Watch out. This is a good "do you understand the stack" question. Drawing it as two layers is worth doing once on paper - it makes the answer effortless.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q14. Mutex, semaphore or spinlock - and when is a spinlock catastrophic?

Say this. A mutex is mutual exclusion with ownership - one holder, and only the owner may release. A semaphore is a counter allowing N holders and has no ownership. A spinlock busy-waits in a loop instead of sleeping. A spinlock is catastrophic when the critical section is long or when there are more threads than cores: you burn a whole core doing nothing, and if the holder gets descheduled the spinner spins for an entire time slice.

Why. Sleeping costs a context switch - a microsecond or so. Spinning avoids it, so spinning wins only when the expected wait is shorter than that.

Watch out. "Spin for very short critical sections on a machine with spare cores; sleep otherwise" is the complete answer.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q15. Why does async I/O not need a thread while waiting?

Say this. Because the waiting is done by the OS and the hardware, not by your code. You register interest in a completion - through IOCP on Windows, epoll on Linux - and return the thread to the pool. When the device finishes, the OS queues a completion notification and a pool thread picks up the continuation.

Why. A blocking read parks a thread on a kernel wait, so the thread exists solely to remember where to resume. Async I/O stores that "where to resume" in a state machine object on the heap instead, which costs bytes rather than a thread.

Watch out. This is the moment Month 1 week 4 and Month 3 week 10 connect. "await maps down to IOCP" is the sentence that shows you understand async rather than just using it.

PART C - Replication, partitioning and caching

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q16. Why can a read replica serve stale data, and how do you hide that from a user?

Say this. Replication is asynchronous - the leader acknowledges the write before followers have applied it, so a read from a follower can miss a just-committed write. You hide it with read-your-writes consistency: route a user's reads to the leader for a short window after they write, or pin them to a replica known to be caught up, or track a version and wait for the replica to reach it.

Why. Synchronous replication would remove the staleness but make every write as slow as the slowest follower, and unavailable if a follower is down. The lag is the price of write availability.

Watch out. The user-visible symptom is "I saved it and it disappeared". That framing shows you have operated a system, not just read about one.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q17. What does quorum mean, and why R + W > N?

Say this. With N replicas, if you write to W and read from R, then R + W > N guarantees the read set and write set overlap by at least one node - so at least one node you read from has the latest write. Common choice is N=3, W=2, R=2.

Why. It is a pigeonhole argument. Any two subsets of a set of N whose sizes sum to more than N must share a member.

Watch out. Tuning R and W trades read latency against write latency. W=N gives fast reads and fragile writes; W=1, R=N is the reverse.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q18. What is split brain?

Say this. A network partition leaves two halves of a cluster each believing the other is dead, so both elect a leader and both accept writes. When the partition heals you have two divergent histories and no automatic way to reconcile them.

Why. It is prevented by requiring a majority quorum to elect a leader: only one side of a partition can hold a majority, so the minority side refuses to serve.

Watch out. This is why cluster sizes are odd numbers. Three or five nodes have an unambiguous majority; four does not.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q19. Why does consistent hashing beat modulo hashing?

Say this. With hash(key) % N, changing N changes the destination of almost every key - add one server and you have to move nearly all your data. Consistent hashing places both servers and keys on a ring and assigns each key to the next server clockwise, so adding a server only moves the keys between it and its predecessor - roughly 1/N of the data.

Why. The modulo binds every key to the current server count. The ring binds each key to a position, and positions do not change when membership does.

Watch out. Plain rings distribute unevenly, so real implementations use virtual nodes - each physical server occupies many ring positions, which smooths the distribution and makes rebalancing granular. Mention that; it is the follow-up.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q20. What does CAP actually say, and what is the common misreading?

Say this. It says that when a network partition occurs, you must choose between consistency and availability - you cannot have both. The misreading is "pick two of three", as if you could trade away partition tolerance. You cannot: partitions are a fact of networks, not a design choice. So the real choice is CP or AP, and only during a partition.

Why. When there is no partition you can have both, which is why PACELC extends it: else, in normal operation, you still trade latency against consistency.

Watch out. This is the single most commonly botched distributed-systems question, so getting it right is disproportionately valuable. Say "partition tolerance is not optional" explicitly.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q21. Strong, eventual, or causal consistency?

Say this. Strong means every read sees the latest write, as if there were one copy. Eventual means replicas converge if writes stop, with no ordering promise in the meantime. Causal is in between: operations that are causally related are seen in order by everyone, while unrelated ones may be seen in any order.

Why. Causal is usually what users actually need. A reply appearing before the message it replies to is unacceptable; two unrelated posts arriving in different orders is not.

Watch out. Anchor it: eventual consistency is fine for a view counter, unacceptable for an account balance. Concrete examples land far better than definitions.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q22. Why is Redis being single-threaded a feature?

Say this. Because every command is atomic with no locking, no context switches and no cache-line contention. That makes the implementation simple and the latency extremely predictable - and it is not the bottleneck anyway, since Redis is usually limited by network and memory bandwidth rather than CPU.

Why. Concurrency in a data structure server means locks, and locks mean contention and complexity. Removing concurrency removes an entire class of bugs and gives you atomicity for free.

Watch out. Modern Redis does use threads for I/O and background tasks - command execution is what stays single-threaded. And one slow command, like KEYS * on a large database, blocks everything. That is the real operational consequence.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q23. LRU, LFU or TTL?

Say this. LRU evicts what has not been touched recently and is the sensible default - it tracks recency, which usually predicts reuse. LFU evicts what is used least often, which is better when popularity is stable but worse when it shifts, because an old hot item lingers. TTL is not really an eviction policy - it is a correctness tool for bounding staleness.

Why. LRU adapts fast and can be fooled by a large scan that evicts everything useful. LFU resists that but adapts slowly.

Watch out. You usually want TTL plus LRU: TTL bounds how wrong the data can be, LRU bounds how much memory it uses. They answer different questions.

PART D - Messaging (your strongest area - own it)

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q24. Explain the delivery guarantees.

Say this. At-most-once: send and do not retry - you may lose messages. At-least-once: retry until acknowledged - you may get duplicates. Exactly-once: no duplicates and no loss, which is not achievable as a delivery guarantee. Almost every real queue, including SQS, gives at-least-once.

Why. The impossibility is simple: after sending, the sender either gets an acknowledgement or it does not. If it does not, it cannot distinguish "the message was lost" from "the acknowledgement was lost", so it must choose between resending and not - duplicate or loss.

Watch out. Say "duplicates are normal, not exceptional". That reframing is what leads to the right design instead of a hunt for a queue that promises exactly-once.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q25. So how do you get exactly-once processing?

Say this. At the consumer, not the transport. Make the handler idempotent: give each message a stable business or idempotency key, and write a deduplication record in the same transaction as the effect. If the record already exists, skip. Then a duplicate delivery is harmless.

Why. The transaction is the crucial part. If you write the effect and the dedup record separately, a crash between them leaves you either processing twice or losing the work - you have just moved the problem.

Instead of. If the effect is not transactional - sending an email, calling a third-party API - you cannot get atomicity, so you need an outbox pattern or a compensating action instead.

Watch out. This is exactly what you built in the job platform. Have the dedup table schema in your head - it is the most likely deep-dive of the whole project.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q26. What is a visibility timeout and what goes wrong with it?

Say this. When a consumer receives a message it becomes invisible to others for a set period rather than being deleted. If the consumer finishes and deletes it, done. If the consumer crashes, the timeout expires and the message reappears for someone else. What goes wrong: processing takes longer than the timeout, the message reappears, and a second consumer starts the same work while the first is still running.

Why. It is a lease, not a lock. The queue cannot know whether a silent consumer is slow or dead, so it must guess with a timer.

Instead of. Extend the visibility timeout with a heartbeat while working, and size the initial timeout from your p99 processing time, not the average.

Watch out. This is the same problem as a distributed lock lease, and it has the same fix - the connection is worth pointing out.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q27. Why do retries need jitter?

Say this. Without it, everything that failed at the same moment retries at the same moment. So a brief downstream blip produces a synchronised wave of retries that keeps the downstream down - a thundering herd. Jitter randomises each delay so the load spreads out.

Why. Exponential backoff alone fixes the rate but not the synchronisation. Both clients wait one second, then two, then four - together, every time.

Watch out. Also cap the total attempts and add a circuit breaker. Retries without a breaker amplify an outage instead of riding it out - retrying harder against a dying service is what turns a blip into an incident.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q28. What is a dead letter queue and what do you actually do with it?

Say this. After N failed attempts a message is moved to a separate queue instead of being retried forever. That stops one poison message blocking the pipeline and preserves it for inspection. Operationally: alert on DLQ depth, inspect the payload and the error, fix the cause, then replay.

Why. Without it, a message that can never succeed is retried indefinitely, consuming capacity and hiding the failure. The DLQ makes the failure visible and bounded.

Watch out. "A DLQ nobody monitors is a data loss mechanism with extra steps." Alerting on depth and having a replay path is the part most candidates never mention.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q29. SQS, RabbitMQ or Kafka?

Say this. SQS is a managed work queue - a message is consumed and deleted, scaling consumers is trivial, DLQ is built in, and there is no infrastructure to run. RabbitMQ is a broker with rich routing - exchanges, topics, per-message acknowledgement - when the routing logic is the hard part. Kafka is a durable partitioned log: consumers track their own offsets, messages remain after being read, so you get replay, multiple independent consumer groups, and ordering within a partition.

Why. The core distinction is queue versus log. A queue forgets; a log remembers. If you might need to reprocess history, or several unrelated consumers need the same stream, you need a log.

Instead of. For your email pipeline SQS was the right call - independent tasks, no replay requirement, already in the AWS estate, managed retry and DLQ. Say that; a justified simple choice beats an unjustified sophisticated one.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q30. Explain Kafka partitions, offsets and consumer groups.

Say this. A topic is split into partitions, each an append-only ordered log. Every message has an offset - its position. A consumer group has each partition assigned to exactly one consumer in the group, and each consumer commits its offset. So parallelism is bounded by partition count, and ordering is guaranteed within a partition but not across the topic.

Why. That design is why Kafka scales: no per-message bookkeeping, just a sequential file and a cursor per consumer. It is also why more consumers than partitions gains you nothing.

Watch out. If you need ordering per entity, partition by that entity's key - all events for one user land in one partition and stay ordered. That is the standard answer to "how do you keep ordering at scale".

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q31. How do you guarantee ordering, and what does it cost?

Say this. Ordering only exists within a single sequential path - one FIFO queue, or one Kafka partition, or one consumer. So you get it by routing everything that must be ordered through one path, keyed by entity. It costs parallelism: that path is now a serial bottleneck, and a slow message blocks everything behind it.

Why. Order and parallelism are fundamentally in tension. Processing two things at once means you cannot promise which finishes first.

Watch out. The good design move is to narrow the ordering requirement - usually you need ordering per user or per document, not globally. Saying that turns an impossible requirement into an easy one.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q32. What is backpressure and why does it matter?

Say this. It is the downstream telling the upstream to slow down, rather than silently accumulating work. Without it, a fast producer and a slow consumer means an unbounded queue - growing memory, growing latency, and eventually a crash or an out-of-memory kill.

Why. A bounded buffer converts a memory problem into a latency problem, which is nearly always the better failure. You want to be slow, not dead.

Watch out. Channel<T> with a bounded capacity is the in-process version. Queue depth alarms and consumer autoscaling are the distributed version. Naming both shows range.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q33. What is the outbox pattern and what problem does it solve?

Say this. The dual-write problem: you need to update the database and publish an event, and there is no transaction spanning both. If the publish fails after the commit you have lost the event; if it succeeds and the commit fails you have published a lie. The outbox writes the event into a table in the same transaction as the data change, and a separate process reads that table and publishes.

Why. Now there is exactly one atomic operation. The publish becomes a retryable at-least-once step, which combined with idempotent consumers is correct.

Watch out. It gives at-least-once publishing, not exactly-once, so consumers still need idempotency. This is a Month 4 topic but it belongs with messaging - and it is a strong thing to have in your project.

PART E - The first three system designs

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q34. Design a URL shortener - what are the real decisions?

Say this. Requirements and scale first - read-heavy by a large factor, so optimise reads. Key generation is the core decision: a counter encoded in base62 is short, dense and guaranteed unique but is sequential and therefore guessable and a write hotspot; a hash of the URL is not sequential but needs collision handling. Then a key-value store, an aggressive cache on the read path since mappings never change, and a 301 or 302 depending on whether you want to count clicks.

Why. The read/write ratio drives everything. Immutable mappings mean cache invalidation is a non-problem, which is unusual and worth saying out loud.

Watch out. The trade-off to name: 301 is cacheable by browsers so it is fast but you lose analytics; 302 gives you every click but costs a round trip every time.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q35. Design a rate limiter - which algorithm and why?

Say this. Token bucket. Each key has a bucket refilling at a fixed rate up to a capacity; a request takes a token or gets 429 with Retry-After. It allows a controlled burst, which real traffic needs, and it is cheap - two numbers per key. Fixed window is simpler but allows double the limit across a boundary. Sliding window log is exact but stores a timestamp per request, so memory grows with traffic.

Why. The state must be shared across instances, so it lives in Redis, and the check-and-decrement must be atomic - a Lua script or an INCR with expiry - otherwise two instances both hand out the last token.

Watch out. The atomicity point is what separates a real answer from a textbook one. It is also exactly what you build in week 18.

Networking, operating systems, replication and data Q&A
Q36. Design a notification service - what is the hard part?

Say this. Fan-out and deduplication. One event can produce many notifications across email, SMS and push, each with different providers, latencies and failure modes. So: an ingestion API, a queue per channel so a slow provider cannot block the others, per-user preference and quiet-hours checks, a dedup key so a retried event does not notify twice, retries with backoff, and a DLQ per channel.

Why. The channels have genuinely different characteristics, so a single shared queue means the slowest provider sets the pace for all of them. Separate queues isolate the failure.

Watch out. Templating and localisation are the other real complexity, and your multilingual work at Casepoint is a genuine credential there.

PART F - The Month 3 self-test

Cover the answers. Anything you cannot say goes in the WEAK tab.

# Say it out loud, no notes
1 The full URL journey, five minutes, without stalling
2 The TCP handshake, and what reliability costs
3 Why TLS uses both asymmetric and symmetric cryptography
4 Head-of-line blocking, and what HTTP/2 fixed and what it did not
5 Why a context switch is expensive - cache and TLB
6 Virtual memory, page faults, and why a fault is not an error
7 How await maps down to IOCP, and why waiting needs no thread
8 Consistent hashing, virtual nodes, and why modulo fails
9 CAP stated correctly, including the common misreading
10 Why exactly-once delivery is impossible and what you do instead
11 Visibility timeout, and what goes wrong when processing is slow
12 Why retries need jitter, and why they need a circuit breaker too
13 SQS versus Kafka, with a real reason for each
14 The dual-write problem and how the outbox solves it

Your advantage in this month. You have used SQS, EventBridge, Redis and SignalR in production. You are not learning Part D from zero - you are learning the vocabulary for things you have already built. Always anchor the answer to your own system: "we hit exactly this with duplicate deliveries in the email pipeline, and the fix was...". That is the answer no other candidate can give.

Month 4 Q&A - Design, LLD and Distributed Systems

Read this on the train. You do not need a laptop, a compiler or two free hours - that is the whole point of these files. Each question has the answer you would say, the reason it is true, and the mistake to avoid. Read one question or twenty; it works either way.

If you only have 20 minutes, read these five

# Question
1 Explain SRP without reciting the definition
2 Why is Dependency Inversion not the same as using a DI container?

4 Why can a distributed lock not be made safe with timeouts alone?
5 What is the dual-write problem and how does outbox solve it?

What this file answers

Everything in the Month 4 checkpoint, plus the LLD round questions Amazon asks explicitly. Part C is the material that separates SDE II from SDE I.

PART A - SOLID, with real violations

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q1. Explain Single Responsibility without reciting the definition.

Say this. "One reason to change" - not "does one thing". A class that formats a report and also emails it has two reasons to change: the layout team and the delivery team. When one changes you risk breaking the other, and two teams end up editing one file.

Why. The unit is a reason for change, which means a stakeholder, not a verb. That is why "does one thing" is misleading - a method that validates, saves and publishes does one business thing and has three reasons to change.

Watch out. Use a real example from your own code. "I had a service that parsed the file and also decided the retry policy" is worth ten textbook definitions.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q2. What does Open/Closed actually look like in practice?

Say this. You should be able to add behaviour without editing existing code. In practice that means the variation point is behind an abstraction - a new payment provider is a new class implementing an interface, not a new branch in a switch that everything already depends on.

Why. Editing working code risks breaking working behaviour. Adding a class cannot break what was already there, so the blast radius of a change is bounded.

Instead of. Do not abstract pre-emptively. Open/Closed is a response to observed change - the second time you edit that switch, extract the abstraction. Doing it on the first is speculative generality.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q3. Give a Liskov violation that compiles fine and breaks at runtime.

Say this. A Square inheriting Rectangle with independent width and height setters. Code written against Rectangle sets width to 4 and height to 5 and asserts the area is 20 - which holds for every rectangle and fails for a square, because setting one dimension changes the other.

Why. Liskov is about behavioural substitutability, not just signature compatibility. The compiler checks the signature; the invariants are what break.

Watch out. A better real-world one: an implementation that throws NotSupportedException for a method on the interface. It satisfies the compiler and violates the contract - a read-only collection implementing IList is the classic.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q4. Why is Dependency Inversion not the same thing as using a DI container?

Say this. Dependency Inversion is a design principle: high-level policy should not depend on low-level detail; both should depend on an abstraction, and the abstraction should be owned by the high-level side. A DI container is a tool that wires up constructors. You can use a container and still violate the principle completely - inject a concrete SqlRepository everywhere and nothing is inverted.

Why. The inversion is about who owns the interface. If your domain layer defines IOrderRepository and the data layer implements it, the dependency arrow points inward and the domain is testable in isolation. If the data layer defines it, nothing changed.

Watch out. This is a favourite question because almost everyone conflates them. Getting it right is a strong signal, and it leads naturally into talking about testability.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q5. When is a design pattern over-engineering?

Say this. When there is only one implementation and no concrete reason to expect a second. A Strategy with one strategy is a switch statement with three extra files and one more indirection to trace when debugging.

Why. Every abstraction has a cost: more files, more indirection, harder navigation. It pays only when it absorbs a change you actually make. If the change never comes, you paid for nothing.

Watch out. Interviewers love a candidate who can say "I would not use a pattern here, and here is why". Enthusiasm for patterns reads as junior; judgement about them reads as senior.

PART B - The patterns that matter

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q6. Strategy or a switch statement?

Say this. Strategy when the behaviours are genuinely independent, likely to grow, and better tested separately - payment providers, pricing rules, export formats. A switch when there are two or three cases, they are stable, and they are short enough to read at a glance.

Why. Strategy converts a compile-time branch into a runtime composition. That buys extensibility and testability and costs indirection.

Watch out. The honest version: refactor the switch to Strategy when you edit it for the third time. "I refactored a switch to Strategy and then judged whether it actually improved" is a mature answer.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q7. How do event handlers cause memory leaks in .NET?

Say this. Subscribing creates a reference from the publisher to the subscriber. If the publisher outlives the subscriber and you never unsubscribe, the subscriber can never be collected - along with everything it references.

Why. The direction is what surprises people. You wrote publisher.Event += handler, so it looks like the subscriber depends on the publisher, but the delegate list lives on the publisher and holds the subscriber alive.

Instead of. Unsubscribe in Dispose, or use weak event patterns. In practice: any long-lived singleton raising events is a leak waiting to happen.

Watch out. A lambda capturing this has the same effect and is harder to spot, because there is no named method to search for.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q8. Decorator or inheritance?

Say this. Decorator when you want to add behaviour to an instance at runtime and combine additions freely - caching plus logging plus retry over the same repository, composed in any order. Inheritance when the behaviour is fixed at compile time and there is a genuine is-a relationship.

Why. Decorator composes; inheritance multiplies. Three optional behaviours by inheritance means eight classes for every combination. By decoration it is three classes you stack.

Watch out. ASP.NET Core middleware is the Decorator pattern - each one wraps the next and can act before and after. Saying that connects Month 2 to Month 4 and is a genuinely good observation.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q9. Should you wrap EF Core in a repository? Argue both sides.

Say this. Against: DbSet<T> is already a repository and DbContext is already a unit of work, so a thin wrapper is duplication that also hides useful capability - you lose composable IQueryable, Include, projections and split queries, or you leak them through anyway. For: it gives you a domain-shaped interface, keeps EF out of the domain layer, makes unit tests trivial, and centralises query logic so you do not have the same filter written twelve times.

Why. The real question is what you are isolating from. If it is "we might swap the ORM" - you will not, and the abstraction will leak. If it is "the domain should not know about EF" - that is a legitimate architectural boundary.

Watch out. Having a genuine opinion with reasons on both sides is the answer. A confident one-sided answer here reads as inexperience, because both are defensible.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q10. Why is Singleton often called an anti-pattern, and when is it still right?

Say this. Because it hides a dependency - anything can reach it globally, so it does not appear in any constructor and cannot be substituted in a test. It also introduces shared mutable state across the whole process. It is still right for genuinely stateless, thread-safe, expensive-to-create things: a configured HttpClient, a logger, a cache.

Why. The problem is the static access, not the single instance. A singleton registered in a DI container and injected through a constructor has the single instance without the global access, which is why that is the pattern everyone actually uses.

Watch out. "Singleton lifetime is fine; the Singleton pattern is usually not" is a crisp way to say it.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q11. Name three anti-patterns you have actually seen.

Say this. Anemic domain model - entities that are just property bags with all the logic in "service" classes, so the rules are scattered and duplicated. Service locator - resolving dependencies from a container inside a class, which hides them and defeats the point of DI. God object - one class that grew until nobody dares change it, usually called Manager or Helper.

Why. All three share a cause: it is easier to add to an existing thing than to create the right new thing. That is also why they grow rather than appear.

Watch out. You have worked on a legacy eDiscovery platform - you have seen these. A specific, unnamed example from real code is far more convincing than the definitions.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q12. Why is untestable code usually badly designed code?

Say this. Because the things that make code hard to test are the things that make it hard to change: hidden dependencies, static state, doing too much, and no seams. If you cannot construct the class without a database, the class knows too much about the database.

Why. A test is just another caller. If a test cannot use it in isolation, no other caller can either - so tomorrow's feature will not be able to reuse it.

Watch out. "Testability and good design are the same conversation" is the line. Interviewers who care about design care about this.

PART C - The hard parts of distributed systems

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q13. Why is two-phase commit avoided in modern systems?

Say this. Because it blocks. The coordinator asks everyone to prepare, then tells everyone to commit. If the coordinator dies after the prepare phase, every participant is holding locks and cannot decide alone whether to commit or abort - so they wait, holding those locks, until it comes back. It converts one node's failure into everyone's unavailability.

Why. The participants have promised they can commit, so they cannot unilaterally abort; but they have not been told to, so they cannot commit. There is no safe local decision.

Instead of. A saga: a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action, so every step commits immediately and failure is handled by compensating rather than by holding locks. You trade atomicity for availability and accept temporary inconsistency.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q14. Explain Raft leader election.

Say this. Every node has a randomised election timeout. A follower that hears nothing from a leader becomes a candidate, increments the term, and requests votes. A node grants one vote per term to the first candidate whose log is at least as up to date as its own. A candidate with a majority becomes leader and starts sending heartbeats.

Why. Randomised timeouts prevent everyone becoming a candidate at once. Requiring a majority guarantees at most one leader per term, and the log-freshness rule guarantees no committed entry is ever lost.

Watch out. Terms are a logical clock. A message from an older term is rejected, which is what makes a returning stale leader harmless.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q15. Why can a distributed lock not be made safe with timeouts alone?

Say this. Because the lock holder can be paused - a long GC pause, a slow disk, a descheduled VM - past the lease expiry without knowing it. The lock is released, another client acquires it, and then the first one wakes up and continues, still believing it holds the lock. Now two clients are in the critical section and neither is wrong from its own point of view.

Why. The lease expires in real time, but the holder's belief expires only when it checks - and it cannot check atomically with the work it is doing.

Instead of. A fencing token: the lock service issues a monotonically increasing number with each grant, and the protected resource rejects any write with a token lower than the highest it has seen. The stale holder's write is refused by the resource itself.

Watch out. This is Kleppmann's critique of Redlock, and it is a genuinely senior topic. Knowing the fencing-token answer sets you apart.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q16. What is the dual-write problem?

Say this. You need to change the database and publish an event, and there is no transaction spanning both. Whichever you do first, a crash in between leaves the system inconsistent: commit then fail to publish means the event is lost; publish then fail to commit means you announced something that did not happen.

Why. There is no ordering that fixes it, because the failure window exists in both orders. You need to make it one atomic operation, which is what the outbox does.

Instead of. The outbox: write the event to a table in the same transaction as the data change, and have a separate publisher read that table. One commit, then an at-least-once publish that can safely be retried.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q17. Choreography or orchestration for a saga?

Say this. Choreography: each service reacts to events and emits its own, with no central controller - loosely coupled, no single point of failure, but the overall flow exists nowhere and is very hard to debug. Orchestration: one coordinator drives each step explicitly - the flow is visible in one place and easy to reason about, at the cost of coupling and a component that must stay available.

Why. It is the classic distributed trade-off: emergent behaviour is resilient and opaque, centralised behaviour is clear and coupled.

Watch out. For anything with money or compliance in it, prefer orchestration. When someone asks "why did this order not ship", you want one place to look.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q18. Explain the circuit breaker states, and why retries alone amplify an outage.

Say this. Closed - calls pass through, failures are counted. Open - the threshold was crossed, so calls fail immediately without touching the downstream. Half-open - after a timeout, let a trial trickle through; success closes it, failure re-opens it. Retries alone amplify because a struggling service receives more load exactly when it can least handle it, so it never recovers.

Why. The breaker converts a slow failure into a fast one, which protects your own threads and gives the downstream room to recover. Failing fast is a feature.

Watch out. Retry plus breaker plus timeout plus jitter is the complete set. Any one on its own is incomplete, and naming all four is the answer.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q19. What is a bulkhead and what does it protect?

Say this. Separate resource pools per dependency, so exhausting one cannot starve the others. If all your threads or connections are in one pool and one downstream goes slow, every request queues behind it - including ones that never needed that dependency.

Why. It is named after ship compartments: the point is to make one flooded compartment survivable rather than fatal.

Watch out. This is a very common real outage shape: an unrelated feature goes down and takes the whole API with it because they shared a connection pool.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q20. What are RED and USE?

Say this. RED is for services: Rate, Errors, Duration - how many requests, how many failed, how long they took. USE is for resources: Utilisation, Saturation, Errors - how busy, how much queuing, how many faults. RED tells you the user is unhappy; USE tells you which resource is why.

Why. They are complementary because a service can be slow with no resource saturated - waiting on a downstream - and a resource can be saturated with users still happy.

Watch out. Pair it with the four golden signals - latency, traffic, errors, saturation - and say they overlap deliberately. Also: measure p95 and p99, never the average. The average hides exactly the requests people complain about.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q21. Why do correlation IDs matter, and where do they have to flow?

Say this. They are the only way to reconstruct one logical operation across many services and asynchronous hops. The ID must be generated at the edge, put in the logging context, and propagated through every boundary - HTTP headers, and crucially the message metadata when you enqueue, so the worker logs under the same ID as the API.

Why. Without it, a failure in a worker is a log line with no path back to the request that caused it. With it, one search reconstructs the whole story.

Watch out. The queue hop is the one people miss. You built this in week 16 - "trace one job end to end using only your logs" is exactly this, and it is a great thing to have done.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q22. What is an SLI, an SLO, and an error budget?

Say this. An SLI is the measurement - "99.2% of requests succeeded in under 300ms". An SLO is the target - "99.9% under 300ms". The error budget is the allowed shortfall: at 99.9% you may fail 0.1%, which is about 43 minutes a month.

Why. The budget turns reliability into a spendable resource. Budget remaining means you can ship risky changes; budget exhausted means you stop feature work and fix reliability. It replaces arguing with arithmetic.

Watch out. 100% is never the target - it is unachievable and the last fraction costs more than it is worth. Saying that shows you understand reliability as an engineering trade rather than an aspiration.

PART D - The LLD round (Amazon tests this explicitly)

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q23. How do you approach a 45-minute LLD from a blank page?

Say this. Five minutes clarifying requirements and explicitly stating what is out of scope. Five listing the nouns - those become your entities. Ten defining the interfaces and where the variation lives. Twenty coding the core classes, with real method bodies for the interesting parts and stubs for the boring ones. Five on edge cases and one alternative you rejected.

Why. Interviewers score whether you got to working code, and whether your class boundaries make sense. Perfect completeness is not expected; a sensible structure and an articulated trade-off is.

Watch out. The most common failure is spending twenty-five minutes on requirements and never writing a class. Set yourself a hard limit and move.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q24. Design a parking lot - what are the real decisions?

Say this. Entities: Vehicle with a size, Spot with a size and occupancy, Level, Ticket, and a PricingStrategy. The real decisions are: how a vehicle maps to eligible spot sizes; how you find a free spot efficiently, which is a free-list or a per-size counter rather than a scan; making pricing a strategy so hourly, daily and flat are separate classes; and thread safety on allocation so two cars cannot take one spot.

Why. The allocation concurrency is the part that separates a real answer from a class diagram. It is the same compare-and-set problem as everywhere else.

Watch out. Have one rejected alternative ready. "I considered a single list of spots scanned linearly and rejected it because lookup becomes O(n) at exactly the busiest time."

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q25. Design a logger - and where does your design differ from a real library?

Say this. Entities: a Logger facade, a Level enum, Sinks (console, file, HTTP), Formatters, and a buffered async writer. Key decisions: level filtering as early as possible so a disabled level costs almost nothing; sinks as an interface for extension; buffering with a background flush so logging never blocks the caller; and deciding what happens when the buffer is full - drop or block.

Why. Serilog adds structured logging: the message template and its properties are kept separate so downstream tools can query on fields rather than grepping strings. That is the biggest difference from a naive design and it is the right thing to mention.

Watch out. "What happens if the sink is down?" is the follow-up. Answer: buffer with a bound, then drop, and never let logging take down the application.

PART E - Your project, defended

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q26. Why a queue at all, and what did it cost you?

Say this. It decouples submission from execution, so the API can accept work in milliseconds and stay responsive under a spike, and workers scale independently. The cost is real: eventual consistency, so the caller must poll or be notified; at-least-once delivery, so every handler needs idempotency; and a whole new class of operational concern - queue depth, poison messages, DLQ monitoring.

Why. You have converted a latency problem into a complexity problem. That is usually the right trade for background work and the wrong one for something the user is waiting on.

Watch out. Never present the queue as free. Naming what it cost is what makes the choice sound like a decision.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q27. Walk me through exactly what happens when a worker dies mid-job.

Say this. The job row stays in a Running state with a lease and a heartbeat timestamp that the worker was updating. When the worker dies the heartbeat stops. A reaper process looks for jobs whose lease has expired and returns them to Pending, incrementing the attempt count. Another worker picks it up. Because the handler is idempotent, any partial work from the first attempt does not double-apply.

Why. The heartbeat is what distinguishes "slow" from "dead" - without it you either kill slow jobs or wait forever for dead ones. The lease is the same lease-expiry problem as a distributed lock.

Watch out. Be honest about the window: a job can be re-run while the original worker is merely paused, which is exactly why idempotency is load-bearing and not decorative.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q28. Where is your bottleneck, and how do you know?

Say this. Name it and give the number. Typically the database on status writes, or the queue receive round trip, or worker CPU on the actual job. You know because you load tested with k6, measured p95 and p99 at increasing load, watched where latency turned upward, and correlated that with queue depth, connection pool usage and CPU.

Why. A bottleneck is where the curve bends, not where you guessed. Having the numbers is what makes this a strong answer rather than a plausible one.

Watch out. This is the question that most reliably exposes a project that was never actually load tested. Have the table of numbers in your README and be able to quote a figure.

LLD, patterns and distributed systems Q&A
Q29. What failure mode did you deliberately not handle, and why?

Say this. Pick a real one and own it. For example: no multi-region failover, because the added complexity and cost would not have taught me anything the single-region design did not, and the recovery objective for a demonstration platform does not justify it. Or: no exactly-once external side effects, because that needs an outbox on the third-party call, and I chose to demonstrate idempotency in the core path instead.

Why. A deliberate, articulated scope decision reads as engineering judgement. "I did not think of it" reads as luck.

Watch out. This is the single best question to prepare for your project, because it distinguishes someone who built something from someone who followed a tutorial. Have your answer written down.

PART F - The Month 4 self-test

Cover the answers. Anything you cannot say goes in the WEAK tab.

# Say it out loud, no notes
1 Each SOLID principle, with a violation you personally encountered
2 Why Dependency Inversion is not the same as a DI container
3 When a design pattern is over-engineering
4 How event handlers leak memory in .NET
5 The case for and against wrapping EF Core in a repository
6 Why 2PC is avoided, and what replaced it
7 Raft leader election, from memory
8 Why a distributed lock is unsafe with timeouts alone, and what fencing tokens fix
9 The dual-write problem and the outbox pattern
10 Circuit breaker states, and why retries alone amplify an outage
11 RED versus USE, and why p99 not average
12 What happens to an in-flight job when its worker dies
13 Your project bottleneck, with a real number
14 A failure mode you deliberately did not handle, and why

Parts C and E are the ones that matter most. Part C is the material Amazon uses to separate SDE II from SDE I. Part E is your project, and your project will be probed harder than anything else on your resume - a weak answer on your own work costs more than a weak answer on a general topic.

Q05 — M5_System_Design_and_Behavioural

Month 5 Q&A - System Design and Behavioural

Weeks 17 to 20. The month you become interview-ready. 34 questions.

Covers: Weeks 17-20. Project phases 2 to 4, the estimation numbers, the classic designs, and the behavioural structure.

Read this on the train. You do not need a laptop, a compiler or two free hours - that is the whole point of these files. Each question has the answer you would say, the reason it is true, and the mistake to avoid. Read one question or twenty; it works either way.

How to use this on a bad week

• 20 minutes on a train: read the five questions in the box below. Nothing else.

• Reading is not learning. After each question, close the file and say the answer out loud once. On a train, mouth it silently - it still works. If you cannot, read it again and move on. You will meet it again.

• Mark what you could not say. Put it in the WEAK tab of the tracker when you get home. That is the only homework.

• This replaces nothing. The tracker still runs the plan. This is what you do with the hours the plan cannot use - the commute, the wait, the evening you are too tired to code.

If you only have 20 minutes, read these five

# Question
1 The nine steps of a system design, in order
2 The estimation numbers you must know cold
3 Why does neither pure fan-out strategy work at scale?
4 How do you avoid overselling inventory without a distributed transaction?
5 Why does Action get 55% of a STAR answer?

What this file answers

Everything in the Month 5 checkpoint - which is the gate to applying. Part A is the numbers to memorise; Part D is the behavioural structure that decides roughly half your Amazon score.

PART A - The design framework and the numbers

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q1. What are the nine steps, in order?

Say this. Clarify requirements. Estimate scale. Define the API. Choose the data model. Draw the high-level architecture. Identify bottlenecks. Scale it. Handle failure. State the trade-offs.

Why. The order is the skill. Candidates who improvise the order ramble and run out of time; candidates who follow a framework sound senior even when the design is imperfect - because the interviewer can follow them.

Watch out. Step 9 is where the round is won. Anyone can draw boxes. "I chose eventual consistency here, so a user may see a stale count - fine for a view counter, unacceptable for an account balance" is what gets you hired.

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q2. How do you budget the 45 minutes?

Say this. Five minutes on requirements and scope. Five on scale estimation. Five on the API. Five on the data model. Ten on the architecture. Ten on bottlenecks, scaling and failure. Five on trade-offs and questions. Watch the clock and say what you are skipping.

Why. Running out of time before you draw anything is the single most common failure. Announcing "I have about ten minutes left so I will focus on the write path" is itself a senior signal.

Watch out. If the interviewer pushes you into a detail early, answer briefly and then say "I want to come back to that once the high-level shape is down" - and then actually come back.

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q3. What estimation numbers must you know cold?

Say this. Powers of two: 2^10 is a thousand, 2^20 a million, 2^30 a billion. So a 32-bit int holds about 4 billion, and 4 KB is a page. Time: 86,400 seconds in a day, so 1 million requests a day is about 12 per second, and 100 million a day is about 1,200 per second. Latency: memory access nanoseconds, SSD read tens of microseconds, network round trip within a datacentre about half a millisecond, cross-continent 100-150 milliseconds, disk seek a few milliseconds.

Why. You need them so you can compute out loud without stalling. The interviewer is watching whether you can reason about magnitude, not whether you are precise.

Watch out. Round aggressively and say you are rounding. "Call it a thousand a second, so ten servers at a hundred each with headroom" is exactly the right register.

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q4. How do you estimate storage for a design?

Say this. Rows per day times bytes per row times retention. Be explicit about the row: an ID is 8 bytes, a timestamp 8, a short string 50-100, a UUID 16. Then add indexes, which are often the same size again, and replication, which multiplies by the replica count.

Why. People forget indexes and replication and then under-estimate by three to five times. Mentioning both unprompted is a strong signal.

Watch out. Then sanity check it. "That is 2 TB a year, which one machine can hold, so I do not need sharding yet" is a conclusion. A number with no conclusion is not an estimate.

PART B - The classic designs, and the one hard part of each

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q5. Why does neither pure fan-out strategy work for a news feed?

Say this. Fan-out on write precomputes each follower's feed when you post - reads are then trivial, but a celebrity with ten million followers causes ten million writes for one post. Fan-out on read assembles the feed at request time - writes are trivial, but every read now queries every followee, which is slow for the common case. So real systems do both: fan-out on write for normal users, and merge celebrity posts in at read time.

Why. The distributions are extreme. Most users have few followers and read often; a few have enormous follower counts. One strategy cannot be right for both ends.

Watch out. Naming this as the celebrity problem and giving the hybrid answer is the expected senior response.

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q6. How do you avoid overselling inventory without a distributed transaction?

Say this. Reserve rather than deduct. On add-to-cart or checkout, create a reservation row with a short expiry, using a conditional update - decrement available stock only if available is greater than zero, in one atomic statement. Payment success converts the reservation to a sale; expiry releases it. A background job sweeps expired reservations.

Why. The atomic conditional update is the whole trick: the database is already a consensus system for a single row, so you use it rather than coordinating across services.

Watch out. Be ready for "what if payment succeeds after the reservation expired?" Answer: a compensating action - refund, or re-reserve if stock allows - and say explicitly that you accept rare oversell over a distributed transaction. That is the saga trade.

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q7. Why are payment systems obsessed with idempotency?

Say this. Because a retry must not charge twice and the network cannot tell you whether the first attempt succeeded. So every charge carries a client-generated idempotency key; the provider stores it and returns the original result for any repeat. Your side does the same for your own writes.

Why. Money is the one domain where at-least-once with a non-idempotent handler is immediately and visibly wrong to the customer.

Watch out. Also: reconciliation. You compare your ledger against the provider's daily and investigate differences, because eventually something will diverge. And webhooks must be idempotent for the same reason - providers retry them.

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q8. How do you deliver a message to a device that is offline?

Say this. Persist first, deliver second. The message is written to storage with a per-conversation sequence number, then pushed to whatever devices are connected. An offline device, on reconnect, sends the last sequence number it has and pulls everything after it. A push notification via FCM or APNs wakes the app so it reconnects sooner.

Why. The connection is a fast path, not the source of truth. Once storage is authoritative, offline delivery is just a resume-from-cursor problem.

Watch out. You did this with SignalR and FCM in VCDoctor - multi-device signalling is exactly the hard part. Use that, and mention per-device cursors, since two devices are at different positions.

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q9. What is the hard part of a file storage design?

Say this. Chunking and deduplication. Split each file into fixed-size chunks, hash each chunk, and store chunks by hash - so an identical chunk is stored once no matter how many files or users contain it. Metadata maps a file to an ordered list of chunk hashes. Sync then only transfers chunks the server does not already have.

Why. It makes resumable upload trivial, makes a small edit to a large file cheap, and gives deduplication for free - all from one decision.

Watch out. The trade-off: fixed-size chunking breaks when you insert bytes near the start, because every subsequent boundary shifts. Content-defined chunking with a rolling hash fixes that at higher CPU cost.

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q10. Compare the rate limiting algorithms.

Say this. Fixed window - a counter per interval. Simplest, but allows double the limit across a boundary. Sliding window log - store every timestamp. Exact, but memory grows with traffic. Sliding window counter - weight the previous window. Good approximation, cheap. Token bucket - refills at a rate up to a capacity. Allows a controlled burst and is usually the right default. Leaky bucket - drains at a constant rate, smoothing output.

Why. They differ in how much burst they permit and how much state they cost. Token bucket wins in practice because real traffic is bursty and rejecting a legitimate burst is worse than allowing it.

Watch out. Whichever you pick, the state must be shared across instances and updated atomically. A per-instance limiter multiplies your limit by the number of instances - a real bug, not a theoretical one.

PART C - Your project, in production terms

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q11. How do you stop one tenant starving the others?

Say this. Per-tenant fairness rather than a single global queue. Either a queue per tenant with round-robin consumption, or weighted fair queueing, plus a per-tenant concurrency cap and a rate limit at the API. Without that, a tenant submitting a hundred thousand jobs owns the whole worker pool.

Why. A single FIFO queue is fair in arrival order, which is not the same as fair between tenants. A bulk submitter legitimately gets everything.

Watch out. This is the multi-tenant version of the bulkhead pattern, and it is a genuinely good thing to have in your project because most demo projects miss it.

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q12. How do you prove tenant isolation rather than assert it?

Say this. A test that tries to read tenant B's job as tenant A and asserts a 404 or 403. Then enforce it in one place - a query filter or repository layer that always applies the tenant predicate - rather than remembering it at every call site.

Why. Isolation implemented per-endpoint will be forgotten on the twelfth endpoint. Implemented once as a filter, it cannot be forgotten.

Watch out. Prefer 404 over 403 for another tenant's resource - 403 confirms the ID exists, which leaks information.

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q13. Liveness or readiness - what is the difference and why does it matter?

Say this. Liveness answers "is this process healthy, or should it be restarted?" Readiness answers "can it serve traffic right now?" A pod warming a cache or waiting for a database is alive but not ready. Getting them backwards is dangerous: if liveness checks a database, a database blip restarts every instance simultaneously.

Why. Liveness controls the restart decision; readiness controls the load balancer. Coupling liveness to a shared dependency turns a dependency outage into a total outage.

Watch out. Liveness should check almost nothing - "is the event loop responsive". Readiness checks dependencies. That distinction is the answer.

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q14. What do p50, p95 and p99 tell you, and why not the average?

Say this. p99 means 99% of requests were faster than this. The average hides the tail: a system with a 50 ms average can have a 3-second p99, and that 1% is who complains. At scale 1% is a lot of people, and a page making twenty calls will hit the p99 on most page loads.

Why. Averages are dominated by the bulk; latency problems live in the tail. Percentiles are the only honest measure.

Watch out. Never average percentiles across servers - it is mathematically meaningless. And measure p99 of what the user experiences, not of one internal call.

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q15. Why do multi-stage Docker builds matter?

Say this. You build with the SDK in one stage and copy only the published output into a runtime-only final image. The compiler, sources, NuGet cache and intermediate files never reach the shipped image - typically a several-hundred-megabyte image becomes under a hundred.

Why. Smaller images pull faster, start faster, and have a smaller attack surface because there is no compiler or shell tooling to exploit.

Watch out. Have your own before-and-after numbers from week 19, and mention running as a non-root user - it is a one-line change interviewers notice.

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q16. What does your CI pipeline protect against, stage by stage?

Say this. Restore and build catches "it does not compile on a clean machine". Unit tests catch logic regressions. Integration tests against real Postgres and Redis catch wiring and SQL problems a mock would hide. Lint and analysers catch a class of bug and enforce consistency. Branch protection stops any of it being bypassed. Then the CD half builds and pushes an image only from a green build.

Why. Each stage is a category of failure caught at the cheapest point. The value is in what it prevents reaching production, not in the pipeline itself.

Watch out. "I built it rather than copying a template" matters here - be able to explain why each stage exists, because a copied pipeline is obvious under one follow-up.

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q17. How do you actually find a bottleneck under load?

Say this. Ramp the load in steps rather than jumping to the maximum. Watch where p95 turns sharply upward - that is saturation. At that point look at what is queuing: connection pool waits, queue depth, CPU, disk. Change one thing, re-measure, confirm the curve moved. Then stop, because the next bottleneck is always somewhere else.

Why. A step ramp shows you the curve; a single big number tells you only pass or fail. The bend in the curve is the information.

Watch out. "I scaled workers from one to four and throughput went up 3.2x, so it scales horizontally but not linearly - the database became the limit" is a genuinely excellent sentence. Have your version of it.

PART D - Behavioural structure

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q18. Why does Action get 55% of a STAR answer?

Say this. Because Action is what is scored. Situation and Task are context the interviewer needs to understand the Action, and Result is the evidence it worked. What they are assessing is what you decided, what you rejected, and why - and all of that lives in Action.

Why. The rubric asks "what did this person do and how did they think". Three minutes of company background gives the interviewer nothing to write down.

Watch out. Two sentences of Situation. Genuinely two. Then your ownership in one, then the bulk on Action, then a number.

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q19. Why does saying "we" cost you the answer?

Say this. Because the interviewer is hiring you, not your team. "We decided to redesign the pipeline" is unscoreable - it could mean you led it or you watched. "I proposed the event-driven design, and the team pushed back on cost, so I built a small prototype to show the numbers" is scoreable.

Why. The signal they need is attribution. Without "I", there is nothing to attribute.

Watch out. Use "we" deliberately where the work genuinely was collaborative. The contrast makes the "I" credible rather than boastful - all-"I" reads as taking credit.

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q20. What makes a Have Backbone story work?

Say this. A real disagreement with someone more senior, argued with data rather than opinion, and then - this is the half people omit - full commitment to whatever was decided, including when you lost. "I disagreed, I made my case with numbers, the decision went the other way, and I implemented it properly and it worked out" is a complete answer.

Why. The principle has two clauses. Candidates prepare the disagreement and forget the commit, which reads as someone who argues and then sulks.

Watch out. This is the most under-prepared principle and you need a genuine example. Start noticing these moments at work now and writing them down the same day - you will not remember them in week 17.

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q21. What makes an Earn Trust story work?

Say this. A time you were wrong, or received hard feedback, and responded well. Not a disguised success - an actual mistake, what it cost, what you did about it, and what changed in how you work.

Why. The principle is testing self-criticism. A candidate who cannot describe being wrong is either not self-aware or not honest, and interviewers read it as the second.

Watch out. Candidates instinctively avoid stories that make them look bad, which is exactly backwards here. The story that makes you look human is the one that scores.

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q22. How do you answer "what would you do differently?"

Say this. Give a real answer with a reason, and make it a design decision rather than a personal failing. "I would have added the dead letter queue in the first iteration instead of the third - we spent two weeks debugging failures that a DLQ would have made visible in an hour."

Why. It is the maturity signal. Every real project has something you would change, and a candidate who says "nothing" has either not reflected or is not being honest.

Watch out. Have one prepared for every story. It is asked constantly and improvising it produces either a non-answer or an unflattering one.

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q23. The interviewer keeps asking "why" until you run out. What do you do?

Say this. Say so, and say how you would find out. "I do not know the exact figure - what I remember is the order of magnitude, and I would confirm it from the CloudWatch metrics." Reaching the edge of your knowledge is the design of the Bar Raiser round, not a failure.

Why. They are calibrating depth, and they cannot do that without finding the edge. Inventing a number is the one response that reliably fails, because it is often detectable and it destroys trust in everything you said before.

Watch out. "I do not know, but here is how I would find out" scores well. "I do not know" and silence does not. The second half is the whole answer.

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q24. How do you quantify a story when you do not have exact numbers?

Say this. Use the order of magnitude and say that is what you are doing. "It was in the region of a hundred thousand records - I do not have the exact figure to hand." That is honest, memorable, and far better than a precise-sounding invention.

Why. Interviewers forget adjectives and remember numbers. "Significantly faster" is forgotten in a minute; "seven to ten hours down to about ninety minutes" is remembered after the loop.

Watch out. Your strongest numbers: 80% reduction, seven-to-ten hours to ninety minutes, 100,000+ records, one worker versus four. Know them cold and pause after saying them.

System design and behavioral Q&A
Q25. Which of your stories is the flagship, and what does that mean for preparation?

Say this. The email pipeline. It means it will be probed hardest and asked most often, so it needs the deepest preparation: what was actually slow and how you measured it, why SQS rather than an alternative, how you handled duplicate delivery, what surprised you, what you would do differently, and what the new bottleneck became.

Why. A weak follow-up on your best story is worse than not telling it, because it suggests the headline number was not really yours.

Watch out. Prepare it as a set of eight answers, not one story. Then it survives any order of questioning.

PART E - The Month 5 gate

This is the most important checkpoint in the plan. Do not start applying to your top targets until these are genuinely true. The plan is eight months precisely so a two-week delay here is affordable - and applying with a half-built project converts a strong candidate into a rejection plus a 6-12 month cooldown, which is far more expensive.

# True?
1 The project is deployed and publicly reachable
2 It survives a worker being killed mid-job, with the job recovered
3 It handles duplicate delivery without double-processing, and I can demonstrate it
4 Retries with backoff and jitter, and a working DLQ with replay
5 A rate limiter that is correct across multiple instances
6 A metrics dashboard and health checks
7 Load tested, with real p95/p99 numbers written down
8 I know my bottleneck and can evidence it with a number
9 CI/CD green, and I built it rather than copying it
10 README complete with an architecture diagram and stated trade-offs
11 15-20 STAR stories written and rehearsed aloud
12 Every high-frequency Amazon principle covered by at least two stories
13 A Have Backbone story that is genuinely mine
14 9 system designs completed, all timed at 45 minutes
15 I can explain the project in 5 minutes, and defend it for 30

If several are "no" - spend the first two weeks of month 6 repairing, then apply. That is the plan working as designed, not the plan failing.

Month 6 Q&A - Interview Rounds and Delivery

Weeks 21 to 24. Applications start. This month is about performance, not knowledge. 26 questions.

Covers: Weeks 21-24. The Google and Amazon loops, how to behave inside a round, what to do when stuck, and the aptitude gates on mid-tier applications.

Read this on the train. You do not need a laptop, a compiler or two free hours - that is the whole point of these files. Each question has the answer you would say, the reason it is true, and the mistake to avoid. Read one question or twenty; it works either way.

How to use this on a bad week

• 20 minutes on a train: read the five questions in the box below. Nothing else.
