# Question
1 What do you do in the first five minutes of a coding round?
2 You are stuck with fifteen minutes left. What do you actually do?
3 The interviewer gives you a hint. How do you take it?
4 What is the Bar Raiser looking for?
5 How do you code with no autocomplete and no compiler?

What this file answers

By now the knowledge is largely built. What is untested is whether you can deploy it in 45 minutes, in English, with someone watching. That is a different skill and this file is about that skill.

PART A - Inside a coding round

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q1. What do you do in the first five minutes of a coding round?

Say this. Restate the problem in your own words and get agreement. Ask about input size, ranges, duplicates, empty input, and whether the input is sorted. Work through one small example by hand. Then state the brute force and its complexity. Only then start on the optimisation.

Why. Every one of those is scored. Clarifying questions demonstrate you do not build the wrong thing; the worked example catches misunderstandings before you have written code; the brute force means your optimisation is visibly a choice.

Watch out. Starting to code in the first minute is the most common self-inflicted wound. It reads as pattern-matching rather than problem-solving, even when the answer is right.

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q2. How do you think aloud without rambling?

Say this. Narrate decisions, not keystrokes. "I need fast lookup of what I have already seen, so a hash set" is a decision. "Now I am writing a for loop" is a keystroke. When you go quiet to think, say so - "give me twenty seconds to think about the edge case" - and then be quiet.

Why. Silence with no explanation reads as being stuck. Constant low-value narration is hard to follow. Announcing your silence solves both.

Watch out. Practise this from week 13, out loud, alone. It feels ridiculous and it is the difference between knowing the answer and being seen to know it.

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q3. You are stuck with fifteen minutes left. What do you actually do?

Say this. Say where you are stuck, precisely - that alone often produces a hint. Then take the brute-force solution and write it, stating that you are securing a working answer first and will optimise if time allows. A working O(n squared) beats an unfinished O(n).

Why. The interviewer needs something to evaluate. An elegant half-solution scores below a complete inelegant one, and stating your reasoning for the fallback shows time management.

Watch out. Do not go silent and keep trying. Fifteen minutes of quiet struggling produces no signal and no code, which is the worst possible outcome.

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q4. The interviewer offers a hint. How do you take it?

Say this. Take it immediately and gratefully, then think out loud about what it implies. "So you are suggesting I look at what I would need at each step - that points at keeping a running set rather than rescanning." Then act on it.

Why. Hints are part of the process; the interviewer wants you to succeed and is calibrating how much help you need. Refusing a hint or ignoring it costs far more than accepting it.

Watch out. Never argue with a hint or push past it silently. Both read badly, and the hint is usually the intended path.

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q5. How do you handle "can you make it faster?" when you think it is optimal?

Say this. Say why you believe it is optimal - "we have to look at every element at least once, so O(n) is a lower bound for time" - and then ask whether they mean space, or a different constraint. Often the question is about space or about a follow-up variation.

Why. Sometimes it is a genuine hint that a better bound exists; sometimes it is a test of whether you can defend your reasoning. Asking converts the ambiguity into information.

Watch out. Do not immediately assume you are wrong and start flailing. Confidence with a stated reason is what is being tested here.

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q6. How do you code with no autocomplete and no compiler?

Say this. Write the signature first, then the skeleton with clear names, then fill in the body. Say aloud what you would normally look up - "I think the method is TryGetValue, I would confirm the exact name". Then dry-run one small example line by line, out loud, with real values.

Why. Google interviews in a shared document. The skill being tested is whether you can hold the code in your head and verify it by reasoning rather than by running it.

Watch out. Two problems a week in a plain text editor from week 9. Candidates who only ever practise in an IDE discover this weakness during the interview, which is the worst possible time.

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q7. What is the code comprehension round and why is it good news for you?

Say this. You are shown unfamiliar code and asked to read it, explain what it does, find bugs and extend it. Google piloted it from 2026 for junior and mid-level roles in place of one coding round. It is good news because reading unfamiliar production code on a large legacy platform is literally your day job at Casepoint - and candidates grounded purely in LeetCode are weak at it.

Why. It tests something interviews historically missed and that real work is mostly made of. Your four and a half years are an advantage here rather than a neutral fact.

Watch out. Practise it: pick an open-source .NET repo, read a subsystem cold for 45 minutes, and explain aloud what it does, how, what you would change and where bugs might hide. Weeks 11, 24 and 27 have this scheduled.

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q8. How do you state complexity so it counts?

Say this. Unprompted, at the end, with a justification. "This is O(n) time because each element is pushed and popped at most once, and O(n) space for the stack in the worst case." Then, if relevant, note the trade you made.

Why. Waiting to be asked loses a point you could have taken. A bare "O(n)" with no reason is indistinguishable from a guess that happened to be right.

Watch out. Amortised is not average. Amortised is a guarantee across a sequence; average is expected over inputs. Using the right one is noticed.

PART B - Inside a design round

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q9. How do you open a system design round?

Say this. Do not design anything for the first five minutes. Ask what the system must do, who uses it, roughly how many, what the read-to-write ratio is, what latency matters, and what is out of scope. Then say the scope back: "so I am designing X for Y users, optimising for Z, and I am excluding W."

Why. Designing before scoping is the fastest way to spend forty minutes on the wrong system. The scoping statement also gives the interviewer a chance to redirect you cheaply.

Watch out. "What would you like me to focus on?" is a legitimate and strong question. Most design prompts are deliberately too large for the time available.

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q10. What do you do when the interviewer says "now scale it to ten times"?

Say this. Find the component that breaks first and say so before changing anything. Usually the database on writes, or a single-instance component holding state. Then apply one fix at a time with a reason - read replicas for read load, a cache for hot keys, sharding when a single writer is the limit, a queue to absorb bursts - and say what each costs.

Why. Naming the bottleneck first shows analysis. Reciting a list of scaling techniques shows memorisation, and interviewers can tell the difference instantly.

Watch out. Every scaling move has a cost: replicas bring staleness, caches bring invalidation, sharding brings cross-shard queries and rebalancing. Say the cost each time.

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q11. How do you handle a topic inside a design you genuinely do not know?

Say this. Name the boundary and reason from what you do know. "I have not run Cassandra in production, so I will not claim specifics - but the property I need here is a wide-column store with high write throughput and tunable consistency, and I would validate that assumption before committing."

Why. Design rounds test judgement under uncertainty, which is the actual job. Confident invention is the failing answer; reasoning from properties is the passing one.

Watch out. This is more common at your level than people expect, because designs deliberately wander into unfamiliar territory. Having a script for it removes the panic.

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q12. What separates a passing design from a strong one?

Say this. The trade-offs, stated unprompted, with the alternative named. Anyone can draw boxes. A strong candidate says "I am choosing eventual consistency for the feed count, which means a user may briefly see a stale number - acceptable here, and I would not accept it for an account balance."

Why. That sentence proves you know there was a decision, you know what you gave up, and you know when the answer would be different. That is seniority in one sentence.

Watch out. If you have five minutes left and nothing else to add, spend them on trade-offs. It is the highest-scoring thing you can say.

PART C - The loops themselves

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q13. What is the Bar Raiser looking for?

Say this. An interviewer from outside the hiring team, trained to protect the long-term hiring bar, with veto power. They will push harder than anyone else, not accept your first answer, and keep asking why until you reach the edge of your knowledge. They are calibrating depth and honesty.

Why. They are deliberately not incentivised to fill this role, so they are the check against a team hiring out of urgency.

Watch out. Reaching your limit is the design of the round, not a failure. "I do not know, but here is how I would find out" scores well. Inventing something reliably fails.

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q14. How is Amazon's loop different from Google's in practice?

Say this. Amazon weaves Leadership Principles into every round, so behavioural is roughly half your score and you can pass every coding round and still be rejected. It also tests LLD explicitly - you code a design. Google weights coding more heavily, makes system design a formal round, has a distinct Googliness round, and decides via a hiring committee that never met you.

Why. The committee is why Google feedback is written for an absent reader: consistency across rounds matters more than any single strong impression.

Watch out. Practical consequence: for Amazon, over-prepare the stories. For Google, over-practise coding without an IDE and narrating clearly.

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q15. What does the hiring committee mean for how you should answer?

Say this. Your interviewers write notes, and people who never met you read those notes. So make yourself easy to write down: state the approach clearly, name the complexity, give a number in your behavioural answers. Anything that only works through charm or tone does not survive transcription.

Why. The packet is the candidate as far as the committee is concerned. Vague brilliance reads as vague.

Watch out. This is why "seven to ten hours down to ninety minutes, about 80%" is so much stronger than "I significantly improved performance". One of those gets written down verbatim.

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q16. Why apply to mid-tier companies first?

Say this. Because interview skill is built by interviewing, and your first two loops will be your worst regardless of preparation. Spending them on companies you do not desperately want converts them from losses into free mocks - and Amazon and Google both have 6-12 month cooldowns after a rejection.

Why. The cooldown is the whole argument. A calibration interview costs you an afternoon; a wasted Amazon attempt costs you a year.

Watch out. Mid-tier companies in India commonly gate on aptitude before a human reads your code, which is why the aptitude intensive sits in weeks 21-22 and nowhere else.

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q17. What aptitude do you actually need, and what can you skip?

Say this. Data interpretation is the highest-frequency section, so drill that most. Then percentages, ratios, averages, profit and loss, time-speed-distance, time and work. Skip deep verbal reasoning. Google and Amazon do not test classical aptitude at all - this is purely to get through mid-tier gates.

Why. The transferable skill is approximation: in data interpretation you rarely need an exact answer, you need to eliminate three of four options fast. That is the same skill as step 2 of a system design.

Watch out. Two focused weeks removes this risk permanently. After that it never needs this much attention again - and if you are short on time, aptitude is the first thing to cut.

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q18. How do you analyse an interview afterwards?

Say this. Within 24 hours, in writing: company, round, questions as close to verbatim as you can remember, what went well specifically, the precise moment you stalled, and the root cause. Then a named repair action with a date.

Why. The root cause is the only field that matters. "I failed the DSA round" is useless. "I did not recognise it as a monotonic stack problem and burned twenty minutes on brute force" is repairable and schedulable.

Watch out. If the same root cause appears three times, your repair method is wrong, not your effort. Change the method - stop solving graph problems and instead implement BFS, DFS, topological sort and union-find from scratch until they are automatic.

PART D - Communication under pressure

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q19. Your English stalls mid-answer. What do you do?

Say this. Stop, and restart the sentence. Do not try to rescue a sentence that has gone wrong - short sentences are clearer and much harder to lose your thread in. "Let me say that more simply" is a perfectly professional thing to say and buys you the reset.

Why. Interviewers are assessing whether they can understand your technical reasoning, not your grammar. A short correct sentence beats a long tangled one every time.

Watch out. Build a phrase bank you can deploy without thinking: "Let me clarify the requirements first", "The trade-off here is", "My initial approach would be brute force, then I would optimise by", "Let me walk through an example to validate this".

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q20. How long should an answer be?

Say this. Answer, then stop. Most answers are 30 to 90 seconds; a STAR story is under three minutes. The most common mistake is continuing to talk after you have finished, because silence feels like failure. Silence is the interviewer's job to fill, not yours.

Why. Over-talking dilutes a good answer and often walks you into a weaker area you were not asked about.

Watch out. Practise the stop. Record yourself and listen for where the answer actually ended versus where you stopped talking - the gap is usually large.

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q21. How do you recover an answer that has gone badly?

Say this. Name it and reset. "I do not think I explained that well - the core point is..." then give the one-sentence version. Interviewers respect the self-correction; it reads as self-awareness rather than weakness.

Why. They are scoring your reasoning, not your first attempt at expressing it. A clean recovery is itself a positive signal.

Watch out. Do not apologise repeatedly or comment on your own nerves. One reset, then move on.

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q22. What do you do in the last five minutes when they ask if you have questions?

Say this. Always have four or five ready, and ask them. Having none signals you are not evaluating them, which weakens your position. Ask about the stack and what is changing, how ownership is divided, what success looks like in six months, and the biggest technical challenge the team faces right now.

Why. It is also your only chance to gather information for a decision you may have to make under time pressure later.

Watch out. For a role you might transfer out of, slip in the mobility question casually: "how many people have moved from the India office to an overseas team in the last couple of years?" That answer tells you the truth - Doc 14 has the full list.

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q23. How do you handle a panel or back-to-back onsite fatigue?

Say this. Treat each round as independent and reset deliberately between them - water, two minutes of quiet, do not replay the previous round. Round four is scored the same as round one, and a candidate who fades is a candidate who scores worse in the afternoon.

Why. Fatigue is a real and under-practised variable. It is why week 31 has two full mock loops in one day.

Watch out. If a previous round went badly, do not mention it in the next one. Each interviewer scores independently and does not know.

Interview rounds and communication Q&A
Q24. What is the single highest-value habit this month?

Say this. Writing the analysis after every interview within 24 hours, with a named root cause. It is what turns interviews into a learning loop rather than a lottery. People who interview for a year without improving are almost always the people who never wrote the analysis.

Why. Without a root cause there is no repair, so the same failure recurs with a different question attached and it feels like bad luck.

Watch out. The INTERVIEWS tab of the tracker has the exact columns. Fill it in on the train home, while it is still fresh - that is a perfect use of your commute.

PART E - The Month 6 checklist

# True?
1 Solving medium problems in under 25 minutes, consistently, narrating throughout
2 Can hold a 45-minute design conversation without freezing or running dry
3 At least 4 external mocks done
4 Can code in a plain text editor without it slowing me down badly
5 All 20 stories rehearsed, randomised, under 3 minutes each
6 A real answer for every high-frequency Amazon principle
7 Applied to Amazon and Google
8 Pipeline still active - 2-3 applications a week going out
9 Every real interview analysed in writing with a named root cause

On rejection. You will be rejected this month, probably several times, possibly by Amazon or Google. That is the expected outcome of the calibration strategy, not evidence the plan failed. Both allow reapplication after a cooldown, and months 7 and 8 exist to convert the pipeline you are building now. Every rejection that produces a named, repaired gap has done its job.

What this file answers

The Month 7 checkpoint, plus the questions that come up when an interviewer decides you are strong and starts probing for the ceiling. Most candidates at your level cannot answer Part B or Part C.

PART A - Kafka in depth

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q1. When does Kafka beat SQS, concretely?

Say this. Three cases. When you need replay - reprocessing history after fixing a bug, or backfilling a new feature. When several independent consumer groups need the same stream, because each tracks its own offset rather than competing for messages. And when you need ordering by key at high throughput, which partitioning gives you.

Why. SQS is a queue: a message is consumed and deleted, so there is nothing to replay and one consumer's read denies it to another. Kafka is a log: reading does not remove, so the same data serves many consumers and many times.

Instead of. SQS wins on operational simplicity - managed, no partition sizing, no rebalancing, built-in DLQ, and per-message visibility timeouts. For your email pipeline it was the right call, and saying so with a reason is stronger than reaching for Kafka.

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q2. Explain consumer group rebalancing and why it hurts.

Say this. Partitions are assigned to consumers in a group. When a consumer joins, leaves or is deemed dead, the group rebalances and reassigns partitions. In the classic protocol every consumer stops consuming during the rebalance - a stop-the-world pause - so a rolling deploy of ten consumers can cause ten pauses.

Why. The group needs a consistent view of who owns what, and the simple way to get that is to stop everyone and redistribute. Incremental cooperative rebalancing was added precisely to avoid this.

Watch out. A consumer that processes a batch for longer than the poll interval is considered dead and triggers a rebalance - which then makes everything slower and can cascade. Tuning max poll records and the interval is the fix.

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q3. How does Kafka guarantee ordering, and what is the limit?

Say this. Within a single partition, messages are strictly ordered by offset. Across partitions there is no ordering at all. So you get ordering per key by partitioning on that key - all events for one user or one document land in one partition.

Why. A partition is a single append-only file with one owner at a time, which is what makes order cheap. Ordering across partitions would require global coordination and destroy the throughput.

Watch out. The consequence is that parallelism is capped by partition count, and you cannot easily increase partitions later without breaking existing key-to-partition mapping. That sizing decision is one of the few genuinely hard-to-reverse Kafka choices.

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q4. What is log compaction and when do you want it?

Say this. Compaction keeps only the latest value for each key, discarding older ones, rather than deleting by age. You want it when the topic represents current state rather than a sequence of events - a table of user profiles, or configuration - so a new consumer can rebuild the full current state by reading from the beginning.

Why. It turns a log into a durable, replayable key-value snapshot. That is the mechanism behind change-data-capture topics and the pattern usually called a log-backed table.

Watch out. It does not guarantee immediate removal - compaction is a background process, so you may still see older versions for a while. And a delete is a tombstone: a null value for the key.

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q5. What are ISR and acks, and how do they relate to durability?

Say this. The in-sync replica set is the replicas caught up with the leader. acks=0 does not wait at all; acks=1 waits for the leader only, so a leader failure right after can lose the message; acks=all waits for every in-sync replica. Combined with min.insync.replicas, that gives you a real durability guarantee.

Why. Durability is a quorum property. Acknowledging from the leader alone means one machine holds the only copy for a window, and that window is where data loss lives.

Watch out. acks=all with min.insync.replicas=1 is a trap - it looks safe and is not, because the ISR can shrink to just the leader. Set it to 2 with a replication factor of 3.

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q6. Kafka claims exactly-once semantics. Is that a contradiction?

Say this. No, but it is narrower than it sounds. Kafka offers idempotent producers - deduplicating retries using a producer ID and sequence number - and transactions that atomically commit both the messages produced and the consumer offsets. So a read-process-write loop entirely within Kafka can be exactly-once.

Why. It works because Kafka controls both sides of the operation. The moment your side effect is outside Kafka - a database write, an email, an HTTP call - the guarantee stops applying and you are back to idempotent handlers.

Watch out. This is the nuance that impresses. "Exactly-once within the Kafka boundary, at-least-once plus idempotency outside it" is the precise answer.

PART B - Stream processing

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q7. Why is event time harder than processing time?

Say this. Event time is when the thing happened; processing time is when you saw it. They differ because of network delays, retries, mobile devices offline for hours, and backfills. So a window over event time cannot simply close when the clock passes its end - late data may still arrive for it.

Why. Processing time gives you a deterministic, immediately closeable window and the wrong answer. Event time gives the right answer and forces you to decide how long to wait.

Watch out. Processing-time results are also non-reproducible: replay the same data and you get different windows. Event-time results are reproducible, which matters enormously for billing or analytics.

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q8. What is a watermark?

Say this. An assertion by the stream processor that it believes it has seen all events with a timestamp earlier than X. When the watermark passes the end of a window, the window is closed and emitted. It is a heuristic about completeness, not a fact.

Why. You cannot know that no more late data will arrive, so you need a decision rule. The watermark is that rule, made explicit and tunable.

Watch out. Anything arriving after the watermark is late data, and you must choose: drop it, send it to a side output, or re-open the window and emit a correction. Naming the three options is the strong answer.

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q9. Tumbling, sliding or session windows?

Say this. Tumbling - fixed, non-overlapping intervals, so every event is in exactly one window. Good for "hits per minute". Sliding - fixed size, advancing by a smaller step, so windows overlap and an event is in several. Good for "average over the last five minutes, updated every minute". Session - dynamic, closing after a gap of inactivity. Good for user sessions, where the natural boundary is a pause rather than a clock.

Why. They differ in whether the boundary is fixed by the clock or by the data. Session windows need per-key state because each key has its own gap timer.

Watch out. Sliding windows multiply the state and the output volume by size divided by step. A 24-hour window sliding every minute is 1,440 open windows per key - a very common cause of unexpected memory blowup.

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q10. How do you count distinct users at scale without exact state?

Say this. HyperLogLog. It gives a cardinality estimate in a fixed small amount of memory - a few kilobytes for billions of items, with a couple of percent error - and it merges, so you can compute per-hour sketches and union them for a day.

Why. Exact distinct counting needs to remember every item seen, so memory grows with cardinality. HLL trades a small bounded error for constant memory, which is almost always the right trade for analytics.

Watch out. Its sibling is count-min sketch for frequency estimation - "is this key hot?" Both are good to name, and both are in Redis, which makes them practical rather than academic.

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q11. What is backfill, and why is replay a design requirement?

Say this. Backfill is reprocessing historical data - because you fixed a bug, added a field, or changed a calculation. It is a design requirement because bugs in stream processing are discovered after the data has flowed, and without replay your only option is to accept permanently wrong history.

Why. This is the concrete argument for a log rather than a queue: a retained log lets you rewind the offset and reprocess. With a queue the data is gone.

Watch out. Backfill competes with live traffic for capacity, and it can produce out-of-order and very-late events that break your watermarks. Running it on a separate consumer group with its own resources is the usual answer.

PART C - Advanced consistency

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q12. Linearizability or serializability - what is the difference?

Say this. They are not the same thing. Linearizability is about single operations on single objects: every operation appears to take effect at one instant, and everyone sees them in the same real-time order. Serializability is about transactions over multiple objects: the result is equivalent to running them one at a time in some order - not necessarily the real-time order.

Why. One is a recency guarantee, the other is an isolation guarantee. A system can be serializable but not linearizable, because it may serialise your transaction before one that actually committed earlier. Strict serializability is both.

Watch out. This is a genuine differentiator - most candidates at your level use the terms interchangeably. Being precise about it signals real reading.

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q13. What is snapshot isolation and what does it permit?

Say this. Each transaction reads a consistent snapshot as of its start time, so readers never block writers. Write-write conflicts are detected and one transaction aborts. What it permits is write skew: two transactions read overlapping data, each writes a different row, so there is no write-write conflict to detect, and together they violate a constraint neither would have broken alone.

Why. The conflict is on a condition across rows, not on a row. Snapshot isolation only watches rows.

Watch out. The classic example is two doctors both going off-call because each sees the other still on. The fix is serializable isolation, or materialising the conflict by locking the thing the condition depends on.

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q14. What are read-your-writes and monotonic reads?

Say this. Read-your-writes: after you write, you always see at least your own write - so your comment does not vanish after you post it. Monotonic reads: you never see time go backwards - once you have seen a value, a later read does not show an older one. Both are per-client session guarantees, weaker than strong consistency but far more useful than plain eventual.

Why. They target the anomalies users actually notice. Full linearizability is expensive; these two remove most of the visible weirdness for a fraction of the cost.

Watch out. You get them practically by pinning a session to one replica, or by tracking a version token and waiting for the replica to reach it. Naming an implementation makes the answer concrete.

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q15. Active-active or active-passive?

Say this. Active-passive: one region serves, the other stands by with replicated data. Simple, no write conflicts, but you waste the standby and failover takes time and is rarely rehearsed. Active-active: both serve. Better utilisation and lower latency for users near each region, but you now have concurrent writes in two places, so you need conflict resolution or partitioning of write ownership by key.

Why. The hard part of active-active is not the infrastructure, it is deciding what happens when the same entity is written in both regions during a partition.

Watch out. The usual real answer is active-active for reads, single-region ownership for writes per entity. That gets most of the benefit without the conflict problem.

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q16. What are RPO and RTO?

Say this. RPO - recovery point objective - is how much data you can afford to lose, measured in time. RTO - recovery time objective - is how long you can afford to be down. RPO drives your replication and backup strategy; RTO drives your failover automation.

Why. They are business decisions, not engineering ones. An RPO of zero requires synchronous replication and therefore higher write latency, so someone has to decide what the data is worth.

Watch out. "We take nightly backups" implies an RPO of up to 24 hours. Saying that out loud is often the first time anyone realises it is unacceptable.

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q17. Why is replication lag operationally dangerous?

Say this. Because it is invisible until it matters. Reads go stale, failover to a lagging replica loses the un-replicated writes, and lag typically grows exactly when the system is busiest - so it is worst during an incident.

Why. A replica applies changes serially from the leader's log. If write volume exceeds the replica's apply rate, the gap grows without bound and there is no natural back-pressure.

Watch out. Alert on lag, not on replica health. A replica can be perfectly healthy and twenty minutes behind, and that is a data-loss risk you cannot see from a ping.

PART D - Time series and geospatial

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q18. Why is cardinality the hard part of a metrics system?

Say this. Each unique combination of metric name and label values is a separate time series to store and index. Adding a label with high cardinality - a user ID, a request ID, a URL with an ID in it - multiplies series count by that cardinality, and memory and query cost go with it. This is the standard way monitoring systems fall over.

Why. The storage is optimised for many points on few series. Reverse that and every optimisation stops working.

Watch out. "Never put an unbounded value in a label" is the rule. Use logs or traces for high-cardinality detail, metrics for aggregates. That division is the answer.

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q19. What is downsampling and why does it work for time series?

Say this. Keep raw resolution for a short retention, then roll up into coarser buckets - one-minute averages for a week, one-hour for a year. It works because nobody queries per-second data from eight months ago; the value of resolution decays much faster than the value of history.

Why. Storage cost is points times retention. Downsampling reduces points per unit time as the data ages, so cost grows logarithmically rather than linearly.

Watch out. Keep min, max and count alongside the average, not just the average - otherwise you lose the spikes, which are the only interesting part of old data.

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q20. How do you find nearby items at scale?

Say this. Reduce two dimensions to one so you can use an ordinary index. Geohashing encodes lat/long into a string where a shared prefix means physical proximity, so a prefix query finds a neighbourhood. Quadtrees recursively subdivide space, adapting depth to density, which handles cities and oceans differently.

Why. Standard indexes are one-dimensional. Any geospatial solution is fundamentally a trick for mapping 2D locality onto a 1D ordering.

Watch out. Geohash has an edge problem: two points either side of a cell boundary can be metres apart with different prefixes. You query the cell plus its eight neighbours. Mentioning that is the mark of someone who has implemented it.

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q21. How does object storage achieve durability without keeping full copies?

Say this. Erasure coding. Split the object into k data shards, compute m parity shards, and distribute all k+m across failure domains. Any k of them reconstruct the object, so you survive m losses while storing only (k+m)/k times the data - roughly 1.5x for 6+3, versus 3x for triple replication.

Why. It is the same mathematics as RAID, applied across machines and racks. You trade CPU on read reconstruction for a large storage saving.

Watch out. The cost is repair traffic and read latency when a shard is missing - reconstruction must fetch k shards from k machines. That is why replication is often preferred for small hot objects and erasure coding for large cold ones.

PART E - The RAG service

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q22. What is actually hard about building a RAG service?

Say this. Retrieval, not generation. If the retrieved context does not contain the answer, no model can produce it. So the hard parts are chunking - how you split documents determines what can ever be retrieved - and hybrid search, because pure vector similarity misses exact terms like error codes, names and IDs.

Why. Everyone focuses on the prompt because that is the visible part. The failure taxonomy is mostly retrieval failures: missing content, wrong chunk boundaries, right chunk ranked too low.

Watch out. Prove retrieval before you add generation. Build the search, measure recall@k on a labelled set, and only then generate. That ordering is itself a strong engineering signal.

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q23. Why is chunking the main quality lever?

Say this. Because a chunk is the smallest unit that can be retrieved. Too large and the embedding is a blur of several topics, so it matches nothing precisely. Too small and it loses the context needed to be useful, and the answer gets split across chunks that are individually unconvincing. Overlapping windows and respecting document structure - headings, paragraphs - both help.

Why. An embedding is one vector for the whole chunk. Its ability to represent meaning degrades as the chunk covers more distinct meanings.

Watch out. Have a number: "I tested three chunk sizes and measured recall@5 on a labelled set of fifty questions." Almost no candidate measures, so measuring is the differentiator.

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q24. Why pgvector rather than a dedicated vector database?

Say this. Because you already run Postgres and know it deeply, so it removes an entire piece of infrastructure, a second consistency model, and a second operational surface. You can join embeddings against your relational metadata in one query, which is exactly what hybrid search and filtered retrieval need.

Why. A dedicated vector database wins at very large scale and on specialised index types. At your scale that advantage is theoretical and the operational cost is real.

Watch out. The reasoning is the interview answer, not the choice. "I chose the boring option because it removed a component and I could justify the limits" is what a senior engineer sounds like.

Advanced distributed systems, streaming and RAG Q&A
Q25. How do you evaluate a RAG system?

Say this. Two layers. Retrieval: recall@k and mean reciprocal rank against a labelled set of questions with known correct chunks. Generation: groundedness - is every claim supported by a retrieved chunk - plus answer correctness. Build a set of fifty to a hundred question-answer pairs once and re-run it on every change.

Why. Without a fixed evaluation set every change is an opinion. With one, you can say "hybrid search moved recall@5 from 0.71 to 0.88", which is an engineering statement.

Watch out. Citations are how you make groundedness checkable at runtime as well as in evaluation. Requiring every claim to cite a chunk makes hallucination visible to the user.

PART F - The Month 7 checklist

# True?
1 Every interview has produced a written analysis with a named root cause
2 Gaps are actually closing, not recurring - and if one recurred three times, I changed the method
3 Can explain Kafka's model and when it beats SQS
4 Can distinguish linearizability from serializability
5 Can explain write skew and which isolation levels permit it
6 4 full mock loops done this month
7 Both projects survive 30 minutes of hostile questioning
8 The RAG service is built, deployed, and has measured recall numbers
9 Pipeline still active

The recurring-gap rule, restated because it matters most this month. If the same root cause appears three times in your analysis log, your repair method is wrong, not your effort. Stop repeating the practice and change its shape: implement the algorithm from scratch from memory until it is automatic, rather than solving more problems that use it. Repetition of failure is not practice.

Month 8 - Rapid Revision Sheet

Weeks 29 to 32. Everything compressed to one line each. This is not for learning - it is for checking what survived.

The other seven files teach. This one tests. Cover the right-hand column, read the left, and say the answer. Anything you cannot say goes in the WEAK tab. That is the entire method.

It is deliberately dense, because by month 8 your risk is no longer missing knowledge - it is failing to retrieve knowledge you already have, under pressure, in a 45-minute window. Consolidate rather than accumulate. The instinct to keep adding topics is the wrong instinct now.

How to use it on a commute

• One section per journey. Cover the answers with your thumb. Say each one out loud, or mouth it silently - it still works.

• Score yourself honestly. Three or more misses in a section means that section is your next Friday.

• Do not re-read the answer and move on. Re-read it, then look away and say it. Reading produces recognition; saying produces recall, and only recall shows up in an interview.

• Part 6 is the highest-value page. Every "why X and not Y" in one table. That is the shape of most follow-up questions.

PART 1 - C# and the runtime, one line each

Prompt Answer
Value vs reference type Value holds the data; reference holds an address. Assignment copies the slot either way
Where does a struct live Wherever it is declared. A field of a class lives on the heap with the object
Boxing cost An allocation plus a copy, then an unbox with a type check
Three accidental boxes Assigning to object; non-generic collections or interfaces; string interpolation of value types
Why strings are immutable Safe sharing, interning, and a cacheable hash - so they make good dictionary keys
Concat in a loop O(n squared) - every += allocates and copies. StringBuilder is O(n) amortised
Object overhead on x64 Header plus method table pointer, 16 bytes before your fields
Static constructor timing Before first static access or first instance, exactly once, thread-safe
Virtual dispatch Through the object's method table - the slot is resolved at runtime
override vs new override replaces in the table; new hides and is resolved at compile time from the reference type
Equals/GetHashCode contract Equal objects must share a hash code. Break it and hash collections lose keys
Dictionary O(1) Average, not worst. Degrades to O(n) with a bad hash distribution
List<T> growth Doubles the array, so Add is O(1) amortised and total copying is bounded by 2n
yield return compiles to An IEnumerator state machine class - nothing runs until the first MoveNext
Deferred execution bug Enumerate the same query twice and everything runs twice - two round trips
IQueryable vs IEnumerable IQueryable builds an expression tree for the provider to translate; IEnumerable runs in memory
Closure allocates A hidden class holding the captured variables - and it extends their lifetime
throw vs throw ex throw preserves the stack trace; throw ex resets it
Exception filter (when) Decides before the stack unwinds, so the original frames are still intact
Finalizer cost Two GC cycles - queue, finalise, then collect on the next pass
GC generations Gen 0 cheap because most new objects are dead; gen 2 expensive because it walks everything
Large object heap Over ~85 KB, collected with gen 2, not compacted by default, so it fragments
Server vs workstation GC Server: a heap and a collector thread per core. Use it for any server workload
What await does Returns to the caller, releases the thread, registers a continuation, resumes via the state machine
async void Cannot be awaited and its exceptions cannot be caught. Event handlers only
.Result deadlock Continuation needs the captured context thread; you are blocking that thread. In ASP.NET Core: starvation, not deadlock
ConfigureAwait(false) Do not capture the context. Needed in library code, not in ASP.NET Core
ValueTask Avoids allocating when the result is usually already available. Await exactly once, never block
CancellationToken Cooperative - a flag the operation checks. Nothing is forcibly terminated
Thread pool starvation Blocking outpaces the slow injection rate. Signature: high latency, low CPU
Framework vs modern .NET Windows-only and machine-wide, versus cross-platform, side-by-side and app-local
CLR / runtime / SDK Execution engine; engine plus libraries to run; plus compilers and tooling to build
Tiered compilation Compile fast first, recompile hot methods with full optimisation
DI lifetimes Singleton per app, scoped per request, transient per resolve
Captive dependency A scoped service captured by a singleton outlives its scope - classically a DbContext
Middleware ordering Fixed at startup by nesting. Auth before authorisation; exceptions first
Why JWTs cannot be revoked Validation is local, so there is nothing to delete. Short expiry, denylist, or a version claim
N+1 One query per row from lazy loading in a loop. Find it in the SQL log, not the C#
Cache stampede A hot key expires and everyone misses at once. Lock, jitter the TTL, or serve stale while refreshing
Study correction: Modern interpolated-string handlers can avoid boxing. Whether a value is boxed depends on the target/overload and compiler lowering; the source shorthand is too broad. Official reference

PART 2 - Databases, one line each

Prompt Answer
How data is stored Fixed-size pages. Clustered index = the table itself, in key order
Index read/write trade Reads seek instead of scanning; every write must update every index, and inserts can split pages
Covering index Contains every column the query needs, so no lookup back to the table
Seek / scan / lookup Navigate directly; read every page; the extra hop back for uncovered columns
When a scan is correct When the query returns a large fraction of the table - sequential beats thousands of random seeks
SARGability A function on the column, or a leading wildcard, prevents a seek. Rewrite as a range
Statistics matter because Cardinality estimates drive plan choice. Stale stats give you nested loops for a million rows
Join types Nested loops for small plus indexed; hash for two large unindexed; merge for two pre-sorted
SQL logical order FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT
ACID Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability - durability via write-ahead log
Read Uncommitted Permits dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms
Read Committed Prevents dirty reads; permits non-repeatable reads and phantoms
Repeatable Read Also prevents non-repeatable reads; permits phantoms
Serializable Prevents all three, using range locks, at a real concurrency cost
Snapshot Consistent point-in-time view, readers do not block; permits write skew
Write skew Two transactions write different rows, no write-write conflict, and together they break a constraint
MVCC vs locking Postgres keeps versions so readers never block; SQL Server locks by default unless snapshot is enabled
Lock escalation Many row locks become one table lock to save memory - and suddenly block everyone. Batch your updates
Deadlock cause and fix Two transactions touching rows in a different order. Fix with a consistent access order
When to denormalise When a hot read path's join cost is measured. You accept two sources of truth and own the sync
Connection pool exhaustion "Timeout expired... obtaining a connection from the pool" - usually a leak or a long transaction, not a slow database

PART 3 - Networking, OS and distributed systems, one line each

Prompt Answer
URL journey DNS, TCP handshake, TLS handshake, HTTP to a load balancer, app, cache, database, response, then assets from a CDN
TCP handshake SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK - one full round trip before any data
Flow vs congestion control Flow protects the receiver (window); congestion protects the network (slow start, backoff)
Head-of-line blocking HTTP/2 fixed it at the HTTP layer; TCP still stalls all streams on loss. HTTP/3 over QUIC fixes that
Why TLS uses both crypto types Asymmetric to authenticate and agree a key; symmetric because it is fast enough for the data
What HTTPS does not hide Which server you contacted, traffic volume and timing, or a malicious endpoint
CORS preflight An OPTIONS request asking permission before a non-simple cross-origin request. Browser-enforced, not server security
WebSocket scaling The connection is state pinned to one server - so you need a backplane and sticky sessions
Context switch cost Register save plus page-table switch, but mostly the cold cache and TLB afterwards
Virtual memory Private address space mapped to physical pages. Gives isolation and lazy allocation
Page fault The normal mechanism for bringing a page in. Only hard faults are slow
Two scheduler layers The OS schedules threads onto cores; the .NET pool schedules work items onto threads
Spinlock catastrophic when The critical section is long, or threads outnumber cores - you burn a core doing nothing
Async I/O needs no thread The OS and hardware do the waiting; the continuation lives in a heap state machine, not on a stack
Replication lag Asynchronous replication means a follower read can miss a just-committed write
Read-your-writes Route a user to the leader briefly after they write, or wait for a version
Quorum R + W > N Read and write sets must overlap by at least one node - pigeonhole
Split brain Both sides of a partition elect a leader. Prevented by requiring a majority - hence odd cluster sizes
Consistent hashing Ring placement, so adding a node moves ~1/N of keys instead of nearly all
Virtual nodes One physical server occupies many ring positions, smoothing distribution
CAP correctly During a partition choose consistency or availability. Partition tolerance is not optional
PACELC And else, with no partition, you still trade latency against consistency
Causal consistency Causally related operations are seen in order; unrelated ones may not be. Usually what users need
Redis single-threaded Atomic commands, no locks, predictable latency - and network-bound anyway. One slow command blocks all
LRU vs LFU vs TTL Recency; frequency; and TTL is a staleness bound, not an eviction strategy. Usually TTL plus LRU
Delivery guarantees At-most-once loses; at-least-once duplicates; exactly-once delivery is impossible
Exactly-once processing Idempotent handler plus a dedup record in the same transaction as the effect
Visibility timeout A lease, not a lock. Slower than the timeout means a second consumer starts the same work
Why jitter Backoff fixes the rate; jitter breaks the synchronisation. Both are needed
DLQ After N failures, park it. Alert on depth, inspect, fix, replay
SQS vs Kafka A queue forgets; a log remembers. Kafka for replay, many consumer groups, or ordering by key
Kafka ordering limit Within a partition only. Parallelism is capped by partition count
Log compaction Keep only the latest value per key - a durable replayable snapshot of current state
acks and ISR acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 on a replication factor of 3. acks=1 can lose data
Event vs processing time When it happened vs when you saw it. Event time is reproducible and needs watermarks
Watermark An assertion that everything before time X has probably arrived. A heuristic, not a fact
2PC avoided because It blocks - a dead coordinator leaves participants holding locks with no safe local decision
Distributed lock unsafe The holder can be paused past the lease. Fix with a monotonic fencing token the resource enforces
Dual-write problem No transaction spans database and broker. The outbox makes it one commit plus a retryable publish
Circuit breaker Closed, open, half-open. Retries without a breaker amplify an outage
Bulkhead Separate pools per dependency, so one slow downstream cannot starve everything
Linearizability vs serializability Single-operation real-time recency, versus multi-object equivalent-to-some-serial-order
RPO vs RTO How much data you can lose, versus how long you can be down
Metrics cardinality Each label combination is a series. Never label with an unbounded value
Erasure coding k data plus m parity shards; any k reconstruct. ~1.5x storage instead of 3x
Geohash edge problem Adjacent points can differ in prefix, so query the cell plus its eight neighbours

PART 6 - Why X and not Y (the follow-up bank)

This is the highest-value page in the file. Almost every "why did you choose that?" is one of these rows.

Choice First when Second when
Two pointers / hash map Already sorted - O(1) space Unsorted and you need indices
Sliding window / prefix sum All positive - shrinking is safe Negatives break monotonicity
BFS / DFS Shortest path or levels Existence, all paths, cycles, topological order
BFS / Dijkstra All edges cost the same Weighted edges - BFS is simply wrong
Dijkstra / Bellman-Ford Non-negative weights Negative edges, or you must detect a negative cycle
Union-Find / DFS Incremental edges, many queries, MST Static graph, one traversal
Heap / full sort Only the top K, or a stream - O(n log k) You need the whole ordering
Greedy / DP A local optimum is provably global You can construct a counterexample
Memoisation / tabulation You have the recursion; sparse state space Stack depth risk, or you want O(1) space
struct / class Small, immutable, short-lived, created in bulk Everything else - it is the right default
Interface / abstract class A capability unrelated types can have Genuine shared state and implementation
Strategy / switch Independent, growing, separately testable Two or three stable, short cases
Decorator / inheritance Compose behaviours freely at runtime Fixed at compile time, real is-a
Task / ValueTask Default - simple and safe Usually completes synchronously in a hot path
lock / Interlocked Several operations must be atomic together A single primitive operation
SemaphoreSlim / lock You need to await inside, or limit to N Simple mutual exclusion, no await
AsNoTracking / tracked Read-only queries - no snapshot taken You intend to call SaveChanges
Include / projection You genuinely need the entities Read-only - project to a DTO, one query, less data
Cache-aside / write-through Default - simple, tolerates staleness A stale read is unacceptable
SQS / Kafka Independent tasks, managed, DLQ built in Replay, many consumer groups, or ordering by key
2PC / saga Almost never - it blocks Cross-service consistency with availability
Choreography / orchestration Loose coupling, no central component The flow must be visible and debuggable
Active-passive / active-active Simplicity, no write conflicts Utilisation and latency, if you can own writes per key
Replication / erasure coding Small hot objects - low read latency Large cold objects - 1.5x instead of 3x
pgvector / vector DB You already run Postgres; join with metadata Very large scale or specialised indexes
Serializable / snapshot You must prevent write skew Readers must never block writers

PART 7 - The 45-minute oral revision outlines

Weeks 29 and 30 ask you to speak for 45 minutes on each area with no notes. That is the most demanding English practice in the whole plan, and it is also the best final check. Use these as the running order.

Area Cover, in this order
C# and .NET Type system and memory; object layout; OOP and dispatch; collections internals; LINQ and deferred execution; delegates and closures; exceptions; IDisposable and the GC; async state machine and the pitfalls; the runtime, JIT and tiering
Databases Pages and B-trees; clustered vs non-clustered; covering indexes; execution plans and SARGability; statistics and plan choice; join algorithms; ACID; isolation levels and anomalies; MVCC vs locking; deadlocks and escalation; normalisation and when to denormalise; connection pooling
Networking and OS The URL journey end to end; DNS; TCP handshake, flow and congestion control; TLS; HTTP versions; WebSockets and scaling; process vs thread; context switching; virtual memory and paging; scheduling; synchronisation primitives; blocking vs async I/O down to IOCP
Distributed systems Replication and lag; quorums; partitioning and consistent hashing; CAP and PACELC; consistency models; caching strategies and failure modes; delivery guarantees and idempotency; DLQ and retries; Kafka model; consensus and Raft; distributed locks; outbox and saga; resilience patterns; observability
Your projects Job platform: architecture, state machine, retries, idempotency, DLQ, priority and fairness, rate limiting, tenant isolation, metrics, deployment, load test numbers, bottleneck, what you would change. RAG: chunking decision, hybrid search, evaluation numbers
Behavioural All 20 stories, randomised, under 3 minutes, Action-heavy, each with a number and a "what I would do differently"

What you have, at this point. Deep .NET knowledge, working pattern recognition, system design competence, two deployed projects with measured numbers, twenty rehearsed stories, and eight months of demonstrated discipline. None of that expires. If there is no offer yet, the correct response is to continue the month 7 loop - repair, mock, apply - at a sustainable level. Most people who reach this point and keep going convert within the following few months.

The failure mode to avoid is concluding the eight months were wasted and stopping. That would be stopping at exactly the point where the accumulated work starts paying.

SQL correction: isolation behavior is engine-specific. PostgreSQL treats Read Uncommitted as Read Committed; Repeatable Read prevents phantom reads but can still allow serialization anomalies. PostgreSQL documentation.
ASP.NET Core correction: with endpoint routing, UseCors belongs after UseRouting and before authorization. Microsoft documentation.
Runtime correction: ThreadPool worker adjustment is not a universal fixed number of threads per second. Microsoft diagnostic guide.

S12 — 12_AI_Assisted_Development_MCP_and_RAG

Full source content: Study-Plan/12_AI_Assisted_Development_MCP_and_RAG.docx. Original wording is retained below. For conflicting statements, use the visible correction and the current execution plan.

AI-Assisted Development, MCP and RAG

Document 12 - A parallel track. Weekend blocks from Month 2, project in Month 7.

Why this is in the plan

Three reasons, in order of importance.

• It is already on your resume. You list GitHub Copilot and Claude AI under AI-Assisted Development. An interviewer will ask about it, and "it helps me code faster" is a weak answer from a candidate at your level. You need a real position on where these tools help, where they hurt, and how you verify their output.

• "How do you use AI tools?" is now a standard question at both Google and Amazon. It probes engineering judgement, not tool familiarity. The wrong answers are equally "I do not use them" and "I use them for everything".

• RAG and MCP are the two concepts that come up most when backend engineers are asked about AI systems. Both are fundamentally backend problems - retrieval, ranking, caching, latency, protocols - which plays directly to your strengths.

One thing this document is not: a machine learning curriculum. You are not becoming an ML engineer. You are becoming a backend engineer who can build and reason about systems that use models.

The hard rule about AI while studying

Never use AI assistance while practising DSA, and never while doing a timed system design. It feels productive and it destroys the exact skill you are training.

Retrieval practice only works when retrieval is actually happening. An AI-completed solution produces the same illusion of fluency as rereading - Doc 00 Section B1 explains why that fails. Use AI freely for the project, for explaining concepts you are stuck on after you have attempted them, and for reviewing code you already wrote. Never for producing an answer you are supposed to be generating from memory.

Track A - AI-assisted development as an engineering practice

What to learn

Topic Substance
Where AI genuinely helps Boilerplate, test scaffolding, unfamiliar API syntax, first-draft documentation, explaining unfamiliar code, refactoring with clear intent, regex, SQL translation
Where AI reliably hurts Novel algorithms, security-sensitive code, anything requiring current library versions, subtle concurrency, business rules it cannot see, and any case where you cannot evaluate the output
The verification discipline You own every line you commit. Read it, understand it, test it. "Copilot wrote it" is not a defence in code review or in production
Context engineering Why these tools fail on large codebases, how to give them the right context, why a focused prompt with the relevant file beats a vague prompt with none
Review-mode usage The highest-value pattern for a senior engineer: write it yourself, then ask the model to critique it. Inverts the risk
Failure modes Hallucinated APIs, plausible-but-wrong concurrency, outdated patterns, confident nonsense on niche topics, silent security holes

Your interview answer (draft it in Month 2, refine all the way through)

Structure it as: what you use it for, what you deliberately do not use it for, and how you verify. A concrete example from your Casepoint work carries far more weight than a general opinion. Something like: used it to generate test scaffolding and to explain an unfamiliar legacy module quickly, did not use it for the retry and concurrency logic in the email pipeline because the failure modes needed reasoning it could not do, and everything it produced went through the same review and test bar as hand-written code.

That answer signals judgement. "I use it for everything, it doubles my speed" signals the opposite.

Track B - LLM fundamentals (only what a backend engineer needs)

Concept What to understand
Tokens Text is split into tokens, not words. Pricing, limits and truncation are all token-based
Context window The working memory of a request. Everything - system prompt, history, retrieved documents - competes for it
Embeddings Text mapped to a vector such that semantic similarity becomes geometric distance. This is the foundation of RAG
Vector similarity Cosine similarity, dot product, Euclidean. Why cosine is usually chosen
Temperature and sampling Determinism vs variety. Why you use low temperature for extraction and classification
System vs user messages Role separation and why instructions in the system message behave differently
Structured output Forcing JSON conforming to a schema. The single most useful feature for backend integration
Function/tool calling The model requests that your code run a function and returns the result into its reasoning. The mechanism underneath agents
Streaming Token-by-token responses, and what that means for your API design and timeouts
Cost and latency Per-token pricing, prompt caching, why prompt size is a performance problem
Hallucination Why models produce confident wrong answers, and why grounding via retrieval is the mitigation

Track C - RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation)

The concept in one paragraph

A model only knows what it was trained on and what you put in its context. RAG solves "answer questions about my data" by retrieving the most relevant chunks of your data at query time and putting them into the prompt as grounding. It is not fine-tuning and it is not training. It is a search problem followed by a prompting problem - which is why it is a backend engineer's territory.

The pipeline, stage by stage

Stage What happens and what can go wrong
Ingest Load documents - PDF, DOCX, HTML, code. Extraction quality sets a ceiling on everything downstream. Bad PDF parsing is the most common silent RAG failure
Chunk Split into passages. Fixed size, recursive, semantic, or structure-aware. Chunk size and overlap are the highest-leverage tuning knobs. Too small loses context, too large dilutes the embedding
Embed Each chunk to a vector via an embedding model. Same model must be used at query time
Store Vectors plus metadata in a vector store. Index type (HNSW, IVF) trades recall against speed and memory
Retrieve Embed the query, find top-K nearest chunks. K is a tuning decision
Rerank Optionally re-score candidates with a stronger model. Usually the biggest single quality improvement after chunking
Augment Build the prompt: instructions, retrieved context, question. Manage the context budget
Generate Model answers from the provided context, and is instructed to say when the context is insufficient
Cite Return sources. Non-negotiable for trust, and it makes the system debuggable

The concepts that separate real understanding from tutorial knowledge

• Hybrid search. Pure vector search fails on exact identifiers, product codes and rare terms. Combining BM25 keyword search with vector search, fused via Reciprocal Rank Fusion, is standard practice and a strong thing to know.

• Chunking strategy is the main quality lever. More than model choice, in most systems.

• Evaluation. Retrieval metrics (recall@k, MRR) versus generation metrics (faithfulness, answer relevance). If you cannot measure it, you cannot improve it - and most RAG demos have no evaluation at all.

• The failure taxonomy. Retrieval missed the chunk; the chunk was retrieved but the answer was not in it; the answer was there and the model ignored it; the model added something not in the context. These have completely different fixes, and being able to name which one you are looking at is the mark of someone who has actually built one.

• Metadata filtering. Tenant, date, document type. In a multi-tenant system this is a security boundary, not a feature - and you already understand tenant isolation from your job platform.

• Cost and latency. Embedding at ingest is a batch cost; retrieval plus generation is per-query latency. Caching, prompt caching and reranking budgets are real engineering decisions.

Why you specifically are well-placed here

RAG is a retrieval and ranking system with a model on the end. Chunking is a data-processing pipeline. Ingestion at scale is a queue and worker problem - which is literally the project you are building in Months 4-5. Multi-tenancy, caching, rate limiting and observability all transfer directly. You are not learning this from zero.

Track D - MCP (Model Context Protocol)

What it is

An open protocol that standardises how applications provide context and capabilities to LLMs. Before it, every AI application wrote bespoke integration code for every tool and data source - an N times M problem. MCP turns that into N plus M: a tool exposes one MCP server, and any MCP-capable host can use it.

The analogy that lands in an interview: MCP is to AI-tool integration what ODBC was to database drivers, or what the Language Server Protocol was to editor tooling. The value is not clever technology; it is that one integration works everywhere.

Architecture

Concept What it is
Host The application the user interacts with - an IDE, a desktop assistant, an agent runtime. Contains one or more clients
Client Maintains a one-to-one connection with a server, handles the protocol
Server Exposes capabilities. Usually a small process you write, wrapping an API, database or filesystem
Tools Functions the model can invoke - model-controlled. This is the primary primitive. "Create a ticket", "run a query"
Resources Data the host can read - application-controlled. Files, records, documents
Prompts Reusable templates the user can invoke - user-controlled. Slash commands, essentially
Transport stdio for local processes; HTTP-based transport for remote servers. Messages are JSON-RPC
Capability negotiation Client and server declare what they support during initialisation

Note the three-way control distinction - model-controlled, application-controlled, user-controlled. It is the design idea most people miss, and naming it demonstrates you read the specification rather than a blog post.

The engineering questions worth having opinions on

• Security. An MCP server is remote code execution with extra steps. Authentication, authorisation, scoping, and the fact that tool descriptions are untrusted input to a model. Prompt injection via tool output is a real attack surface.

• Tool design. Too many tools confuse the model; too few make it useless. Descriptions are effectively prompts and should be written as such.

• Idempotency and side effects. A model may call your tool twice. You have already solved this pattern in your job platform.

• Error handling. Errors are read by a model, so they should be actionable in natural language, not stack traces.

• Observability. Logging what the model called, with what arguments, and what came back. Debugging agents is largely a logging problem.

The build - a RAG service in .NET (Month 7)

Deliberately small. Four weekend blocks in Weeks 25-28. It is a supporting artefact, not a rival to your main project. If it starts competing with interview preparation, cut its scope, not your preparation.

Why this stack

Use PostgreSQL with pgvector rather than a dedicated vector database. You already know Postgres deeply after Month 2 Week 8, it removes an entire piece of infrastructure, and "I used pgvector because operationally I would rather not run a second datastore for this scale" is exactly the kind of trade-off reasoning that scores well. It is also a genuinely common production choice.

Phases

Phase Scope
1 (Wk 25) ASP.NET Core API. Document ingest endpoint. Text extraction. Chunking with configurable size and overlap. Store chunks in Postgres. Reuse your job platform's worker pattern for async ingestion
2 (Wk 26) Embeddings generation. pgvector column and index. Vector similarity search. POST /query returning top-K chunks with scores. No model call yet - prove retrieval works before adding generation
3 (Wk 27) Generation with grounded prompting and citations. Structured JSON output. Streaming response. "I do not know" behaviour when context is insufficient
4 (Wk 28) Hybrid search (BM25 + vector, fused). A small evaluation set of ~20 question/answer pairs with recall@k measured. Metadata filtering for multi-tenancy. Caching. README with architecture, trade-offs and evaluation results
Optional An MCP server exposing your job platform as tools - submit a job, check status, inspect the DLQ. Small, and it demonstrates both protocols working together

What makes it interview-worthy

Not that it exists - RAG demos are common. What makes it worth discussing is the evaluation set and the honest numbers. Almost nobody measures. Being able to say "hybrid search improved recall@5 from 0.62 to 0.81 on my evaluation set, and reranking added another 0.06 at 200ms latency cost" puts you in a very small group.

Free resources

Resource For
Microsoft Learn - AI for .NET developers learn.microsoft.com/dotnet/ai The canonical .NET path. Microsoft.Extensions.AI, vector data abstractions, tutorials
Semantic Kernel docs and GitHub Microsoft's orchestration framework for .NET. Agents, plugins, memory
Kernel Memory (GitHub) Microsoft's open-source RAG service. Read the source - it is a well-built reference implementation
Model Context Protocol modelcontextprotocol.io The official specification. Read the spec, not summaries of it
MCP C# SDK github.com/modelcontextprotocol/csharp-sdk Build MCP servers in .NET
Anthropic documentation docs.anthropic.com Prompting, tool use, structured output, context management. Applies broadly
pgvector github.com/pgvector/pgvector Vector search in the database you already know
Anthropic and OpenAI cookbooks (GitHub) Working patterns for RAG, evaluation and tool use
Free tiers Most providers have free or low-cost tiers sufficient for a study project. Local embedding models via ONNX avoid API cost entirely

Schedule

When What

M3 Sat (one block) Track B. LLM fundamentals. Tokens, embeddings, tool calling, structured output
M4 Sat (one block) Track C theory. The RAG pipeline and the failure taxonomy
