S13 — 13_Aptitude_and_Quantitative_Preparation

Full source content: Study-Plan/13_Aptitude_and_Quantitative_Preparation.docx. Original wording is retained below. For conflicting statements, use the visible correction and the current execution plan.

Aptitude and Quantitative Preparation

Document 13 - A parallel track. 15-20 minutes, two to three times a week.

An honest framing first

You asked for aptitude, so here it is - but you deserve an accurate picture of where it matters, because misallocating time here would be expensive.

Where it matters Reality
Google SWE loop Classical aptitude is not tested. No quant round, no logical reasoning round
Amazon SDE loop Classical aptitude is not tested in the technical loop. Amazon's assessments do include work-style and work-simulation components, which are not aptitude tests
Mid-tier and Indian product companies Frequently tested. Online assessments commonly include quantitative aptitude, logical reasoning and verbal sections as a gate before the technical rounds
Service companies and mass recruiters Heavily tested, often as the primary filter
System design (both targets) Quantitative estimation matters a great deal. Back-of-envelope capacity estimation is step 2 of the nine-step framework

So the strategy is: keep aptitude light and continuous, and treat estimation skill as the part that genuinely feeds your Google and Amazon preparation. In Month 6 your application ladder starts with mid-tier companies specifically to calibrate - and those are exactly the ones with aptitude gates. Being filtered out by a percentages question before anyone looks at your code would be an avoidable and irritating way to lose a calibration opportunity.

Time budget: 15-20 minutes, two to three times per week. Slot it into the last block of Tuesday and Thursday. It should never displace DSA or system design.

Part 1 - Quantitative aptitude

Topic What to drill
Number system Divisibility rules, factors, LCM and HCF, remainders, unit digits, base conversion
Percentages Increase/decrease, successive percentages, percentage change vs point change
Ratio and proportion Direct and inverse, partnership, mixtures and alligation
Averages Weighted averages, effect of adding or removing a term
Profit and loss Cost/selling price, discount chains, marked price, false weights
Simple and compound interest Formulae, half-yearly and quarterly compounding, the difference between SI and CI
Time, speed and distance Relative speed, trains, boats and streams, average speed
Time and work Work rates, combined work, efficiency, pipes and cisterns
Permutations and combinations Arrangements, selections, circular arrangements, repetitions
Probability Basic, conditional, complementary events, dice and cards
Mensuration Areas, volumes, surface areas of standard shapes
Progressions AP and GP, sums, nth term
Data interpretation Tables, bar charts, pie charts, line graphs, caselets. Highest frequency section in most assessments

The skill that actually transfers

Approximation and mental estimation. In a data interpretation section you rarely need exact answers - you need to eliminate three of four options quickly. That same skill is what step 2 of a system design demands. Practise deliberately: round aggressively, compute the order of magnitude first, only refine if the options are close.

Part 2 - Logical reasoning

Topic What to drill
Number and letter series Pattern identification, missing terms
Analogies and classification Relationship identification, odd one out
Coding-decoding Letter shifts, substitution, symbol coding
Blood relations Family tree diagramming
Direction sense Displacement and final position
Syllogisms Venn diagram method. Learn the diagram method, do not reason verbally - verbal reasoning on syllogisms is where people lose marks
Seating arrangement Linear, circular, facing inward/outward. Grid method
Puzzles Floor puzzles, scheduling, matrix puzzles. Highest time cost per question - triage these
Clocks and calendars Angles, odd days, day-of-week calculation
Cubes and dice Painted cubes, opposite faces
Statement and assumption/conclusion Formal logic on prose
Data sufficiency Judging whether the information suffices, without solving. Genuinely useful for interview requirement-clarification too

Part 3 - Verbal

Lightest priority of the three. Your stated goal is clear technical communication, and this section overlaps with that only partially.

• Reading comprehension - the section worth practising, because it is also reading-speed practice for technical documentation.

• Sentence correction and error spotting - subject-verb agreement, tenses, articles, prepositions. This is where your English gap is most likely to show in an assessment.

• Para jumbles - sentence ordering. Trains coherent structuring, which helps your spoken explanations.

• Vocabulary - lowest return. Do not build word lists; it is not a good use of your hours.

Part 4 - Technical aptitude

Common in online assessments, and directly relevant to interviews.

• Output prediction - given a code snippet, what does it print. Pointer/reference semantics, operator precedence, integer overflow, short-circuit evaluation. You already own most of this after Month 1.

• Complexity questions - identify the Big-O of a given loop nest or recursion. Directly from your DSA track.

• Pseudocode tracing - dry-run a routine and produce the final state.

• SQL output questions - joins, group by, null behaviour. Directly from Month 2 Week 8.

• OS and networking multiple choice - directly from Month 3.

Note that four of five of these are already covered by your main track. Technical aptitude needs almost no separate study - just a few practice sets to get used to the multiple-choice format and the time pressure.

Part 5 - Estimation for system design (the part that matters most)

This is aptitude that Google and Amazon do test, inside the system design round. Memorise these.

Powers of two

Power Approximate value Name
2^10 1 Thousand 1 KB
2^20 1 Million 1 MB
2^30 1 Billion 1 GB
2^40 1 Trillion 1 TB
2^50 1 Quadrillion 1 PB

Latency numbers to reason with

Operation Rough order of magnitude
L1 cache reference ~1 ns
Main memory reference ~100 ns
SSD random read ~100 microseconds
Round trip within the same datacentre ~500 microseconds
Disk seek (spinning) ~10 ms
Round trip India to US ~150 ms

You do not need these to be exact. You need to know that memory is roughly a thousand times faster than SSD, that a cross-continent round trip dwarfs everything local, and that these ratios drive your caching and replication decisions.

The estimation drills

Given Compute in under 2 minutes
100M daily active users, 10 requests each Average QPS, then peak QPS at 3x
500M writes/day, 1 KB each Daily storage, yearly storage, with replication factor 3
1M QPS reads, 10 KB responses Bandwidth required
10 TB of data, 1 TB per node Node count, plus replication overhead
100k concurrent WebSocket connections Memory and connection budget per server, servers needed

Practise one of these every time you do a system design. Say the numbers out loud - stating estimates confidently is a scored signal, and stating them hesitantly reads as guessing even when the number is right.

Free resources

Resource For
IndiaBix indiabix.com The standard free bank for quantitative, reasoning and verbal, with explanations
GeeksforGeeks - Aptitude Topic-wise theory plus practice sets, plus their technical aptitude sections
PrepInsta (free sections) Company-specific assessment patterns for Indian recruiters
Khan Academy If any underlying maths is genuinely shaky - ratios, probability, algebra. Free and well built
Latency numbers every programmer should know Widely available reference. Print it and keep it visible
System Design Primer - estimation section Back-of-envelope worked examples

Schedule

Month Aptitude work
M1-M2 Tue/Thu last 15 min. Quantitative fundamentals: number system, percentages, ratios, averages, profit/loss, TSD, time and work
M3-M4 Tue/Thu 15 min. Logical reasoning: series, syllogisms (diagram method), seating, puzzles, blood relations, directions. Plus estimation drills inside every system design
M5 Tue/Thu 15 min. Data interpretation, which is the highest-frequency section. Plus verbal light touch
M6 Weeks 21-22 Intensive: 30 min/day for two weeks. Full timed mock assessments before the mid-tier applications land. This is when it actually pays
M7-M8 Maintenance only. One timed set per week if assessments are still coming in

The discipline for this track

• Always timed. Untimed aptitude practice is nearly worthless - the entire difficulty is speed.

• Learn the shortcut method, not the school method. These sections are designed so the long method does not fit in the time.

• Triage ruthlessly. In a real assessment, skipping two hard puzzles to secure eight easy questions is the correct play. Practise skipping - it is a trained skill and most people are bad at it.

• Keep a separate small error log. Same principle as the Weak List: bias your revision towards what you got wrong.

• Do not let this expand. If aptitude is eating more than 20 minutes on a weekday, it is stealing from work that matters more for your actual targets.

Career, Interviews and Relocation Playbook

Document 14 - the merged replacement for the old Documents 14, 15 and 16. Behavioural stories, target companies, visa routes, and every question you will be asked.

This one document now holds everything that is about getting the job rather than building the skill. Documents 02-09 build the engineer. This document converts that engineer into an offer, in a country with a path to permanent residency.

It replaces three documents that used to be separate and kept cross-referencing each other: the behavioural and STAR bank, the compensation and target-company list, and the interview question bank. They are one document because in practice you use them in the same week, for the same conversation. Months 05 to 09 still refer to this as Doc 14 - the number is unchanged on purpose so those references still resolve.

PART 0 - What activates when

This is a reference document, not a reading assignment. Nine parts, and they switch on at different times. Only Part 1 needs anything from you before Month 5.

Part What it is Activates What you do
1 Behavioural mastery and the STAR story bank Setup day, then Month 5 Weeks 17-20 From day one: two minutes of work journal, daily. Nothing else until Month 5
2 The relocation reality - visas, routes, timelines Month 4 (read it once, early) Read it. Then start the paperwork in Part 2 immediately - it has months of lead time
3 Target companies, ranked by path to residency Month 5 Week 20 Run the LinkedIn test on 20 names before you apply to any of them
4 How to verify a company before you apply Month 5 Week 20 Twenty minutes per company. Non-negotiable
5 Compensation - India and after relocation Month 5 Week 20 Know your numbers before any recruiter call
6 Application strategy, week by week Month 6 Week 21 This is the sequence you actually apply in
7 Interview questions and answers Month 5 Week 20, then constantly Say every answer aloud five times. This is the largest part of the document
8 The verification checklist Before every application Every volatile number in this document, with the official source that owns it
9 The one-page summary Whenever you feel lost Read it in two minutes

The one thing to do today: start the work journal in Part 1. Everything else in this document can wait for Month 4. The journal cannot, because in Month 5 you need twenty stories and you will not remember them.

PART 0A - August 2026 route research addendum

Added 25 August 2026, after the rest of this document was written. It records where newer information appears to contradict Parts 2, 3 and 6.

Status: UNVERIFIED. This came from a single round of research on 25 August 2026 and the fact-checking pass was stopped before it finished - one claim of twenty-one was independently confirmed. Nothing here should change an application decision until the three items at the end of this part have been checked against the official sources named. It is recorded now, rather than quietly folded into Parts 2 and 3, because acting on the existing Canada ranking without checking it could cost months - and because being confidently wrong about immigration rules is worse than knowing you have not checked.

Where this document now looks out of date

Section What this document says What the August 2026 research indicated (unverified) What to do
Part 2 and 3A - Canada Ranked first of every country here. Express Entry can grant permanent residency before you land, with no job offer. Estimated CRS for this profile is about 429. No general or all-programme draw since 23 April 2024 (that cut-off was 529) and no STEM draw since 11 April 2024 (491). Arranged-employment CRS points were abolished on 25 March 2025, so a job offer no longer adds points. The draws actually running in 2026 require Canadian experience, French, or an occupation you do not hold. Note the three-year BCA is NOT the obstacle here - CRS pays the same 120 points for any programme of three years or longer. VERIFY FIRST. If it holds, sitting in the pool at 429 converts at close to zero, and Canada becomes a French-language or provincial-nomination route rather than a file-and-wait one.
Part 2 and 3L - United States Ranked last. Highest pay, worst permanence. Confirmed, and sharper than written. Cold applications from India to unrelated US employers convert at under 2 per cent - treat as zero, since roughly 65 per cent of H-1B approvals are renewals. Selection is now wage-weighted rather than a flat lottery. A three-year BCA is not a US bachelor equivalent on its own: H-1B survives it through a credential evaluation plus the three-for-one experience rule, but EB-2 requires a single-source four-year degree and is structurally closed to you. The research rated an L-1 transfer through a current employer as the only clean route - and that is not available here, see the note below. Drop the United States as an active channel. With no employer transfer available and EB-2 closed, there is no route worth spending hours on. Revisit only from inside a different employer that has proven mobility.
3E - Ireland The best all-round fit for your exact profile. A three-year BCA may be assessed at NFQ Level 7 rather than Level 8. If so you move off the Critical Skills threshold near EUR 40,904 and on to the no-degree threshold near EUR 68,911. VERIFY FIRST. If it holds, Ireland is materially harder than this document assumes, and the Critical Skills line in the cover letter template needs changing.
3D, 3F and 3I - Germany, Netherlands, Poland Listed, but ranked below Canada and New Zealand. Possibly the strongest three for this profile, precisely because none of them gate on the degree. Germany has an IT-specialist route that reportedly waives the degree requirement for three or more years of IT experience - but see the 29 August 2026 note in Part 0B: German-language proficiency appears to be required as a rule on that route, and it may be a separate residence permit rather than the EU Blue Card itself, carrying a higher salary floor. The Netherlands highly skilled migrant route is salary-only with no degree test, and the reduced under-30 threshold keeps applying with the same employer after you turn 30. Poland is the second largest Blue Card issuer in the EU, and Relativity runs a .NET eDiscovery office in Krakow - a direct domain match, and the only company in this document checked against live evidence. Raise in priority, pending verification. SUPERSEDED 29 August 2026 as to the resume: the Blue Card wording was removed from the Europe resume and cover letter, because eligibility depends on the Germany check that has not been done. Do not put it back. State only that sponsorship is required and leave the route for a call - see Part 0B.
Part 6 - application sequence Week 22 is the centre of gravity: Canada and New Zealand. If the Canada finding holds, the centre of gravity moves to Germany, the Netherlands and Poland - the three channels that do not gate on the degree and that accept cold applications from India. The research rated an internal transfer as the highest-conversion move by a wide margin, but that requires an employer that actually moves people, which rules out the current one. Re-sequence only after verifying. Do not rewrite Part 6 on the strength of this addendum alone.

The three things to verify before acting on any of this

Each is a single lookup against a primary source. Add them to the Part 8 checklist, which already holds every other fact here that moves on a government timetable.

Claim What to check Source that owns the answer
Canada - Express Entry Whether general or STEM draws have resumed at all, and the current cut-offs. This is the single claim the whole Canada ranking rests on. canada.ca / IRCC
Germany - EU Blue Card The IT-specialist route, and whether it genuinely waives the degree requirement for your years of experience. make-it-in-germany.de / BAMF
Ireland - NFQ level What level a three-year BCA is assigned, and therefore which salary threshold applies to you. NARIC Ireland / enterprise.gov.ie

A fourth thing to resolve, and it is the one that decides whether the Canada conclusion above is right at all. The research contradicted itself on the CRS score: its summary said about 429, while its own detailed claim computed 450 to 470 for the same profile. The figure quoted in the Canada row above is 429. That spread crosses several draw cut-offs, so recompute it directly from the official CRS tool before acting on it, and correct this addendum with the answer.

Two inputs nobody has supplied are what make that calculation uncertain: exact age, which costs points every year from the late twenties, and marital status, which changes how the whole grid is scored. Fix those two and the CRS number stops being a guess.

The full evidence behind this addendum - 136 individual claims with dates, sources and confidence levels - is saved in the repository at CONTEXT.md (Part D), at the repository root. That file also records what the research explicitly could not answer and what was never asked. Read it before commissioning any further research, so the same ground is not covered twice.

Settled 25 August 2026 - the internal transfer route is closed

The current employer does not offer overseas transfer or relocation. That is now a known fact, not an open question, and it closes several things at once: the L-1 route in Part 2, the "you are already L-1 eligible" note in Part 2, and the Part 8 checklist row that asks HR about India-to-US mobility precedent. None of those need chasing. Treat this addendum as superseding them.

This matters more than it first looks, because the research rated an internal transfer as the highest-conversion move available - 25 to 40 per cent, against under 2 per cent for cold US applications. Losing it removes the best route and the only clean path into the United States in one go.

What survives is the strategy, not the employer. Route 1 in Part 2 - join an India office, move later - still works, but only through a company that actually moves people, which is exactly what Part 3M lists. So Part 3M changes from a fallback into a live parallel track: a role at an India-based employer with proven mobility is worth taking on its own terms, because it restores the transfer route that the current job cannot provide.

Immediate consequence for the application list: with no transfer available and EB-2 closed to a three-year degree, the United States has no route worth spending hours on. Direct applications to Germany, the Netherlands and Poland, plus Part 3M employers in India, are where the hours go until the three verifications above come back.

Provisional order of effort

The order the rest of this addendum implies, written out so it is actionable without further interpretation. It is provisional: rows 1 and 4 move if the Germany and Canada checks come back differently, and row 5 moves on the Ireland check. It replaces nothing in Part 6 until then - treat it as the working order while the verifications are outstanding.

Sequence Poland or Germany first for hit rate, the Netherlands first for net pay.

A role here is worth taking on its own terms, not as a consolation.

Overlaps with item 1 at Relativity in Krakow, which is why that one company is worth applying to first.

7 Australia points routes (subclass 189) Nil ACS deducts years of experience for a BCA, as Part 2 already warns. The employer-sponsored route is the only sensible one and it sits behind items 1 to 3.

Two things this order does not change. The Week 21 calibration applications inside India still happen exactly as Part 6 has them - interview skill is built by interviewing, and those remain the cheapest place to build it. And the Week 20 gate still stands: none of the above is a reason to start applying to the companies you actually want before the project exists.

PART 0B - What this document does not tell you

Added 29 August 2026. Part 0A corrected the country ranking. This part corrects something the ranking cannot fix on its own, and it applies to Parts 2, 3, 6 and 9 alike.

Status: UNVERIFIED, exactly as Part 0A. Every figure below comes from the same single research run, whose fact-checking pass was stopped before it finished. The full evidence is in CONTEXT.md Part D at the repository root. Treat these as orders of magnitude, not as numbers, and never quote one to an employer or on a form.

Verification attempt, 29 August 2026 - what could and could not be checked

Ten web requests were spent trying to close the four Part 0A verifications. The outcome is worth recording, because it changes how these gaps can ever be closed at all.

• Five official sources refused automated access outright, returning HTTP 403: canada.ca on two separate pages, ind.nl, make-it-in-germany.de and bmi.bund.de. That independently reproduces what the August research reported about canada.ca, so it is not a one-off. The practical consequence: these verifications cannot be completed by any research tool. They have to be done by you, in a browser, as a person. Do not commission more research expecting a different result - it will fail the same way.

• Germany - the no-degree IT route does appear to exist, which is the good news. But two details surfaced that the August research did not record: German-language proficiency appears to be required as a rule on that route, and it may be a separate residence permit rather than the EU Blue Card itself, carrying a higher salary floor than the EUR 45,934.20 quoted above. This does not close the question, it sharpens it - the thing to establish is which of the two routes you actually qualify for, because they are not the same permit and do not have the same threshold.

• Netherlands - one genuinely new and favourable fact. IND states that the reduced under-30 salary criterion keeps applying after you turn 30, for as long as you stay with the same employer. The under-30 threshold is therefore a condition at the point of hire, not a deadline that closes the route. The tables above have been corrected. Note also that IND publishes amounts valid 1 July to 31 December, so the January figures quoted here may already be superseded.

• Ireland - the NFQ Level 7 reading was repeated by a secondary source, which is not independent confirmation, because the August research relied on the same class of source. What did emerge is the cheap way to settle it: NARIC Ireland runs a free searchable database of foreign qualifications, and where a qualification is not listed you can request a generic comparability statement through an online form. Do that before spending any effort on Ireland - it either opens the market or closes it.

• Canada - no progress at all. Neither the rounds-of-invitations page nor the CRS criteria page could be reached. The CRS contradiction of 429 against 450 to 470 is still open and is still the first thing to settle, using the official CRS tool yourself.

The flaw this part fixes

Part 2 ranks countries by how quickly the visa becomes permanent, and by how strong the .NET market is. Both are real questions. Neither is the question that decides the outcome, which is whether any employer in that country will sponsor an unknown mid-level engineer who is currently in Surat and needs a visa. That column does not exist anywhere in this document, so the whole thing reads as a menu: choose a country, follow the steps, arrive. It is not a menu.

A country can have a two-year path to permanent residency and still be unreachable, because the hard part happens before any of that. Read Part 2 as "what happens after you land". Read the table below as "how likely you are to land at all". Where the two disagree, this one governs.

How likely each channel actually is

Probability of at least one sponsored offer within twelve to eighteen months, per channel, assuming sustained effort in that channel.

Channel Odds Why it sits there
Poland - EU Blue Card 20-30% The best cold-application hit rate on this list. Second-largest Blue Card issuer in the EU, and Indian nationals are the largest recipient group EU-wide. Relativity runs a .NET eDiscovery office in Krakow, which is a direct domain match.
Netherlands - highly skilled migrant 15-25% Salary-only, no degree test. The employer must be an IND recognised sponsor, and that register is public and searchable. The under-30 threshold is far lower than the 30-and-over one - and per IND the reduced under-30 criterion keeps applying after you turn 30 for as long as you stay with the same employer, so the age matters at the point of hire rather than for ever.
Germany - EU Blue Card 15-25% An IT-specialist route reportedly waives the degree requirement for three or more years of IT experience. Two cautions added 29 August 2026: German-language proficiency appears to be required as a rule on that route, and it may be a separate residence permit rather than the EU Blue Card itself, with a higher salary floor. Establish which route applies to you before building a plan on it. Improves with A1 to B1 German, which also shortens the settlement clock from 27 months to 21.
India employers with proven mobility - Part 3M Parallel track Now the only remaining way to reach a transfer route at all, since the current employer offers none. Worth taking on its own terms rather than as a fallback.
Ireland 8-15% Hinges entirely on whether a three-year BCA is graded NFQ Level 7 or Level 8. Level 7 moves the salary bar from roughly EUR 40,904 to roughly EUR 68,911, which is a senior salary, not a mid-level one.
United Kingdom 8-12% Approval is straightforward once an employer commits, and the degree is not a personal barrier because the RQF level attaches to the occupation. But main-applicant Skilled Worker applications fell 39 per cent in the year to 30 June 2026 - the collapse is in employer willingness to sponsor at all.
Australia - subclass 482 5-10% A skills assessment is mandatory for Indian passport holders before you can even lodge, which is three to six months of lead time before the first application. The points route 189 is effectively closed to software engineers.
New Zealand - AEWV 5-10% Realistically needs you on the ground. The residence pathways added in 2026 reward people already in New Zealand accumulating local experience; they do not help a cold application from Surat.
Canada under 5% from abroad Estimated CRS about 429 against draws this profile cannot enter. A job offer has been worth zero CRS points since 25 March 2025. Reachable only through French to NCLC 7 or a provincial nomination.
United States - cold applications under 1% Treat as zero. Roughly 65 per cent of H-1B approvals are renewals, so the programme mostly serves people already inside the country. Selection has been wage-weighted since February 2026.

Across all channels together: roughly 50 to 65 per cent of landing at least one sponsored role within eighteen months. That figure assumes 200 to 400 targeted applications plus an active referral campaign. It is not the probability of applying to thirty companies and waiting. The single largest cause of failure here is stopping after the first fifty rejections, which is the normal shape of this process rather than a signal about you.

What this means in practice

• The operative plan is the provisional order of effort in Part 0A, not the week-by-week sequence in Part 6. Germany, the Netherlands and Poland carry about 70 per cent of the overseas hours, because they are the three channels that neither gate on the degree nor need an employer transfer.

• Do not write "eligible for an EU Blue Card" on the Europe resume, whatever Part 6 says. That claim was removed from the resume on 29 August 2026 because eligibility depends on the Germany verification in Part 0A, which has not been done. Say only that you require sponsorship, and leave the route to be discussed on a call.

• The four verifications in Part 0A are still outstanding, and the CRS contradiction - 429 against 450 to 470 for the same profile - is still unresolved. Until those come back, this part is direction, not instruction.

• The Week 20 gate in Part 6 still stands, and nothing here is a reason to move it. Odds this low are a reason to arrive with the project built and load tested, not a reason to start applying sooner.

What would actually move these numbers

• French to NCLC 7. The only move fully under your control that reopens Canada - worth about 62 CRS points and, more importantly, entry to a draw category whose cut-offs have run 382 to 420 rather than the 500s. It is a 12 to 24 month commitment on top of full-time work, so decide it deliberately or not at all.

• Applying to the Netherlands while you are still under 30. The reduced threshold appears to keep applying with the same employer after you turn 30, so this is a cliff at the moment of hire rather than a deadline for the whole plan - which makes it an argument for applying there early, not for panicking about a birthday.

• A second post-secondary credential. A one-year qualification on top of the BCA is worth more CRS than its cost suggests, and a full master's is what reopens EB-2 in the US - though neither produces an invitation on its own.

• The distributed job platform existing, deployed and load tested. It is the only item on this list that improves every channel at once, and it is the one already scheduled.

PART 1 - Behavioural mastery and the STAR story bank

Behavioural is roughly half your Amazon score, the Bar Raiser can veto on it alone, and it is the round that strong engineers most reliably underprepare. You can be excellent at everything in Documents 02-09 and still not get an offer if this round is weak.

You already have unusually good raw material: four and a half years of real production work with real numbers. What you do not yet have is structure, quantification and delivery. This part converts one into the other.

Start today: the work journal

Two minutes per working day. One line: what problem came up, what I decided, what happened.

This is the single highest-return habit in the entire plan relative to effort. In Month 5 you need 20 detailed stories. Without a journal you will be trying to recall incidents from eight months earlier, and you have told me you forget quickly. With a journal you will have 150+ raw entries to select the best 20 from.

Start it the same day you start Month 1. Not in Month 5.

Amazon's 16 Leadership Principles - what each actually probes

High-frequency principles are marked. Roughly six appear in about 85% of interviews.

Principle What the interviewer is really testing Typical question
Customer Obsession (HF) Do you start from the user, or from the technology Tell me about a time you went beyond requirements for a customer
Ownership (HF) Do you act outside your job description; do you think long-term Tell me about something you fixed that was not your responsibility
Invent and Simplify Do you find simpler solutions rather than more complex ones Tell me about a time you dramatically simplified something
Are Right, A Lot Judgement under incomplete information; do you seek disconfirming views Tell me about a decision you made with insufficient data
Learn and Be Curious Do you learn beyond what is required of you Tell me about something you taught yourself recently
Hire and Develop the Best Do you raise others. Mentoring counts even without direct reports Tell me about someone you helped grow
Insist on the Highest Standards Do you accept "good enough" Tell me about a time you refused to accept substandard work
Think Big Can you see beyond the immediate ticket Tell me about a time you proposed something larger than asked
Bias for Action (HF) Do you move with calculated speed under uncertainty Tell me about a time you acted without full information
Frugality Can you do more with less Tell me about achieving something with constrained resources
Earn Trust (HF) Candour, self-criticism, treating others well Tell me about receiving difficult feedback
Dive Deep (HF) Do you go to root cause or stop at symptoms Tell me about the hardest bug you debugged
Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit (HF) Will you challenge, and then commit fully either way Tell me about disagreeing with your manager
Deliver Results (HF) Do you finish, despite obstacles Tell me about delivering under a hard deadline
Strive to be Earth's Best Employer Team environment, empathy, growth of others Tell me about improving your team's working life
Success and Scale Bring Broad Responsibility Second-order consequences, ethics, impact beyond the feature Tell me about considering the wider impact of a decision

The two most under-prepared

• Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit. Needs a genuine disagreement with someone more senior, argued with data, followed by full commitment whichever way it resolved. The "and commit" half is what candidates omit, and it is half the principle. Start noticing these moments at work now.

• Earn Trust. Needs a story where you were wrong, or received hard feedback, and responded well. Candidates instinctively avoid stories that make them look bad, which is exactly backwards - this principle is testing self-criticism.

Google - "Googliness and Leadership"

Less codified than Amazon's LPs, but the themes are consistent.

Theme What they look for
Collaboration Do people want to work with you. Concrete examples of working across teams
Comfort with ambiguity Do you freeze without complete requirements, or do you move sensibly
Intellectual humility Can you say "I was wrong" and "I do not know"
Bias to action with judgement Do you ship, without being reckless
Care for the user Same instinct as Customer Obsession, phrased differently
Doing the right thing Ethics, pushing back on bad decisions
Growth of others Mentoring, code review culture, documentation

Google also probes how you respond to being challenged mid-answer. An interviewer may push back on something you said to see whether you defend it with reasoning, or fold immediately, or become defensive. The correct response is to engage with the substance: "That is a fair point - let me reconsider. The reason I chose that was X, but if Y is true then you are right that Z would be better."

Your story bank - the extraction template

For every story, fill this in. One page each. Twenty of them.

Field Content
Title A short handle you can find quickly. "Email pipeline 80% optimisation"
Situation Two sentences of context. Resist explaining the whole company
Task What you specifically owned. Not the team's goal - yours
Action The bulk of the story. What you investigated, what you decided, what you rejected and why, how you executed, who you worked with
Result Quantified. Numbers, percentages, time saved, incidents prevented
Learning What you would do differently. Never skip this - it is what separates a story from a boast
LPs it serves Usually three to five, depending on emphasis
Follow-up answers Pre-written answers to the probes listed below

Time budget within the answer

Part Share Note
Situation 15% Context only
Task 15% Your ownership, stated clearly
Action 55% This is what is scored
Result 15% Numbers, then the learning

The two fatal delivery errors

• Spending three minutes on Situation. Interviewers score Action. A long setup burns the clock and gives them nothing to write down.

• Saying "we" throughout. "We decided", "we built", "we improved" gives the interviewer nothing to attribute to you. Use "I" for your decisions and actions, and "we" only where genuinely collaborative - the contrast then reads as honest rather than self-aggrandising.

Your candidate stories - starting material

From your resume and roles. Expand each into the full template; add more from the journal as it grows.

Story Strongest principles
Email processing 7-10h to 1-1.5h (~80%) using SES, EventBridge, SQS Deliver Results, Dive Deep, Ownership, Insist on Highest Standards, Invent and Simplify. Your flagship - it will be asked about repeatedly, so it must be your deepest story
FOIA backend features for US federal agencies Customer Obsession, Earn Trust, Success and Scale Brings Broad Responsibility
Legacy refactoring and platform modernisation at Casepoint Ownership, Think Big, Are Right A Lot
SQL query optimisation on large eDiscovery datasets Dive Deep, Deliver Results
Multilingual content processing Customer Obsession, Learn and Be Curious
100,000+ record datasets at Zibma while holding performance Dive Deep, Frugality
Payment gateway integrations - Stripe, PayPal, CCAvenue Bias for Action, Deliver Results, Earn Trust (money correctness)
Vonage video integration in VCDoctor Learn and Be Curious, Deliver Results
SignalR one-to-one messaging and FCM multi-device signalling Invent and Simplify, Dive Deep
ERP reporting for multiple institutions and roles Customer Obsession, Ownership
Building .NET Core APIs into an existing ASP.NET application Think Big, Invent and Simplify
Production incident you resolved (pick the hardest) Dive Deep, Ownership, Bias for Action
A disagreement with a senior colleague or manager Have Backbone; Disagree and Commit - find a real one
A time you were wrong or received hard feedback Earn Trust - find a real one
Helping a junior developer Hire and Develop the Best
Your distributed job platform project Learn and Be Curious, Think Big, Ownership, Dive Deep

Notice two rows say "find a real one". Those are your gaps. Do not invent them - interviewers probe hard and fabricated stories collapse under follow-up. Look through your journal, and start watching for these situations at work now.

The follow-up probes (this is where interviews are actually won or lost)

Your first answer gets you maybe 40% of the score. The follow-ups get the rest. Pre-write answers to these for every story.

• What was the data behind that decision?

• What alternatives did you consider, and why did you reject them?

• What was your specific contribution, as opposed to the team's?

• What was the hardest part, technically?

• Who disagreed with you, and how did you handle it?

• What went wrong that you did not anticipate?

• How did you measure success? What were the numbers before and after?

• What would you do differently now?

• What did you learn that you applied later?

• How did this affect the customer or the business?

• How long did it take, and did that match your estimate?

• What happened after you left it - did it hold up?

The Bar Raiser will keep going until you reach the edge of your knowledge. That is the design of the round, not a sign it is going badly. When you reach the edge, say so: "I do not know the exact figure - what I remember is the order of magnitude, and here is how I would confirm it." That scores well. Inventing a number does not, and it is often detectable.

Common question bank

Ownership and delivery

• Tell me about a time you took on something outside your role.

• Tell me about a deadline you thought you would miss.

• Tell me about a project you owned end to end.

• Tell me about a time you had to make a decision without your manager.

Conflict and backbone

• Tell me about disagreeing with your manager or a senior engineer.

• Tell me about convincing someone who initially disagreed.

• Tell me about a time you were overruled. What did you do next?

• Tell me about difficult feedback you received.

Failure and learning

• Tell me about your biggest professional mistake.

• Tell me about a time you missed a deadline.

• Tell me about something that failed in production because of your change.

• Tell me about a time you did not know how to proceed.

Technical depth

• Tell me about the most complex system you have worked on.

• Tell me about the hardest bug you have debugged.

• Tell me about a performance problem you solved.

• Tell me about a technical decision you would reverse today.

Collaboration

• Tell me about working with a difficult colleague.

• Tell me about working across teams.

• Tell me about mentoring someone.

• Tell me about improving a team process.

Rehearsal protocol

Month Behavioural work
M1-M4 Journal only. Two minutes a day. No rehearsal yet - you are collecting raw material
M5 Wk 17-20 Write all 20 stories in the full template. Five per week. Map to the LP matrix
M5 Wk 20 Record every story. Listen back once. Cut anything that is not Action
M6 Rehearse randomised and cold. No warning, no preparation time. Under 3 minutes each
M7 Re-record your three weakest each week. Practise follow-up probes specifically
M8 Fully randomised. Have someone else pick

The randomisation rule. From Month 6, never rehearse stories in a fixed order. Shuffle them, or have someone pick at random. Stories rehearsed in sequence become a memorised script, and memorised scripts are audible - they sound rehearsed rather than remembered, which reads as inauthentic. Know the situation, the decisions, the reasoning, the result and the lesson. Never memorise sentences.

PART 2 - The relocation reality

You told me you want to move abroad, that applying directly from India feels hard, and that you would rather join a company with a real relocation path than chase the highest-prestige name. That is a sound strategy, and this part is built around one refinement of it: rank countries by whether the visa leads to permanent residency, not by salary.

A work visa tied to one employer is not the same thing as living somewhere. If the goal is to settle, the question that decides everything is: how long from landing to a status that is mine rather than my employer's? That single question reorders the entire target list, and it moves the United States - the highest-paying destination - to the bottom.

Your priorities, restated

Rank Priority What it means for targeting
1 Path to permanent residency Does this visa become PR, and in how many years? Canada, New Zealand, Australia, Germany and Ireland are 2-3 years. The US is decades for an Indian national
2 Sponsorship that actually happens The company appears on a government sponsor register, or has named engineers who moved from India. Not "we support mobility"
3 Stack fit (.NET) You interview and work in C#. Target companies where .NET is core, not tolerated. This is your single biggest conversion advantage and most candidates ignore it
4 Salary in real terms Net of tax and cost of living, not gross. A EUR 70k Berlin offer and a GBP 70k London offer are not the same life
5 Prestige Nice, not the objective. A FAANG badge you cannot relocate from does not serve your goal

The single most important idea in this part. A mid-size .NET product company in Toronto, Auckland, Dublin or Amsterdam that hires Indians directly is a better vehicle for your actual goal than a FAANG India role where you are one of tens of thousands competing for a handful of transfer slots. Prestige and mobility are not the same thing. Optimise for the one you want.

The route nobody told you about: you are already L-1 eligible [STRUCK 29 August 2026 - THIS WHOLE SECTION IS VOID, see the note below and Part 0B]

STRUCK 29 August 2026 - why this section is void: the current employer does not offer overseas transfer or relocation, so there is no L-1 for anyone to file. Part 0A settled that on 25 August 2026. The section is left in place rather than deleted so the reasoning stays visible, but nothing in it is actionable - do not raise it with your manager, and skip the Part 7 F6 script. See Part 0B.

You joined Casepoint in May 2025. Casepoint is a US-headquartered company and you have been employed by its India entity for over a year. The L-1 intracompany-transfer requirement - one continuous year with the foreign entity in the preceding three years - you already meet it.

This matters more than it sounds, for four reasons:

• No lottery. L-1 is not subject to the H-1B cap or the annual lottery. It is filed when the company decides to file it.

• Not covered by the 2025 H-1B fee. The September 2025 proclamation imposing a USD 100,000 payment applies to new H-1B petitions, not L-1. That fee has made many US employers stop sponsoring H-1B for mid-level engineers, which makes the L-1 route relatively more valuable, not less [VERIFY: current status - this proclamation has been challenged in court]

• L-1A has a real green-card path. L-1B specialised-knowledge transferees queue in EB-2/EB-3, where the India backlog runs into decades. L-1A managers can use EB-1C, where the India backlog is dramatically shorter. If a US move matters to you, the long game is a management track, not a senior-engineer track [VERIFY: monthly State Department Visa Bulletin]

• You are in the right domain. Casepoint serves US federal agencies. FOIA and eDiscovery work is exactly the "specialised knowledge" an L-1B petition needs to argue, and you have fifteen months of it.

What to actually do: this is a conversation with your own manager, not an application. The script for it is in Part 7, Section F6 - it is a genuinely delicate conversation and doing it badly can mark you as a flight risk. Two things to confirm first, quietly: whether the India entity and the US entity have a qualifying corporate relationship (parent, subsidiary, branch or affiliate), and whether anyone has moved Surat-to-US before. Ask HR the second question as curiosity about the company, not as a request.

The honest caveat. Even a successful L-1 puts you in the US on a status tied to Casepoint, in the country with the worst permanence prospects for an Indian national. Treat it as a high-earning few years and a strong resume line, not as emigration. If you want to settle, Canada, New Zealand and Australia below are strictly better.

Why the US is ranked last despite paying the most

CONFIRMED and hardened, 25 August 2026 - see Part 0A. Three additions. Cold applications from India convert at under 2 per cent, so the practical advice is not "rank it last" but "do not spend hours on it at all". EB-2 is structurally closed to a three-year BCA, because it requires a single-source four-year degree. And the L-1 escape hatch this section relies on is not available - the current employer does not offer transfer or relocation - so the United States should be dropped as an active channel rather than merely ranked last.

This is the conclusion most Indian engineers resist, so here it is plainly. On an H-1B or L-1 you are working in the United States on a status that belongs to your employer. Changing jobs is a legal event. Being laid off starts a countdown measured in weeks. Your spouse may not be able to work. And because employment-based green cards are capped per country of birth, the queue for an Indian national in the main professional categories is long enough that people plan their children's citizenship around it rather than their own.

None of that makes the US a bad idea. It makes it a specific idea: go for high earnings and a strong resume over a defined number of years, with your eyes open, ideally on an L-1A management track that opens EB-1C. Do not go expecting to settle.

If your goal is... Then target
Permanent settlement Canada or New Zealand first, then Australia, Germany, Ireland. All four give a real path measured in single-digit years
Out of India fastest, PR later Poland or Malta into the EU, or the UAE. Then use EU mobility or a second move
Maximum earnings, flexible later US or Switzerland. Go in knowing it is a chapter, not a destination
Europe lifestyle plus strong .NET demand Netherlands, Ireland, Germany, Nordics, UK. All excellent .NET markets
English-speaking, .NET-heavy, real PR path Ireland, New Zealand, Canada. [STRUCK 29 August 2026 - these are now the three hardest on the list, not the best match. Ireland is gated on the NFQ grading, New Zealand realistically needs you on the ground, and Canada sits at an estimated CRS of 429 against draws this profile cannot enter. See Part 0B.]

The paperwork you must start before Month 6

This is the part of the plan with the longest lead times and the least effort. None of it competes with studying, and starting it late costs you months you cannot recover. Do it on the weekends of Month 4 and 5.

Item Lead time Why now
IELTS General Training 4-8 weeks Required for Canada Express Entry. Book it, sit it once, and know the score. Results are valid two years
Educational Credential Assessment (WES) 6-12 weeks Canada requires your BCA assessed against Canadian standards. This is pure administration and it blocks your Express Entry profile until it is done [VERIFY: wes.org current turnaround]
Express Entry profile Same day, once the above exist Costs nothing to sit in the pool. Your score can only be drawn if the profile exists
ACS skills assessment (Australia) 8-12 weeks Required for the points routes. Be aware ACS deducts years of your experience depending on how closely your degree matches ICT - with a BCA expect a deduction, which is exactly why the employer-sponsored 482 route suits you better than the points routes [VERIFY: acs.org.au]
Passport validity and pages 2-6 weeks Check it has more than a year left. A short-dated passport delays every visa in this document
A clean digital footprint One evening LinkedIn matching your resume exactly, a GitHub with the job platform pinned and a real README. Overseas recruiters screen on these before they call

One point about age. Canada's CRS and Australia's points test both award maximum points in your late twenties and start deducting from around thirty. That is the strongest argument in this entire document for starting the paperwork this month rather than at the end of the plan. The study plan takes eight months; the points clock does not pause for it.

PART 3 - Target companies, ranked by path to residency

This is your apply list, ordered by the ranking in Part 2: countries where the visa becomes permanent come first, and Indian big tech comes near the end. That ordering will feel wrong the first time you read it, because it puts companies you have never heard of above companies everyone has. That is the point. You are optimising for where you can end up, not for whose name your friends will recognise.

How to read these tables

Route What it means and what you do
Direct Hires from abroad and sponsors the visa itself. You apply to the overseas job posting from India. Check the country's public sponsor register first (Part 4)
Transfer Has an India office. You join in India, perform, and move internally after the eligibility period. Slower, but a much easier first door
Direct + Transfer Both are open. These are your best targets - you can apply overseas now and still have the India option as a fallback

A necessary warning about this whole part. Company hiring policy changes quarterly, sponsor licences lapse, India offices open and close, and a company that sponsored freely in 2025 may have stopped. Treat every row here as a starting hypothesis to be tested, not a fact. Part 4 tells you how to test one in twenty minutes, and you should test every company before you spend an evening on its application. The lists are here to stop you staring at a blank page - not to be trusted. [VERIFY: every row, via the sponsor registers and the LinkedIn test in Part 4]

Evidence status of these company lists - added 29 August 2026

The warning above is right, and it is the most important sentence in Part 3. Here is what it means concretely. Of every company named in this part, exactly one has been checked against live evidence: Relativity's Krakow engineering office, which had .NET roles advertised in August 2026 with published salary bands. Everything else here is a hypothesis assembled from what the company builds and what stack it is known to use. That is a sound way to build a starting list. It is not a sponsorship finding, and it is not what the individual rows below sound like.

Treat every phrase of this kind as unverified, wherever it appears below: "routine visa sponsor", "well-known accredited employer", "real sponsorship", "provides real relocation support", "a genuinely routine India-to-Canada movement pattern", "the transfer route is real", "hires Indian engineers". Not one of those was checked against a sponsor register or against named engineers who actually moved. Part 4 is how you check one, and it takes twenty minutes. Do it before every application, not before the first.

Five places where the evidence in CONTEXT.md Part D actively disagrees with the text below:

• Nuix, in 3C and 3K, is described as .NET. The research found it appears to be Java-leaning and could not confirm the stack. Part 9 also names it as a best-fitting company. Check the stack before spending an application on it.

• Magnet Forensics, in 3A and 3K, is marked Direct. Its sponsorship policy was explicitly not verified.

• The Canadian banks row in 3A says they use the Global Talent Stream and offer real sponsorship. The research's own assessment is the opposite: Canadian employers do not routinely use the Global Talent Stream for mid-level backend engineers hired from India, because the business case rarely closes against a deep local talent pool.

• Epiq, Consilio, Lighthouse and KLDiscovery in 3K are described as having a real transfer route. The research listed them as probable but unverified transfer vectors.

• Microsoft, Amazon and Google offices marked Direct in 3A and elsewhere. The research found that large product companies with India entities move people almost exclusively as internal transfers at senior level, rather than hiring from abroad at mid-level.

And one row that is under-weighted rather than wrong. Relativity appears in 3K under its Chicago head office, with Krakow mentioned as an aside. Krakow is the part that matters: it is the most precisely matched opportunity found anywhere in this research, in the country with the best sponsorship odds for an Indian national, and Part 0A puts it first. Treat Relativity Krakow as a 3I row, not as a footnote to a US row.

PART 4 - How to verify a company before you apply

Every company says it supports mobility. Most do not, in practice. And every job board is full of overseas postings from companies that cannot legally sponsor you. Twenty minutes of checking per company saves you evenings of wasted applications, and it is the difference between a pipeline and a lottery ticket.

Check 1 - the government sponsor register (do this first)

Several countries publish a list of employers legally permitted to sponsor a foreign worker. If a company is not on the list, the conversation is over before it starts - no amount of enthusiasm from a hiring manager can fix it. This is the highest-value five minutes in your entire job search and almost nobody does it.

Country What to check Where
UK Register of licensed sponsors (workers). Downloadable as a spreadsheet - get it once and filter it against the company names in Section 3H gov.uk - search "register of licensed sponsors workers" [VERIFY: updated frequently]
Netherlands Public register of recognised sponsors. A highly skilled migrant permit is legally impossible without one ind.nl - "Public Register Recognised Sponsors"
New Zealand List of accredited employers. Accreditation is required before they can hire you on an AEWV immigration.govt.nz - employer accreditation
Australia Accredited sponsor status. Not every sponsor is accredited, but accredited ones get priority processing, so it is a good filter homeaffairs.gov.au [VERIFY: what is published changes]
Ireland Employment permit statistics list the companies actually granted permits. Also look for Trusted Partner status enterprise.gov.ie - employment permit statistics
Canada There is no single register, but quarterly LMIA statistics name employers, and Job Bank postings indicate LMIA-supported roles canada.ca - LMIA statistics [VERIFY]
Germany, Poland, Malta, Nordics No public register. Fall back on Check 2 below Use the LinkedIn test

Check 2 - the LinkedIn test (do this before every single application)

• Search the company name plus "Software Engineer", and filter the location to Toronto, Auckland, Sydney, Dublin, Amsterdam, Berlin, Copenhagen, London or Krakow.

• Open ten profiles. Look at their career history, not their current title.

• Did any of them start at that company in India and later appear in the foreign office? Or did any of them move to that country from India at all?

• If several did, relocation is real. If none did, the mobility programme is marketing.

• Bonus signal: how many engineers in that office have Indian names and non-local university degrees? A team that already contains migrants is a team whose manager has done the paperwork before and is not afraid of it.

This single check is worth more than any recruiter's assurance. Do it for every company on your shortlist, and record the answer in the application tracker in Document 11 so you never repeat the work.

Check 3 - questions to ask the recruiter (ask early, not after the offer)

For an overseas role you are applying to directly

• Is this role open to candidates who require visa sponsorship? - Ask this in the first message. It costs you nothing and saves you weeks.

• Does the company hold a sponsor licence, and have you sponsored engineers from outside the country recently?

• Who covers the visa costs, the relocation, and the dependant applications?

• What is the realistic start date, allowing for visa processing?

• Is the role permanent and local-contract, or a fixed-term deputation?

For an India role you intend to transfer out of

• How many engineers moved from the India office to an overseas office in the last two years?

• Is this role part of a global team, or does it sit in an India-only cost centre? This is the question that catches the trap.

• Is there a formal internal mobility programme, and what is the eligibility period?

• Does the company sponsor work visas for transferring employees, and who bears the cost?

• Are there open roles in the overseas offices that an internal candidate could apply to today?

Many Global Capability Centres in India are structured as cost centres that deliver work for teams abroad but never move people into them. The work looks global; the career is not. That second question is how you tell the difference before you sign.

Red flags

• Nobody at the company has ever moved from India to an overseas office.

• The recruiter answers "we support it case by case" and cannot name a single case.

• The company is not on the sponsor register for a country that publishes one.

• The India entity is a separate legal subsidiary with no corporate relationship to the foreign entity. The L-1 route legally requires a qualifying relationship.

• The role is explicitly staffed to support a foreign team rather than to be part of one.

• The overseas job posting says "must have existing right to work" - believe it, and move on.

• A recruiter asks you to pay anything at all, for a visa, a placement, or a "processing fee". This is always a scam. Legitimate employers pay sponsorship costs, never the candidate.

PART 5 - Compensation

Where you are now

Rs 6.21 LPA at 4.5 years is substantially below market, before any of this plan. Market rate for your experience today is roughly Rs 12-18 LPA at services companies and Rs 18-35 LPA at product companies. You are being paid roughly a third of your market value.

That is not a criticism - it is common for engineers in smaller firms in tier-2 cities - but it reframes everything. A large jump is not something this plan creates. It is something already owed to you that this plan helps you collect.
