RM — Software_Engineer_6_8_Month_Master_Roadmap

Full source content: Software_Engineer_6_8_Month_Master_Roadmap.docx. Original wording is retained below. For conflicting statements, use the visible correction and the current execution plan.

6–8 Month Software Engineer Transformation Roadmap

Primary stack: C# / .NET / ASP.NET Core | Goal: Deep engineering knowledge + top product-company interview readiness

How to use this course

This is not an interview-cramming plan. The goal is to turn practical development experience into deep software-engineering understanding. Interviews are the final validation: DSA, system design, low-level design, behavioral communication, and technical depth.

• Monday–Friday: 2 focused hours/day.

• Saturday–Sunday: full study/build days; use them for project work, deeper topics, tests, and revision.

• Every concept follows: Learn → Understand → Explain → Code → Recall → Apply → Revise.

• Use active recall instead of rereading. Close the notes and explain concepts from memory.

• Revision cadence: Day 1, Day 3, Day 7, Day 14, Day 30.

• Maintain one Master Notes document and one Roadmap/Revision Tracker. Do not write giant notes; capture the mental model, why, internals, example, pitfalls, and questions.

Target outcome by Month 6

• Strong C# and modern .NET fundamentals rather than framework-only usage.

• Interview-ready DSA with pattern recognition and complexity analysis.

• Solid CS fundamentals: networking, operating systems, databases, concurrency.

• Ability to design backend systems and explain trade-offs.

• Ability to discuss distributed systems, queues, caching, retries, idempotency, scaling, and failures.

• One serious distributed backend project that demonstrates engineering depth.

• Behavioral stories based on real work experience.

• Clear, simple technical English—not perfect English.

• Begin applications in Month 6; use Months 6–8 for interview conversion and deeper specialization.

Your weekly operating system

Day Time Primary work
Mon 2h C#/.NET deep learning + DSA
Tue 2h C#/.NET/CS + DSA
Wed 2h Backend/DB/Networking + DSA
Thu 2h CS/System Design + DSA
Fri 2h Revision + active recall + weekly interview questions
Sat Full day Deep topic + project + DSA + speaking
Sun Full day Project + weekly test + revision + planning

Month 1 — C# + .NET Foundations + DSA Basics

Week 1: C# types, value/reference types, stack/heap mental model, classes, objects, constructors, access modifiers. DSA: Big-O, arrays.

Week 2: OOP, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction, interfaces, composition. DSA: strings, HashMap/HashSet.

Week 3: Collections, IEnumerable/ICollection/IList/IQueryable, LINQ, deferred execution, delegates, lambdas. DSA: two pointers, sliding window.

Week 4: async/await, Task, exceptions, IDisposable, using, dependency injection basics. DSA: stack, queue, binary search.

• Outcome: explain what you use in C# instead of only knowing syntax. Build small console/API exercises.

Month 2 — Advanced C# + ASP.NET Core + SQL

Week 5: Task vs Thread, thread pool, concurrency vs parallelism, lock, race conditions, deadlocks, CancellationToken.

Week 6: .NET Framework vs modern .NET, CLR/runtime/SDK, ASP.NET Core hosting, Kestrel, middleware, request pipeline, configuration, logging.

Week 7: Web API architecture, controllers, services, DI lifetimes, authentication/authorization, JWT, EF Core, tracking vs no-tracking.

Week 8: SQL deeply: indexes, execution plans, joins, transactions, ACID, isolation levels, locks, deadlocks, normalization/denormalization.

• DSA: linked lists, recursion, trees, BST, heap. Start timed easy/medium problems.

Month 3 — CS Fundamentals + Networking + Concurrency + System Design Basics

Week 9: HTTP, DNS, TCP, TLS, REST, HTTP methods/status codes, connection lifecycle, WebSockets and SignalR.

Week 10: OS fundamentals: process, thread, memory, scheduling, synchronization, deadlock.

Week 11: Databases: storage/index concepts, transactions, isolation, replication basics, SQL vs NoSQL, caching basics.

Week 12: queues and asynchronous systems: SQS/RabbitMQ concepts, producer/consumer, acknowledgements, retries, DLQ, idempotency, ordering.

• System Design starts: URL shortener, rate limiter, notification service. DSA continues with graphs/BFS/DFS and intervals.

Month 4 — LLD + Distributed Systems + Project Build

Week 13: SOLID and object-oriented design. Implement Parking Lot and Logger in C#.

Week 14: design patterns: Strategy, Factory, Observer, Adapter, Decorator, Builder. Apply them only where useful.

Week 15: distributed systems: load balancing, caching, replication, sharding, partitioning, eventual consistency, CAP concepts.

Week 16: Project Phase 1 — Distributed Job Processing Platform: requirements, architecture, API, PostgreSQL schema, queue, worker model.

• DSA: medium-heavy practice. System design: file storage, chat, job processing.

Month 5 — Advanced System Design + Project + Behavioral

Week 17: Project Phase 2 — retries, exponential backoff, DLQ, idempotency, priority, worker scaling.

Week 18: Project Phase 3 — Redis, rate limiting, authentication, structured logging, metrics, health checks.

Week 19: Project Phase 4 — Docker, CI/CD, AWS deployment, load testing, failure testing, performance measurement.

Week 20: system design: notification platform, ecommerce/order processing, payment workflow, feed, large-scale messaging.

• Behavioral: build STAR stories from real work: performance optimization, production issue, disagreement, ownership, failure, difficult requirement, collaboration.

Month 6 — Interview Launch Month

• DSA: timed medium problems, pattern revision, weak-area repair. Add selected hard problems only where useful.

• System Design: 2–3 timed designs/week. Practice requirements, API, data model, high-level architecture, scaling, failure handling, trade-offs.

• LLD: 1–2 designs/week in C#.

• Behavioral: 8–12 polished STAR stories; practice speaking without memorized scripts.

• Resume/project: polish GitHub README, architecture diagrams, benchmarks, trade-offs, tests, deployment, and project explanation.

• Start applications. Use early interviews as calibration; keep studying while interviewing.

Month 7 — Interview Conversion + Advanced Gaps

• Analyze every interview: DSA pattern missed, CS gap, communication gap, design gap.

• Target company-specific interview patterns while preserving fundamentals.

• Advanced distributed systems: Kafka concepts, consumer groups, partitioning, ordering, outbox, saga, circuit breaker, observability.

• Do weekly full mock loops: DSA + system design/LLD + behavioral.

• Continue project improvements only when they create a strong engineering story.

Month 8 — Peak Performance / Optional Extension

• Consolidate rather than endlessly adding topics.

• DSA: repeat missed problems from memory; maintain a personal pattern sheet.

• System design: 10–15 canonical designs from scratch.

• CS: oral revision of C#, .NET, DB, OS, networking, distributed systems.

• Behavioral: randomized question practice.

• Applications/interviews continue. Use the month to close specific weaknesses rather than follow a fixed syllabus.

Master topic map

C#: Types; memory; OOP; interfaces; generics; collections; LINQ; delegates/events; exceptions; IDisposable; async/await; Task; threading; concurrency; GC; reflection/attributes basics; performance.

.NET / ASP.NET Core: Framework vs modern .NET; CLR/runtime/SDK; hosting; Kestrel; middleware; request pipeline; DI; configuration; logging; Web API; authentication; authorization; JWT; EF Core; background services; caching; testing.

DSA: Big-O; arrays; strings; hashing; two pointers; sliding window; stack/queue; binary search; linked lists; recursion; trees; heaps; graphs; intervals; greedy; backtracking; dynamic programming.

Databases: SQL; indexes; query plans; joins; transactions; ACID; isolation; locks; deadlocks; normalization; denormalization; replication; partitioning; SQL vs NoSQL.

Networking: DNS; TCP; TLS; HTTP/HTTPS; REST; WebSockets; SignalR; load balancers; connection lifecycle.

Distributed systems: Queues; pub/sub; caching; retries; DLQ; idempotency; ordering; consistency; replication; sharding; partitioning; rate limiting; circuit breakers; distributed locks; outbox/saga concepts; observability.

System Design: Requirements; APIs; data model; architecture; bottlenecks; scaling; cache; queue; database choice; failure handling; monitoring; trade-offs.

LLD: SOLID; composition; interfaces; Strategy; Factory; Observer; Adapter; Decorator; Builder; clean code; testability.

Engineering practice: Git; code review; testing; Docker; CI/CD; security; performance profiling; logging; metrics; deployment.

Communication: Self-introduction; explain a technical concept simply; clarify requirements; think aloud; STAR behavioral stories; concise English.

Memory system — mandatory

• Keep a one-page concept note for each major topic.

• After learning, close the material and explain it from memory.

• Use Day 1 / 3 / 7 / 14 / 30 retrieval reviews.

• Every Sunday, take a no-notes weekly test.

• Every month, take a cumulative test covering old topics.

• Keep a 'Forgotten / Weak' list. Anything you miss returns to the next review cycle.

• For important concepts, implement a tiny example and explain one real production use case.

• Do not measure progress by videos watched. Measure: problems solved, concepts recalled, designs completed, project milestones, and mock performance.

DSA rule

Do not chase a problem count. Aim for pattern recognition. For every problem record: brute force, optimized idea, why it works, time complexity, space complexity, and one variation. Re-solve missed problems after 1, 3, 7, and 14 days.

System Design rule

Never memorize a diagram. For every design: clarify requirements → estimate scale → define APIs → choose data model → propose architecture → identify bottlenecks → add cache/queue/scaling → discuss failures and consistency → explain trade-offs.

Project: Distributed Job Processing Platform

• ASP.NET Core API for submitting and querying jobs.

• PostgreSQL for durable job metadata.

• Queue for asynchronous processing.

• Multiple workers for horizontal scaling.

• Redis for caching/rate limiting where appropriate.

• Retries with backoff and dead-letter handling.

• Idempotency and duplicate-message handling.

• Priority and worker concurrency controls.

• Authentication/authorization.

• Structured logs, metrics, health checks and failure simulation.

• Docker + CI/CD + AWS deployment.

• Load testing and a written performance/architecture report.

Weekly test template

• Explain 5 concepts without notes.

• Solve 2 DSA problems under time pressure.

• Explain 1 system design for 10–15 minutes.

• Implement 1 small C# example from memory.

• Speak for 2 minutes about one technical topic in English.

• Write down 3 things you forgot and schedule them for review.

Definition of 'ready to apply'

You do not need to know everything. Begin applying in Month 6 when you can consistently solve common medium DSA patterns, explain core C#/.NET/DB/networking concepts, complete a 45-minute system design conversation, explain your project deeply, and answer behavioral questions using real experience. Months 6–8 are intentionally both learning and interview periods.

Compact version of the plan

6–8 months | 2 hours Mon–Fri + full weekends. M1: C#/.NET foundations + DSA basics. M2: advanced C#/.NET + SQL + concurrency. M3: OS + networking + databases + queues + first system design. M4: LLD + distributed systems + start serious project. M5: finish/deploy project + advanced system design + behavioral. M6: interview launch + timed DSA/design + mocks + applications. M7: analyze interviews + advanced distributed systems + company-specific preparation. M8: optional consolidation and interview conversion. Use active recall and 1/3/7/14/30-day spaced reviews throughout.

F01 — 01_PROJECT_BLUEPRINT_DISTRIBUTED_AI_ENGINE

Full source content: FAANG-Master-Plan/01_PROJECT_BLUEPRINT_DISTRIBUTED_AI_ENGINE.md. Original wording is retained below. For conflicting statements, use the visible correction and the current execution plan.

Project correction: target/benchmark values are goals until measured. Implement atomic database-local effect plus deduplication where possible; downstream idempotency or reconciliation is required for external effects. A marker alone is not an exactly-once guarantee. Use .NET 10 LTS for a new study project, or confirm the target employer’s runtime; the old .NET 8 references are preserved.

🛠️ Portfolio Showcase Project: Distributed Fault-Tolerant Job & AI Task Engine

Project Title: NexusQueue — High-Throughput Distributed Task Engine with Resilience, Concurrency Control & AI Task Processing

Tech Stack: C# / .NET 8 / ASP.NET Core Web API, PostgreSQL (Durable Storage + pgvector), Redis (Distributed Locks + Caching), RabbitMQ / AWS SQS (Message Broker), Docker, Kubernetes (KEDA), Prometheus & Grafana, Semantic Kernel.

1. Why This Project? (Why Not Another CRUD App?)

FAANG interviewers see thousands of generic Todo apps, E-commerce storefronts, and basic CRUD APIs. They immediately dismiss them.

This project is deliberately engineered to prove SDE-2 Seniority by solving the exact distributed systems problems tested in System Design interviews:

1. Asynchronous Decoupling & Queueing (Handling traffic spikes without crashing).

2. Horizontal Worker Auto-Scaling (Using Kubernetes and KEDA based on queue depth).

3. Idempotency & Deduplication (Handling network retries and duplicate message deliveries).

4. Distributed Concurrency & Locks (Preventing race conditions using Redis Redlock / distributed mutexes).

5. Dead-Letter Queues (DLQ) & Exponential Backoff with Jitter (Handling poison pills and transient failures).

6. Modern AI Task Integration (RAG with pgvector) (Demonstrating high-value production AI engineering skills).

7. Production Observability & Load Testing (Prometheus metrics, structured logging, and k6 benchmark reports reaching 5,000+ RPS).

Study correction: Treat benchmark figures in source plans as proposed targets/examples, not measured achievements. Record hardware, workload, errors, percentile latency and date before claiming a result.

2. Project Architecture Diagram


graph TD

    Client[Web / Mobile Clients] -->|REST / gRPC| LB[NGINX / K8s Ingress]

    LB --> API1[ASP.NET Core API - Pod 1]

    LB --> API2[ASP.NET Core API - Pod 2]





    API1 -->|Idempotency Check & Rate Limit| Redis[(Redis Cluster)]

    API1 -->|Write Job Metadata State: PENDING| Postgres[(PostgreSQL DB)]

    API1 -->|Publish Job Message| Queue[RabbitMQ / AWS SQS]





    Queue -->|Consume Task| Worker1[Worker Pod 1]

    Queue -->|Consume Task| Worker2[Worker Pod 2]

    Queue -->|Consume Task| WorkerN[Worker Pod N - Auto-scaled by KEDA]





    Worker1 -->|Distributed Lock / Token Bucket| Redis

    Worker1 -->|Execute AI RAG / Document Embeddings| SemanticKernel[Semantic Kernel + OpenAI/Local LLM]

    Worker1 -->|Store & Query Vector Embeddings| PgVector[(PostgreSQL + pgvector)]

    Worker1 -->|Update State: COMPLETED / FAILED| Postgres

    Worker1 -->|Poison Pill after 3 retries| DLQ[Dead Letter Queue]





    API1 -->|Prometheus Metrics: Latency, QPS| Prometheus[Prometheus]

    Worker1 -->|Queue Lag, Error Rates| Prometheus

    Prometheus --> Grafana[Grafana Dashboard]

3. When to Build It: 5-Phase Project Timeline

You do NOT build the project all at once while ignoring DSA. You build it iteratively in structured weekend modules:


┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐

│                        PROJECT MILESTONE SCHEDULE                      │

├───────────────┬───────────────┬───────────────┬────────────────────────┤

│ WEEKS 11 – 13 │ WEEKS 14 – 16 │ WEEKS 17 – 18 │ WEEKS 19 – 20          │

│ Phase 1: Core │ Phase 2: Dist │ Phase 3: AI & │ Phase 4: K8s, Metrics  │

│ API & Queue   │ Locks & DLQ   │ Vector RAG    │ & Load Benchmark       │

└───────────────┴───────────────┴───────────────┴────────────────────────┘

🔹 Phase 1: Core Ingestion API & Queue Decoupling (Weeks 11–13)

• What You Build:

1. ASP.NET Core 8 Web API with Clean Architecture / Vertical Slice Architecture.

2. Endpoints: POST /api/v1/jobs (Enqueue job), GET /api/v1/jobs/{id} (Check status).

3. PostgreSQL schema for Job metadata: Id (UUID), JobType, Payload (JSONB), Status (Pending, Processing, Completed, Failed), RetryCount, CreatedAt, UpdatedAt.

4. RabbitMQ exchange and queue bindings using MassTransit or raw RabbitMQ.Client in C#.

5. Background Worker Service (BackgroundService / IHostedService) consuming messages from the queue.

🔹 Phase 2: Distributed Resilience & Concurrency (Weeks 14–16)

• What You Build:

1. Idempotency Interceptor: Check Idempotency-Key header against Redis with TTL. If key exists, return cached response; otherwise acquire lock and proceed.

2. Distributed Locking: Implement distributed mutual exclusion using Redis (SETNX / RedLock) so multiple workers never process the same tenant resource simultaneously.

3. Resilience Policy (Polly): Exponential backoff with jitter on transient failures ($2^n \times \text{base} + \text{jitter}$).

4. Poison Pill Isolation: After 3 failed attempts, route message to a dedicated Dead-Letter Queue (DLQ) and record failure root cause in PostgreSQL.

🔹 Phase 3: High-Value AI Task Pipeline (Weeks 17–18)

• What You Build:

1. Add an AI task type: DOCUMENT_INDEXING_AND_RAG.

2. Integrate Microsoft Semantic Kernel in C#.

3. Worker extracts document text, chunks into overlapping passages (500 tokens with 50-token overlap).

4. Generate vector embeddings using OpenAI API or local Ollama/HuggingFace embeddings model.

5. Store embeddings in PostgreSQL with the pgvector extension using HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) index.

6. Endpoint: POST /api/v1/jobs/query performing cosine similarity semantic search and augmented context synthesis.

🔹 Phase 4: Containerization, Kubernetes & Production Observability (Weeks 19–20)

• What You Build:

1. Multi-stage Dockerfile producing a lean, production-grade ~90MB container image.

2. docker-compose.yml orchestrating API + Worker + PostgreSQL + Redis + RabbitMQ.

3. Kubernetes Deployment manifests:

* Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps, Secrets, Liveness & Readiness probes.

* Configure KEDA (Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling) to auto-scale Worker Pods from 1 to 10 instances based on RabbitMQ queue depth!

4. Prometheus metrics export (/metrics) exposing:

* Ingestion RPS, P95/P99 latency, active queue length, worker processing time, DLQ failure count.

5. Grafana Dashboard visualizing real-time throughput.

🔹 Phase 5: Load Testing & Performance Benchmark Defense (Week 20)

• What You Build:

1. Write a k6 load testing script simulating 5,000 requests per second.

2. Benchmark the system under failure: intentionally kill a worker pod or disconnect Redis to prove zero message loss.

3. Write a 2-page GitHub README architecture defense containing:

* System Architecture Diagram.

* Scale & Capacity Calculations.

* Bottlenecks Identified & Fixed (e.g. PgBouncer connection pooling, Redis index optimization).

* Benchmark charts proving P99 latency $< 45\text{ms}$.

Study correction: Treat benchmark figures in source plans as proposed targets/examples, not measured achievements. Record hardware, workload, errors, percentile latency and date before claiming a result.

4. How to Talk About This Project in FAANG Interviews

In SDE-2 System Design and Resume rounds, you will guide the interviewer to this project:

*"In my personal system, NexusQueue, I designed a distributed task platform capable of handling thousands of background operations and AI pipelines asynchronously. The core architectural challenge was ensuring exactly-once processing semantics over an at-least-once message broker. I solved this by implementing distributed locks via Redis SETNX combined with database-level idempotency keys. Under load testing at 5,000 RPS, we observed database connection exhaustion, which I resolved by introducing PgBouncer connection pooling and tuning worker batch sizes, maintaining a P99 latency under 45ms even during simulated worker node crashes."*
Study correction: Treat benchmark figures in source plans as proposed targets/examples, not measured achievements. Record hardware, workload, errors, percentile latency and date before claiming a result.

This level of explanation immediately demonstrates Senior SDE-2 competence.

10. What to deliberately ignore

Saying no is part of the strategy. Each of these is either paid, redundant, or an active time sink for your situation.

Skip Why
Paid courses (Educative, Interview Kickstart, AlgoExpert, Scaler) Everything above covers the same ground free. Documented cases exist of free-only preparation reaching the same outcomes

A note on books

Two books are worth owning if you ever choose to spend money, and only these two: Designing Data-Intensive Applications (Kleppmann) and System Design Interview Vol 1 (Alex Xu). S10 — 10_Project_Distributed_Job_Platform_Spec

Full source content: Study-Plan/10_Project_Distributed_Job_Platform_Spec.docx. Original wording is retained below. For conflicting statements, use the visible correction and the current execution plan.

Project correction: target/benchmark values are goals until measured. Implement atomic database-local effect plus deduplication where possible; downstream idempotency or reconciliation is required for external effects. A marker alone is not an exactly-once guarantee. Use .NET 10 LTS for a new study project, or confirm the target employer’s runtime; the old .NET 8 references are preserved.

Project Specification - Distributed Job Processing Platform

Document 10 - Built across Months 4 and 5. Your primary engineering artefact.

Why this project

A CRUD API proves you can use a framework. This project proves you can reason about failure, concurrency, scale and trade-offs - which is exactly what an SDE II or L4/L5 interview is trying to establish.

It is also deliberately close to work you have already done. Your Casepoint email-processing pipeline using SES, EventBridge and SQS is the same shape of problem. That is not a coincidence - it means you can build this fluently and defend it from genuine experience rather than tutorial memory.

The one-sentence pitch (memorise this)

A multi-tenant distributed job processing platform in .NET that accepts job submissions over HTTP, durably persists them, distributes them to horizontally scalable workers via a queue, and guarantees each job completes exactly once despite worker crashes, duplicate deliveries and downstream failures.

Non-negotiable requirements

If any of these are missing, the project has not done its job. Build against this list, not against what feels comfortable.

Capability Must demonstrate
Durable submission Job survives an API restart between submission and processing
Asynchronous processing Real queue, real separate worker process. Not an in-memory BackgroundService pretending
Horizontal scaling Run 1 worker, then 4. Throughput must measurably increase. With numbers
Crash recovery Kill a worker mid-job. The job must be recovered and completed, not lost
Idempotency Deliver the same message twice. The job must execute once
Retries Exponential backoff with jitter, bounded attempts
Dead letter queue Poison messages land in a DLQ, are inspectable, and can be replayed
Priority High-priority jobs preempt a backlog of low-priority jobs
Fairness One tenant flooding the queue must not starve others
Rate limiting Correct across multiple API instances, not per-instance
Multi-tenancy Tenant A provably cannot read or affect tenant B's jobs
Observability Structured logs with correlation IDs, metrics, health checks
Deployment Docker, CI/CD, running on AWS
Evidence Load test results with p50/p95/p99, and a written bottleneck analysis

Architecture

Components

Component Responsibility
API service (ASP.NET Core) Job submission, status queries, DLQ inspection and replay, auth, rate limiting
Worker service (.NET worker) Consumes from the queue, executes handlers, manages state transitions, heartbeats
PostgreSQL Durable job metadata, state, attempt history, idempotency keys, outbox
Queue (SQS in AWS; RabbitMQ locally) Work distribution, visibility timeout, DLQ
Redis Status read cache, distributed rate limiting, worker registry
Prometheus + Grafana Metrics and dashboards

Job state machine

Define this explicitly and enforce illegal transitions in code. Interviewers ask about it.

State Transitions to
Pending Queued (on successful enqueue), Cancelled
Queued Running (worker claims it), Cancelled
Running Completed, Failed, Retrying, Orphaned (heartbeat lost)
Retrying Queued (after backoff), DeadLettered (attempts exhausted)
Orphaned Queued (reclaimed by the reaper)
Failed DeadLettered
Completed / Cancelled / DeadLettered Terminal

The three hard problems (and your answers)

Problem Your solution
Duplicate delivery. The queue guarantees at-least-once, so the same message will eventually arrive twice Idempotency key per job. A processed_jobs table with a unique constraint. Worker attempts an insert first; a unique-violation means already processed, so acknowledge and skip
Worker crash mid-job. The job is Running but nobody is running it Worker heartbeats every N seconds. A reaper process finds Running jobs whose heartbeat is stale past a threshold, transitions them to Orphaned, then re-queues. Combined with idempotency, a job that actually completed before the crash will not re-run its side effects
Dual write. You must both save the job and enqueue the message, and either can fail Transactional outbox: write job and outbox row in one DB transaction, then a relay publishes from the outbox and marks it sent. At-least-once publish, made safe by idempotency

These three answers are the heart of your interview story. Be able to draw each failure on a whiteboard and explain exactly where your design catches it.

Build phases

Phase 1 - Walking skeleton (Month 4, Week 16)

• Solution structure: Api, Worker, Contracts, Infrastructure, plus test projects.

• Docker Compose: Postgres, Redis, RabbitMQ.

• POST /jobs persists a job as Pending; GET /jobs/{id} returns status.

• EF Core schema and migrations. Job entity, state enum, attempt count.

• Enqueue on submit, worker consumes, transitions Running then Completed.

• Serilog structured logging with a correlation ID flowing API to worker.

• Health check endpoints. README started with an architecture diagram.

Phase 2 - Reliability (Month 5, Week 17)

• Retry policy: exponential backoff with jitter, configurable max attempts.

• Dead letter queue with an inspection endpoint and a replay endpoint.

• Idempotency keys and the processed_jobs dedup table.

• Transactional outbox with a relay.

• Worker heartbeats and the orphan reaper.

• Job priority with a priority-aware consumer.

• Per-tenant fairness (round-robin or weighted).

• Failure simulation documented: kill worker, kill DB, flood queue, add latency.

Phase 3 - Production concerns (Month 5, Week 18)

• Redis cache-aside for status reads, with correct invalidation on state change.

• Distributed rate limiting (token bucket in Redis), 429 with Retry-After.

• Authentication, plus tenant isolation with a test proving cross-tenant denial.

• Prometheus metrics: submitted, completed, failed, queue depth, duration histogram.

• Grafana dashboard.

• Liveness vs readiness probes, correctly distinguished.

• Integration tests with Testcontainers against real Postgres and Redis.

Phase 4 - Ship and prove (Month 5, Week 19)

• Multi-stage Dockerfiles, non-root user, image size optimised and measured.

• GitHub Actions: build, test, lint on PR; image push on merge.

• AWS: ECS or EC2, RDS Postgres, ElastiCache Redis, real SQS, IAM least privilege, billing alarm.

• k6 load tests: baseline, ramp, sustained, spike.

• Scale workers 1 to 4, re-measure, prove horizontal scaling with numbers.

• Written performance and architecture report committed to the repo.

The README - treated as a deliverable, not an afterthought

Many interviewers will read your README and never run your code. It is the artefact, and it should be written from Week 16, not bolted on in Week 19.

Section Content
One-paragraph pitch The memorised sentence from page 1
Architecture diagram Excalidraw, embedded as an image
Why this exists The problem it solves. Not "a demo project"
Design decisions Each with the alternative you rejected and why
Failure modes table Failure, detection, response, observed behaviour
Performance results Load test numbers, p50/p95/p99, throughput at 1 vs 4 workers
Bottleneck analysis Where it breaks, why, evidenced
Trade-offs and limitations Be honest. Stating a known limitation is a senior signal
What I would do next Shows you know where the edges are
How to run it docker compose up and it works. Test this on a clean machine

Interview questions you must be able to answer about it

• Why a queue rather than direct processing? What did that cost you?

• What happens if a worker dies mid-job? Walk me through the recovery, second by second.

• How do you guarantee exactly-once processing on an at-least-once queue?

• Why Postgres and not a NoSQL store? What would change if jobs were 100x larger?

• How would you handle a job that takes six hours?

• Your queue backs up to a million messages. What breaks first, and what do you do?

• How would you make this multi-region?

• Where is your bottleneck, and how do you know? (Have the numbers ready.)

• What would you do differently if you started again?

• How would you add a job that depends on another job completing first?

Rehearse all ten out loud. They are the most likely questions and the answers should be fluent, not constructed on the spot.

Scope discipline

The project must be finished by the end of Month 5 because Months 6-8 belong to interviewing. Two rules protect that:

• No new features after Week 19. Polish and documentation only.

• When you are tempted to add something, ask whether it demonstrates a distributed-systems property you cannot already demonstrate. A React admin dashboard does not. A saga across two services might - and still probably is not worth the time.

📖 Master Curriculum Encyclopedia (CodeWithShubham & CodeLLDWithShubham Integration)

This encyclopedia integrates every single branch, sub-pattern, design pattern, and algorithm from your reference mindmaps:

• CodeLLDWithShubham Mindmap: OOP Fundamentals, 5 Class Relationships, 8 Design Principles, 5 SOLID Principles, 5 UML Diagrams, and all 23 Gang of Four (GoF) Design Patterns.

• DSA Patterns (CodeWithShubham) Mindmap: Arrays, Strings (KMP, Rabin-Karp), Stacks, Queues, Linked Lists, Recursion & Backtracking, Trees (Views, Traversals, BST), Heaps, Graphs (Shortest Paths, Topo Sort, DSU, Bipartite), Trie, DP (1D, Knapsack, LCS, LIS, Grid, MCM), Greedy, Bit Manipulation, all 8 Sorting Algorithms, and Range Queries (Segment & Fenwick Trees).

🏛️ PART 1: Low-Level Design (LLD) Complete Breakdown

1. OOP Fundamentals

• Classes & Objects: Blueprints, memory instantiation on heap vs stack in C#, object lifecycle.

• Constructors: Default, parameterized, copy constructors, static constructors in C#, constructor chaining (this(), base()).

• Encapsulation: Data hiding, information hiding, getters/setters, properties with backing fields.

• Abstraction: Hiding implementation complexity, exposing essential contracts via interfaces and abstract base classes.

• Inheritance: is-a relationship, single vs multiple interface inheritance in C#, virtual, override, new keywords.

• Polymorphism:

* Compile-time (Static): Method overloading, operator overloading.

* Runtime (Dynamic): Method overriding via virtual method table (vtable).

• Abstract Classes: Partial implementation, abstract methods, when to use vs interfaces.

• Access Modifiers: public, private, protected, internal, protected internal, private protected.

• Static: Static classes, static methods, static constructors, static fields (thread safety considerations).

• Enums: Strongly typed constants, flags enums ([Flags]), underlying types (byte, int).

2. Class Relationships (UML Notations & Semantics)

• Association (-->): General uses-a relationship between two independent classes (e.g., Order uses EmailService).

• Dependency (..>): Weakest relationship; one class depends on another as a method parameter or local variable (temporary interaction).

• Aggregation (◇--): has-a relationship with weak ownership (Whole-Part). The child can exist independently of the parent (e.g., Department has Professors; if department dissolves, professors still exist).

• Composition (◆--): has-a relationship with strong ownership. The child's lifetime is bound to the parent's lifetime (e.g., House and Rooms; destroying the house destroys the rooms).

• Realization (..▷): Interface implementation or abstract contract realization (class Car : IVehicle).

3. Core Design Principles

• DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself): Extract reusable logic; single source of truth for business rules.

• KISS (Keep It Simple, Stupid): Avoid premature optimization; prefer simple, readable code over clever one-liners.

• YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It): Implement only what is currently required; avoid building speculative features.

• Separation of Concerns (SoC): Break software into distinct sections where each section addresses a separate concern (e.g., Presentation vs Business Logic vs Data Access).

• Coupling (Loose vs Tight): Measure of dependency between modules. Aim for loose coupling via interfaces.

• Cohesion (High vs Low): Measure of how strongly related the responsibilities inside a single class are. Aim for high cohesion (a class does one cohesive job).

• Composition Over Inheritance: Prefer composing objects with interfaces rather than inheriting deep hierarchies (avoids fragile base class problem).

• Law of Demeter (Principle of Least Knowledge): A method of an object should only call methods belonging to: its own class, parameters passed in, objects it instantiated, or its direct member fields. Don't chain calls like a.GetB().GetC().DoSomething().

4. SOLID Principles (The 5 Pillars)

1. SRP (Single Responsibility Principle): A class should have only one reason to change. Separate domain entities from persistence, formatting, and validation.

2. OCP (Open-Closed Principle): Software entities should be open for extension, but closed for modification. Implement new behavior by adding new classes/strategies, not modifying existing tested code.

3. LSP (Liskov Substitution Principle): Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types without altering program correctness (e.g., classic Rectangle vs Square violation).

4. ISP (Interface Segregation Principle): Clients should not be forced to depend on interfaces they do not use. Split fat interfaces into smaller, cohesive role interfaces (IReadable, IWritable rather than IReadWriteAdminSuperService).

5. DIP (Dependency Inversion Principle): High-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions. Abstractions should not depend on details; details should depend on abstractions (Dependency Injection).

5. UML Diagrams for Interviews

• Class Diagram: Visualizing classes, fields, methods, access modifiers (+, -, #), and relationships (Inheritance, Composition, Aggregation, Dependency).

• Use Case Diagram: Actors, system boundaries, use cases, <<include>> and <<extend>> relationships.

• Sequence Diagram: Chronological interaction between objects over time; lifelines, synchronous messages, asynchronous calls, return messages, activation bars.

• Activity Diagram: Workflow and business logic flowchart; decision diamonds, fork/join parallel nodes.

• State Machine Diagram: States, transitions, events, guards, actions (critical for designing Elevators, Vending Machines, Order fulfillment).

6. All 23 Gang of Four (GoF) Design Patterns

A. Creational Patterns (5)

1. Singleton: Ensures a class has only one instance, with a global access point. In C#: Thread-safe double-checked locking or Lazy<T>.

2. Builder: Separates the construction of a complex object from its representation (e.g., fluent query builder, complex document generator).

3. Factory Method: Defines an interface for creating an object, but lets subclasses decide which class to instantiate.

4. Abstract Factory: Creates families of related or dependent objects without specifying their concrete classes (e.g., DarkTheme vs LightTheme UI components).

5. Prototype: Creates new objects by cloning an existing instance (in C#: ICloneable or memberwise clone).

B. Behavioral Patterns (10)

1. Strategy: Defines a family of algorithms, encapsulates each one, and makes them interchangeable at runtime (e.g., Payment strategies, Pricing rules).

2. Iterator: Provides a way to access elements of an aggregate object sequentially without exposing its underlying representation (IEnumerator<T> in C#).

3. Command: Encapsulates a request as an object, thereby letting you parameterize clients with different requests, queue or log requests, and support undo/redo.

4. Observer: Defines a one-to-many dependency so that when one object changes state, all its dependents are notified automatically (Event-driven architectures).

5. State: Allows an object to alter its behavior when its internal state changes (e.g., Elevator: IdleState, MovingUpState, MovingDownState).

6. Template Method: Defines the skeleton of an algorithm in a method, deferring some steps to subclasses without changing algorithm structure.

7. Chain of Responsibility: Passes a request along a chain of handlers. Each handler decides either to process the request or pass it to the next handler (e.g., ASP.NET Core Middleware pipeline).

8. Visitor: Separates an algorithm from the object structure on which it operates (e.g., Tax calculation across different product types).

9. Mediator: Defines an object that encapsulates how a set of objects interact, preventing direct dependencies between them (e.g., MediatR library in .NET, Air Traffic Controller).

10. Memento: Captures and externalizes an object's internal state so the object can be restored to this state later (Undo/Redo checkpoints).

C. Structural Patterns (8)

1. Adapter: Converts the interface of a class into another interface clients expect (wrapping legacy APIs or third-party SDKs).

2. Facade: Provides a simplified, unified high-level interface to a complex subsystem.

3. Decorator: Attaches additional responsibilities to an object dynamically without subclass explosion (e.g., CachingDecorator, LoggingDecorator around repositories).

4. Composite: Composes objects into tree structures to represent part-whole hierarchies. Lets clients treat individual objects and compositions uniformly (e.g., File System folders and files).

5. Proxy: Provides a surrogate or placeholder for another object to control access to it (e.g., Virtual Proxy for lazy loading, Remote Proxy, Protection Proxy).

6. Bridge: Decouples an abstraction from its implementation so that the two can vary independently (e.g., Shape and Color hierarchies).

7. Flyweight: Reduces memory footprint by sharing common state among multiple fine-grained objects (e.g., Character glyph rendering in text editors, game particle systems).

⚡ PART 2: Data Structures & Algorithms (DSA) Complete Breakdown

1. Array Patterns

• Kadane’s Algorithm: Max Subarray Sum, Max Product Subarray (tracking min & max), Circular Subarray Sum (Max of normal subarray vs TotalSum - MinSubarray).

• Prefix Sum: 1D Prefix Sum, 2D Prefix Sum (Matrix range queries), Subarray Sum Equals K (Map<sum - k, count>).

• Two Pointers: Opposite Ends, Fast and Slow (Reader-Writer), 3Sum (duplicate skipping logic), 4Sum, Container With Most Water, Trapping Rain Water.

• Dutch National Flag: 3-way partition (low, mid, high) sorting 0, 1, 2 in $O(N)$ single pass.

• Sliding Window: Fixed size, Variable size, At Most $K$ difference technique.

• Intervals & Matrix: Merge Intervals, Insert Interval, Non-Overlapping Intervals, Spiral Matrix, Rotate Image.

2. String Patterns

• Two Pointers / Palindromes: Valid Palindrome, Longest Palindromic Substring (expand around center vs DP).

• Sliding Window on Strings: Longest Substring Without Repeating Characters, Minimum Window Substring, Find All Anagrams in a String.

• Pattern Matching Algorithms:

* KMP (Knuth-Morris-Pratt): Precomputing the Longest Prefix Suffix (LPS) array in $O(M)$ time to search patterns in $O(N)$ time without backtracking.

* Rabin-Karp: Rolling hash matching.

* Z-Algorithm: Constructing the Z-array in $O(N)$ linear time.

• String Hashing & Frequency: Group Anagrams (Prime hashing vs sorted key).

3. Stack Patterns

• Monotonic Stack: Next Greater Element I & II, Previous Smaller Element, Largest Rectangle in Histogram ($O(N)$ height expansion), Daily Temperatures.

• Balanced Parentheses: Valid Parentheses, Minimum Remove to Make Valid Parentheses, Longest Valid Parentheses.

• Min Stack: $O(1)$ GetMin() using auxiliary min-stack or value encoding (2 * val - min).

• Expression Evaluation: Infix to Postfix conversion, Evaluating Reverse Polish Notation (RPN), Basic Calculator I & II.

4. Queue Patterns

• Circular Queue: Ring buffer array implementation with head and tail pointers.

• Monotonic Deque: Sliding Window Maximum ($O(N)$ double-ended queue).

• Queue using Stacks & Stack using Queues: Amortized $O(1)$ push/pop mechanisms.

5. Linked List Patterns

• Reversals: Iterative reversal, Recursive reversal, Reverse Linked List II (between $m$ and $n$), Reverse Nodes in k-Group.

• Fast & Slow Pointers: Middle of Linked List, Detect Cycle, Find Cycle Origin (Floyd’s Tortoise and Hare proof).

• Merging: Merge Two Sorted Lists, Merge K Sorted Lists (Min-Heap approach in $O(N \log K)$).

• Pointer Mutation: Remove Nth Node From End of List, Reorder List, Palindrome Linked List.

• Doubly Linked List: Implementing an LRU Cache & LFU Cache in $O(1)$ time.

6. Recursion & Backtracking Patterns

• Subsets & Subsequences: Subsets I (distinct elements), Subsets II (handling duplicates with sorting and skip loop).

• Combinations: Combination Sum I, II, III.

• Permutations: Permutations I, Permutations II (swap in-place vs visited array).

• Board & Matrix Backtracking: Word Search, Rat in a Maze, N-Queens (validating diagonals and columns), Sudoku Solver.

7. Tree Patterns

• Traversals: Inorder, Preorder, Postorder (Recursive + Iterative using Stack), Level Order (BFS), Zigzag Level Order, Boundary Traversal.

• Tree Views: Top View (Horizontal distance tracking), Bottom View, Left View, Right View.

• Tree DP (Bottom-Up): Maximum Depth, Diameter of Binary Tree, Balanced Binary Tree, Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum, Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA).

• Construction & Serialization: Construct from Inorder + Preorder, Construct from Inorder + Postorder, Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree.

• Binary Search Tree (BST): Validate BST (passing down valid range bounds), Kth Smallest Element, Inorder Successor, LCA of BST, Convert Sorted Array to BST.

8. Heap / Priority Queue Patterns

• Min-Heap & Max-Heap Basics: Array representation (parent = (i-1)/2, left = 2i+1, right = 2i+2), Heapify operations.

• Top-K Elements: Kth Largest Element in an Array, Top K Frequent Elements.

• Two Heaps Pattern: Find Median from Data Stream (balancing sizes of Max-Heap and Min-Heap).

• K-Way Merge: Merge K Sorted Lists, Smallest Range Covering Elements from K Lists.

9. Graph Patterns

• Representations: Adjacency Matrix vs Adjacency List.

• BFS & DFS: Number of Islands, Max Area of Island, Rotting Oranges (Multi-source BFS), Clone Graph.

• Cycle Detection:

* Undirected: BFS/DFS with parent pointer, or Disjoint Set Union (DSU).

* Directed: 3-Coloring DFS (0 = Unvisited, 1 = Visiting in current path, 2 = Completely visited).

• Topological Sort (DAG): Kahn’s Algorithm (In-degree queue), Course Schedule I & II, Alien Dictionary.

• Shortest Path Algorithms:

* Unweighted: Standard BFS ($O(V + E)$).

* Non-Negative Weighted: Dijkstra’s with Min-Heap ($O((V + E) \log V)$).

* Negative Weights: Bellman-Ford (detecting negative cycles in $O(V \cdot E)$).

* All-Pairs Shortest Path: Floyd-Warshall ($O(V^3)$).

• Disjoint Set Union (DSU / Union-Find): Path Compression + Union by Rank ($O(\alpha(N))$), Number of Connected Components, Redundant Connection, Kruskal’s Minimum Spanning Tree (MST).

• Bipartite Graph: 2-Coloring via BFS/DFS (Is Graph Bipartite?).

• Strongly Connected Components (SCC): Kosaraju’s Algorithm (2-pass DFS with transposed graph) & Tarjan’s Algorithm.

10. Trie Patterns

• Prefix Tree: Insert, Search, StartsWith in $O(L)$ time.

• Applications: Word Search II (Trie + Backtracking grid search), Search Suggestions System.

• Bitwise Trie: Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array ($O(32N)$ time).

11. Dynamic Programming Patterns

• 1D Linear State: Fibonacci, Climbing Stairs, House Robber I & II, Decode Ways.

• 0/1 Knapsack: Subset Sum, Partition Equal Subset Sum, Target Sum (traversing capacity backwards).

• Unbounded Knapsack: Coin Change I & II, Rod Cutting (traversing capacity forwards).

• Longest Common Subsequence (LCS): LCS, Edit Distance, Longest Palindromic Subsequence, Shortest Common Supersequence.

• Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS): $O(N^2)$ DP table and $O(N \log N)$ Binary Search using Patience Sorting / Tails array.

• Grid DP: Unique Paths I & II, Minimum Path Sum, Cherry Pickup.

• Interval DP & MCM: Matrix Chain Multiplication, Burst Balloons, Palindrome Partitioning II.

• DP on Trees & Bitmask DP: Tree independent sets, Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP) on small $N \le 16$.

12. Greedy Patterns

• Interval Scheduling: Activity Selection, Non-overlapping Intervals, Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons.

• Array Greedy: Jump Game I (maximum reachable index) & Jump Game II, Gas Station (circular greedy balance).

13. Bit Manipulation Patterns

• XOR Invariants: $a \oplus a = 0$, $a \oplus 0 = a$. Single Number I, II (bit counters modulo 3), and III (isolating lowest set bit diff & -diff).

• Bitwise Tricks: Checking if $K$-th bit is set, Brian Kernighan’s Algorithm for counting set bits (n = n & (n - 1)), Checking Power of 2 (n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0), Reverse Bits.

14. All 8 Sorting Algorithms

• Comparison Sorts:

* Bubble Sort: $O(N^2)$ adjacent swaps with early-exit flag.

* Selection Sort: $O(N^2)$ finding minimum element in unsorted partition.

* Insertion Sort: $O(N^2)$ shifting elements; near $O(N)$ for almost-sorted arrays.

* Merge Sort: $O(N \log N)$ divide-and-conquer; stable; requires $O(N)$ auxiliary memory.

* Quick Sort: $O(N \log N)$ average, $O(N^2)$ worst case; in-place; partitioning schemes (Lomuto vs Hoare).

* Heap Sort: $O(N \log N)$ in-place using Max-Heap; unstable.

• Non-Comparison Sorts:

* Counting Sort: $O(N + K)$ non-comparison sorting for bounded integer keys.

* Radix Sort: $O(D \cdot (N + K))$ digit-by-digit sorting using Counting Sort as a stable subroutine.

15. Advanced Range Queries (Segment & Fenwick Trees)

• Segment Tree:

* Complete binary tree over an array supporting Range Sum / Range Minimum Query and Point Updates in $O(\log N)$ time.

* Lazy Propagation for Range Updates in $O(\log N)$.

• Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree - BIT):

* Space-efficient array-based tree using two's complement lowest set bit (i & -i) for Prefix Sum queries and Point Updates in $O(\log N)$ time with minimal code.

Full source content: Study-Plan/TRACKER.xlsx. Original wording is retained below. For conflicting statements, use the visible correction and the current execution plan.

Sheet: START

B1 Software Engineer Transformation - Tracker
B2 Open this every day. It is the only file you need to know what to do.
B4 START DATE (a Monday)
C4 2026-08-24 00:00:00
C5 Change that one yellow cell and every date in the whole workbook moves with it. It must be a Monday.
B7 HOW TO USE THIS
B8 1. Every morning
C8 Open the DAILY tab. Press Ctrl+F, type today's date, and work that one row. That is the whole system.
B9 2. Every evening
C9 Put an x in the Done column. Add anything you could not recall to the WEAK tab. Write one line in the JOURNAL tab.
B10 3. Every Friday
C10 No new material. Work only the WEAK tab - the items with the oldest dates first.
B11 4. Every Sunday
C11 Take the weekly test (6 tasks, listed below). Then read next week's row in the WEEKS tab.
B12 5. Every month end
C12 Fill one column of the DASHBOARD tab. Three numbers. Nothing else.
B14 THE DAILY 2 HOURS
B15 0:00 - 0:10
C15 Explain yesterday out loud, notes closed. Badly is fine. NEVER skip this - it is the highest-leverage habit in the plan.
B16 0:10 - 1:15
C16 Today's topic, from the DAILY tab. Short notes only.
B17 1:15 - 1:55
C17 DSA. One or two problems. Log all six fields in the DSA tab.
B18 1:55 - 2:00
C18 Weak List, journal line, tomorrow's one-line plan.
B19 Tue and Thu
C19 Add 15 minutes of aptitude at the end. That is the only variation.
B21 THE SUNDAY TEST - 6 tasks, no notes
C22 Explain 5 concepts from this week aloud, recorded
C23 Solve 2 DSA problems, 25 minutes each
C24 Talk through 1 system design for 10-15 min (from week 12)
C25 Implement 1 small C# example from memory, no IDE help
C26 Speak 2 minutes in English on one technical topic
C27 Write down 3 things you forgot - they go straight to the WEAK tab
B29 IF YOU FALL BEHIND
B30 Missed 2-3 days
C30 Ignore it. Carry on from today. Do NOT try to catch up.
B31 Missed a week
C31 Skip to the current week. Put the missed topics in the WEAK tab.
B32 Missed two weeks
C32 Same, and move the START DATE cell forward two weeks.
B33 Missed a month
C33 Restart the current month only. Never restart the plan.
B34 Too tired today
C34 The 30-minute version: 10 min recall + 15 min one DSA problem + 5 min journal. Never zero.
B36 WHAT THE TABS ARE FOR
B37 DAILY
C37 All 224 days. One row per day. This is the tab you live in.
B38 WEEKS
C38 The 32-week overview. Read one row every Sunday.
B39 WEAK
C39 Everything you got wrong. Drives every Friday. THE most important tab.
B40 DSA
C40 One row per problem, six fields. The log is where pattern recognition is built.
B41 REVIEW
C41 The 1/3/7/14/30-day ladder. Type the date you learned it; the rest calculates.
B42 DESIGNS
C42 All 18 system designs and 5 LLDs, with the week each is due.
B43 STORIES
C43 Your 20 STAR stories mapped to Amazon's 16 principles. No column may be empty.
B44 JOURNAL
C44 One line per working day. This becomes your 20 stories in month 5.
B45 APPLY
C45 Every application, with the sponsor-register and LinkedIn checks.
B46 INTERVIEWS
C46 Every interview, with a named ROOT CAUSE and a repair date.
B47 DASHBOARD
C47 Three numbers a month. The only progress measure that matters.
B49 The whole plan in one line
C49 Recall yesterday, learn one thing, solve one problem, write down what you got wrong. Repeat for eight months.

S11 — 11_Trackers_and_Templates

Full source content: Study-Plan/11_Trackers_and_Templates.docx. Original wording is retained below. For conflicting statements, use the visible correction and the current execution plan.

Trackers and Templates

Document 11 - Copy these into your working documents. Use them daily.

How to set this up

Keep it simple. One spreadsheet with several tabs, plus one notes document. Do not spend a weekend building a system - the system is not the work.

Artefact Where it lives
Master Notes One document, one page per concept, six-question frame
Weak List Spreadsheet tab. The most important tab
DSA Log Spreadsheet tab, one row per problem
Spaced Review Tracker Spreadsheet tab, driven by dates
Work Journal Plain text file, one line per working day, append only
STAR Story Bank One document, one page per story
Interview Analysis Log Spreadsheet tab, from Month 6
Application Tracker Spreadsheet tab, from Month 6

Template 1 - Master Notes (one page per concept)

Field Fill in
Concept
Date learned
What is it? One sentence, junior-developer level
Why does it exist? What problem forced its invention
Mental model The analogy or picture you use
How does it work internally? The mechanism. This is the interview level
Example Smallest code or scenario that demonstrates it
Real use from my work Casepoint, Vision, Zibma, or a project. Always fill this in
Common mistakes What people get wrong, including what you got wrong
Trade-offs What it costs. Nothing is free
When would I NOT use it? The question that proves depth
Interview questions on this Three you would expect
My own explanation Written from memory, notes closed
Review dates D1 __ / D3 __ / D7 __ / D14 __ / D30 __

Keep each page short. A page that takes 40 minutes to write and is never reread is worse than a page that takes 10 minutes and gets retrieved five times.

Template 2 - Weak List

Every failure to recall, explain or solve goes here immediately. This list drives Friday sessions and Sunday tests.

Item Added Source Attempt 1 Attempt 2 Cleared
Why .Result deadlocks 12 Sep Weekly test Failed Passed
Consistent hashing 3 Oct Recall Failed
Course Schedule II 8 Oct DSA Failed Failed

Rules: an item leaves the list only after two consecutive successful recalls at least seven days apart. If the list has not grown in two weeks, you are not testing yourself hard enough.

Template 3 - DSA log

Problem Diff Pattern Brute O Opt O Key insight Variation Re-solve
Two Sum E Hashing O(n^2) O(n) Complement lookup in a map If sorted, two pointers D1 D3 D7
Course Schedule M Topo sort - O(V+E) Cycle detection via in-degree Return the order itself D1 D3

The "key insight" column is the one that matters. If you cannot write it in one sentence, you have not understood the problem - you have only made it pass.

Template 4 - Spaced review tracker

Concept D1 D3 D7 D14 D30
async state machine 2 Sep 4 Sep 8 Sep 15 Sep 1 Oct
Isolation levels 20 Oct 22 Oct 26 Oct 2 Nov 18 Nov

Mark each cell pass or fail. A fail resets the ladder to D1 and adds the item to the Weak List.

Template 5 - Weekly test (every Sunday, no notes)

# Task Pass condition
1 Explain 5 concepts from this week, aloud, recorded Correct and coherent, no notes
2 Solve 2 DSA problems, 25 min each Working solution, complexity stated
3 Talk through 1 system design, 10-15 min (from M3) All nine steps, in order
4 Implement 1 small C# example from memory Compiles, no IDE assistance
5 Speak 2 minutes in English on one technical topic Clear, no long stalls
6 Write 3 things you forgot Added to Weak List with dates

Template 6 - Monthly cumulative test (last Sunday)

Covers everything from Month 1 onward, not just the current month. This is the test that catches silent forgetting.

# Task Pass condition
1 10 concepts, drawn randomly from all months 8 of 10 correct
2 4 DSA problems, mixed, timed 3 of 4 solved in time
3 1 full system design, 45 min Complete, with trade-offs stated
4 3 STAR stories, randomly chosen (from M5) Under 3 min, Action-heavy
5 Explain your project for 5 min (from M4) Fluent, no notes
6 The month checkpoint table from that month's document Honest yes/no on every row

Template 7 - Work journal (daily, two minutes)

Format: Date - problem - what I decided - outcome.

Date Entry
18 Aug Bulk export timing out at 50k records. Chose to batch and stream rather than raise the timeout. Cut memory use, export finished in 4 min
19 Aug Disagreed with the proposed retry-on-every-failure approach - would have hammered a failing downstream. Argued for backoff plus circuit breaker. Accepted
20 Aug Root-caused an intermittent null in the ingest path to a race on a shared dictionary. Replaced with ConcurrentDictionary

Every one of those lines is a potential STAR story. That is the entire point.

Template 8 - STAR story matrix

Rows are your stories, columns are the principles. Mark which stories serve which. Every column must have at least two marks. A column with zero marks is an interview you are going to lose.

Story Cust Obs Owner Dive Deep Bias Act Backbone Deliver
Email pipeline 80% X X X
FOIA features X X
Payment integration X X
Disagreement story X
Hard feedback story

Extend the columns to all 16 principles. Build this in Month 5 Week 20.

Template 9 - Interview analysis log (from Month 6, within 24 hours)

Company Round Result What went badly Root cause Repair scheduled
(example) DSA Rejected Stalled 20 min on the approach Did not recognise monotonic stack Re-drill monotonic stack, 3 Nov

The root cause column is the only one that matters. "Did badly" is not a root cause. "Did not recognise the pattern", "knew it but could not explain it aloud", "ran out of time on requirements", "froze when challenged" - those are root causes, and each has a different repair.

Template 10 - Application tracker

Company Role Applied Referral Stage Next action Date
(example) SDE II 5 Nov Yes Phone screen Prepare LP stories 12 Nov

Rule: 2-3 applications per week, every week, from Week 21 onward. A pipeline that empties while you wait on one company is the most common self-inflicted delay in a job search.

The progress dashboard

Update monthly. These are the only numbers worth tracking.

Metric M2 M4 M6 M8

Problems re-solved from memory
Concepts passing the D30 review

Note what is not on this list: hours studied, videos watched, pages read, tutorials completed. Those measure input. Every metric above measures output, which is the only thing an interview can observe.

Every foundation prompt with an added answer or practice outline

Every foundation prompt with an added answer or practice outline

Start here · All questions · Every topic

Read one question/section, close it, and explain it from memory. Reading alone does not mark a coding/design exercise complete. Every original source block has a stable ID for coverage and links. Original schedules are retained as historical context; use the revised daily tracker for execution.

The first part preserves the complete original prompt list. The second supplies answers and design/behavioral starting outlines for every technical question, listed design and behavioral prompt. These outlines start practice; they are not complete implemented designs or invented personal stories.

QS — system-designdistributed-systems foundation

Full source content: Q-and-A/system-designdistributed-systems foundation.docx. Original wording is retained below. For conflicting statements, use the visible correction and the current execution plan.

1. System Design fundamentals — add these

• What is horizontal vs vertical scaling?

• What is stateless vs stateful architecture?

• When should you use a load balancer?

• L4 vs L7 load balancer?

• Reverse proxy vs API gateway?

• What is service discovery?

• Client-side vs server-side service discovery?

• What is DNS and how does DNS-based load balancing work?

• What is CDN and when should you use it?

• What is caching and what are cache-aside, write-through, write-back and read-through?

• What are cache invalidation strategies?

• What is cache stampede/thundering herd and how do you prevent it?

• What is consistent hashing and why is it useful?

• What is database sharding?

• What are good shard keys and bad shard keys?

• What is hot partition/hot key and how do you handle it?

• SQL vs NoSQL — when would you choose each?

• When should you use a relational database vs document/key-value/wide-column database?

• What is database indexing and what are the trade-offs?

• What is replication vs partitioning?

• What is leader-follower replication?

• What is read-after-write consistency?

• What is eventual consistency?

• What is strong consistency?

• What is quorum read/write?

• What is CAP theorem, and what does it actually mean?

• What is PACELC?

• What is backpressure?

• What is asynchronous vs synchronous communication?

• Queue vs pub/sub vs event stream?

• What is at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery?

• What is idempotency and how do you design an idempotent API?

• What is API versioning?

• Pagination: offset vs cursor-based?

• How do you handle large API responses?

• What is request hedging?

• What is graceful degradation?

• What is graceful shutdown?

These are high-priority because they form the vocabulary needed to solve almost every system-design problem.

2. Database internals — important gap

Your current material talks about transactions and isolation, but I'd add:

• What is a database transaction?

• What are dirty reads, non-repeatable reads and phantom reads?

• Optimistic vs pessimistic locking?

• Row-level vs table-level locking?

• What is MVCC?

Priority: High for SDE-II.

The clock/time questions are especially worth adding because they often separate basic distributed-systems knowledge from deeper understanding.

4. Kafka/streaming — only a few more

Month 7 is already excellent here. I would only add:

• What happens when there are fewer consumers than partitions?

These are enough. Don't turn Kafka into a separate six-week subject unless the target role specifically requires it.

GAP-01-001 — What is horizontal vs vertical scaling?

Answer / starting outline. Vertical scaling gives one machine more resources; horizontal scaling adds machines. The former has hardware/failure-domain limits, while the latter needs traffic distribution and coordination. Example: add API replicas behind a balancer; shared session state and database capacity must still be addressed.

Practice. Close the answer and explain the mechanism; draw one concrete flow, state a failure case and defend an alternative. For a design outline, develop APIs, data schema, estimates and failure recovery before treating it as a completed design.

GAP-01-002 — What is stateless vs stateful architecture?

Answer / starting outline. A stateless service instance does not require locally retained client session state to handle the next request. Durable state lives elsewhere. Stateful components retain identities, partitions or sessions that influence placement and recovery. Stateless APIs still depend on stateful databases; they are not systems without state.

Practice. Close the answer and explain the mechanism; draw one concrete flow, state a failure case and defend an alternative. For a design outline, develop APIs, data schema, estimates and failure recovery before treating it as a completed design.

GAP-01-003 — When should you use a load balancer?

Answer / starting outline. Use a load balancer to distribute traffic across healthy instances and provide a stable endpoint. Select health checks and routing behavior deliberately. It does not cure a saturated database, and retries through a balancer can duplicate side effects.

Practice. Close the answer and explain the mechanism; draw one concrete flow, state a failure case and defend an alternative. For a design outline, develop APIs, data schema, estimates and failure recovery before treating it as a completed design.

GAP-01-004 — L4 vs L7 load balancer?

Answer / starting outline. L4 routing operates on transport information such as addresses and ports. L7 routing understands application protocol fields such as HTTP paths and headers, enabling richer rules but adding processing and protocol responsibilities. TLS termination and connection persistence influence the choice.

GAP-01-005 — Reverse proxy vs API gateway?

Answer / starting outline. A reverse proxy forwards requests to upstream servers and may terminate TLS or cache. An API gateway adds API-oriented concerns such as routing, authentication integration, quotas and aggregation. Products overlap; choose by required behavior rather than their label.

Practice. Close the answer and explain the mechanism; draw one concrete flow, state a failure case and defend an alternative. For a design outline, develop APIs, data schema, estimates and failure recovery before treating it as a completed design.

GAP-01-006 — What is service discovery?

Answer / starting outline. Service discovery maps a logical service name to usable instances. Static configuration works at small stable scale; DNS, registries or orchestrator services handle changing membership. Discovery must address stale entries and unhealthy instances.

Practice. Close the answer and explain the mechanism; draw one concrete flow, state a failure case and defend an alternative. For a design outline, develop APIs, data schema, estimates and failure recovery before treating it as a completed design.

GAP-01-007 — Client-side vs server-side service discovery?

Answer / starting outline. With client-side discovery, callers obtain instance locations and choose a destination. With server-side discovery, a proxy or balancer selects the instance. Clients gain routing control but more complexity; centralized routing simplifies clients while adding an infrastructure dependency.

Practice. Close the answer and explain the mechanism; draw one concrete flow, state a failure case and defend an alternative. For a design outline, develop APIs, data schema, estimates and failure recovery before treating it as a completed design.

GAP-01-008 — What is DNS and how does DNS-based load balancing work?

Answer / starting outline. DNS maps names to records such as IP addresses. DNS-based balancing returns different destinations, sometimes considering geography or health. Resolvers cache responses according to TTL and their behavior, so failover is not instantaneous and individual request distribution is imprecise.

Practice. Close the answer and explain the mechanism; draw one concrete flow, state a failure case and defend an alternative. For a design outline, develop APIs, data schema, estimates and failure recovery before treating it as a completed design.

GAP-01-009 — What is CDN and when should you use it?

Answer / starting outline. A CDN serves/cacheable content from locations near users, reducing origin traffic and user latency. Suitable data includes static assets and appropriately configured public responses. Cache keys, TTLs, invalidation and private-content permissions are essential; accidental caching of personalized data is a security bug.

GAP-01-010 — What is caching and what are cache-aside, write-through, write-back and read-through?

Answer / starting outline. Cache-aside: application reads cache, then storage on a miss and populates cache. Read-through: cache performs that loading. Write-through: writes pass through cache to storage. Write-back: cache acknowledges before durable storage is updated, requiring durability/recovery. Choose using acceptable staleness, write load and failure consequences.

Practice. Close the answer and explain the mechanism; draw one concrete flow, state a failure case and defend an alternative. For a design outline, develop APIs, data schema, estimates and failure recovery before treating it as a completed design.

GAP-01-011 — What are cache invalidation strategies?

Answer / starting outline. Strategies include TTL expiry, explicit deletion on writes, event-driven invalidation and versioned keys. Each has race windows or propagation delay. State acceptable staleness, define the source of truth, and consider stale fills arriving after invalidation.

Practice. Close the answer and explain the mechanism; draw one concrete flow, state a failure case and defend an alternative. For a design outline, develop APIs, data schema, estimates and failure recovery before treating it as a completed design.

GAP-01-012 — What is cache stampede/thundering herd and how do you prevent it?

Answer / starting outline. A stampede occurs when many requests simultaneously miss or expire a popular entry and hit the origin. Mitigate with per-key request coalescing, jittered expiries, background refresh, stale-while-revalidate and origin concurrency limits. A lock requires failure and expiry handling.

Practice. Close the answer and explain the mechanism; draw one concrete flow, state a failure case and defend an alternative. For a design outline, develop APIs, data schema, estimates and failure recovery before treating it as a completed design.

GAP-01-013 — What is consistent hashing and why is it useful?

Answer / starting outline. Consistent hashing maps keys and nodes onto a ring or related structure so membership changes remap a subset of keys rather than nearly all of them. Virtual nodes improve balance. It does not inherently fix hot keys, replication correctness or uneven item sizes.

Practice. Close the answer and explain the mechanism; draw one concrete flow, state a failure case and defend an alternative. For a design outline, develop APIs, data schema, estimates and failure recovery before treating it as a completed design.

GAP-01-014 — What is database sharding?

Answer / starting outline. Sharding partitions data across independently managed storage nodes, commonly by a key. It scales storage/write capacity but complicates cross-shard joins, transactions, routing and rebalancing. Partitioning inside one database does not necessarily mean distributing across machines.

Practice. Close the answer and explain the mechanism; draw one concrete flow, state a failure case and defend an alternative. For a design outline, develop APIs, data schema, estimates and failure recovery before treating it as a completed design.

GAP-01-015 — What are good shard keys and bad shard keys?

Answer / starting outline. A useful shard key distributes load and supports common access patterns. Tenant ID can preserve locality but a huge tenant creates a hotspot. Time alone may send all new writes to one partition. Consider cardinality, skew, range queries, growth and resharding before choosing.

Practice. Close the answer and explain the mechanism; draw one concrete flow, state a failure case and defend an alternative. For a design outline, develop APIs, data schema, estimates and failure recovery before treating it as a completed design.

GAP-01-016 — What is hot partition/hot key and how do you handle it?

Answer / starting outline. A hot key/partition receives disproportionate traffic. Use caching, fan-out replicas, write aggregation, splitting/salting when semantics allow, dedicated capacity or tenant limits. Salting spreads writes but makes reads/aggregation more complex; measure skew before changing placement.

Answer / starting outline. Choose relational storage when transactions, constraints and joins suit the data/access patterns. NoSQL covers several distinct models, not one trade-off. Choose a concrete document, key-value or wide-column store for its actual query/consistency/operational properties. Neither category automatically guarantees higher scale or weaker consistency.

GAP-01-018 — When should you use a relational database vs document/key-value/wide-column database?

Answer / starting outline. Relational: structured relationships and transactional invariants. Document: aggregate-shaped records and queries matching those aggregates. Key-value: direct key access with simple values. Wide-column: partition-key and ordered-range access at scale. Test required queries, transaction boundaries, indexes and operational cost.

GAP-01-019 — What is database indexing and what are the trade-offs?

Answer / starting outline. An index is an additional access structure that avoids scanning every row for supported predicates/orderings. It costs storage and maintenance on writes. Composite order, selectivity and query shape matter. The planner may still prefer a scan, so inspect the plan and representative measurements.

GAP-01-020 — What is replication vs partitioning?

Answer / starting outline. Replication keeps copies of the same data for availability/read capacity. Partitioning splits data into subsets for size/load management. They often coexist: each shard may have replicas. Replication can lag; partitioning introduces placement and cross-partition operations.

GAP-01-021 — What is leader-follower replication?

Answer / starting outline. A leader accepts writes and followers reproduce its changes. Synchronous and asynchronous acknowledgment choices trade latency against durability/failover guarantees. A failover process must avoid divergent leaders and define what happens to acknowledged but unreplicated writes.

GAP-01-022 — What is read-after-write consistency?

Answer / starting outline. Read-after-write means a client can observe its completed write in subsequent reads under a stated scope. Route those reads to the leader, carry a replication position or use a stronger consistency path. A random asynchronous replica may serve older data.

GAP-01-023 — What is eventual consistency?

Answer / starting outline. Eventual consistency says replicas converge if updates stop and the replication/conflict-resolution process succeeds. It does not give a maximum staleness duration without another bound. Define conflict rules and user behavior while replicas disagree.

GAP-01-024 — What is strong consistency?

Answer / starting outline. Strong consistency is an overloaded term; specify the property. Linearizability makes each operation appear atomic between invocation and completion and respects real-time order. A consistent snapshot or serializable transaction is a different guarantee. Discuss which reads/writes and scope receive it.

GAP-01-025 — What is quorum read/write?

Answer / starting outline. A quorum contacts enough replicas to meet a configured read/write rule. R+W>N ensures overlap for the same replica set, but overlap alone does not prove linearizability. Version selection, concurrent writes, membership changes and repair behavior determine the actual guarantee.

GAP-01-026 — What is CAP theorem, and what does it actually mean?

Answer / starting outline. CAP concerns a network partition: a system cannot guarantee both linearizable consistency and availability as formally defined for all operations during the partition. It is not a general instruction to pick any two features permanently. State which operations reject, wait or serve potentially stale results.

GAP-01-027 — What is PACELC?

Answer / starting outline. PACELC asks: during a partition, how do availability and consistency trade off; otherwise, how do latency and consistency trade off? Synchronously coordinating distant replicas adds normal-operation latency even when no partition exists.

GAP-01-028 — What is backpressure?

Answer / starting outline. Backpressure communicates or enforces that a downstream stage cannot keep up, so upstream work slows or is bounded. Use bounded queues, concurrency limits and flow control. An unlimited in-memory queue hides saturation until memory/latency failure.

Practice. Close the answer and explain the mechanism; draw one concrete flow, state a failure case and defend an alternative. For a design outline, develop APIs, data schema, estimates and failure recovery before treating it as a completed design.

GAP-01-029 — What is asynchronous vs synchronous communication?

Answer / starting outline. Synchronous communication waits for a response in the current request flow; asynchronous messaging decouples submission from later processing. Async reduces temporal coupling but adds delivery, ordering, state/status and retry complexity. async/await in code does not by itself make a business workflow asynchronous.

GAP-01-030 — Queue vs pub/sub vs event stream?

Answer / starting outline. A work queue distributes tasks among competing consumers. Pub/sub fans notifications to subscriptions. An event stream stores ordered records within partitions for replay and independent consumer progress. Products can support multiple styles; choose delivery, retention, ordering and replay requirements.

GAP-01-031 — What is at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery?

Answer / starting outline. At-most-once permits loss but avoids redelivery at the stated delivery layer. At-least-once permits redelivery and needs idempotent effects. Exactly-once requires a precise boundary and atomic coordination/deduplication. Delivery and business effects are different; an external side effect may not share the messaging transaction.

GAP-01-032 — What is idempotency and how do you design an idempotent API?

Answer / starting outline. Use a client-provided idempotency key scoped to caller/operation, a request fingerprint, a unique constraint and stored outcome/state. Concurrent duplicates must converge on one operation. Reject key reuse with different payloads. Define expiry/replay behavior and coordinate dedup state with the effect wherever an atomic boundary exists.

GAP-01-033 — What is API versioning?

Answer / starting outline. Version an API when a change breaks a supported client contract. Strategies include path, header or negotiated media type; maintain compatibility and a retirement policy. Adding fields is only safe if clients tolerate them. Version request/response semantics and events deliberately.

GAP-01-034 — Pagination: offset vs cursor-based?

Answer / starting outline. Offset pagination skips a number of ordered rows; large offsets can be costly and concurrent changes can shift pages. Cursor/keyset pagination continues after a stable ordering key, often including a unique tie-breaker. It suits sequential feeds but complicates arbitrary page-number jumps.

GAP-01-035 — How do you handle large API responses?

Answer / starting outline. Use pagination, projections, bounded page sizes, compression where useful and streaming for suitable workflows. Huge responses consume memory and bandwidth and make retry/cancellation expensive. Maintain authorization on every page and avoid silently truncating required results.

GAP-01-036 — What is request hedging?

Answer / starting outline. Hedging sends a second equivalent request after a delay to reduce tail latency, then uses an acceptable result and cancels the other if possible. GAP-04-013 — Kafka vs RabbitMQ vs SQS vs Pub/Sub — when would you choose each?

Answer / starting outline. Kafka suits retained partitioned streams and replay. RabbitMQ suits brokered routing/work queues with its delivery features. Compare retention, ordering scope, throughput, latency, operational burden and cloud coupling.

GAP-06-011 — How do you estimate queue depth?

Answer / starting outline. Over an interval, backlog grows by arrivals minus completions. In a stable system, Little’s law relates average items in system L = arrival rate λ × average time W. Queue-only depth uses queue waiting time; include in-flight work only if W covers it. For an outage, accumulate incoming work and calculate recovery rate.

GAP-06-012 — How do you calculate availability?

Answer / starting outline. Time availability = available duration / total observed duration under a defined policy; request availability uses eligible successful requests / eligible requests. At 365 days/year, 99%, 99.9%, 99.99%, 99.999% allow about 3.65 days, 8.76 hours, 52.56 minutes and 5.256 minutes of annual downtime respectively. State window and exclusions.

Answer / starting outline. Use a tested database failover/recovery plan, bounded connection retries and explicit degraded behavior. Determine whether acknowledged data can be lost. Reject operations whose invariants cannot be guaranteed; never accept durable work solely in memory.

Practice. Close the answer and explain the mechanism; draw one concrete flow, state a failure case and defend an alternative. For a design outline, develop APIs, data schema, estimates and failure recovery before treating it as a completed design.
